articles.title: Basic Blood Cell Types: Erythrocytes, Leukocytes, And Platelets
articles.markdown: # Basic Blood Cell Types: Erythrocytes, Leukocytes, And Platelets # Introduction Blood is a specialized connective tissue containing various cell types suspended in plasma, each originating from multipotent hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow.  This article reviews the basic types of blood cells, including red blood cells, white blood cells (composed of granulocytes and agranulocytes), and platelets.  Morphologic characteristics, functional roles, and common pathologic alterations are discussed.  Hematopoiesis and cell lineages are explored in detail in a separate article. # Red blood cells Red blood cells (RBCs), or erythrocytes, are the most abundant blood cells, accounting for approximately 40%-45% of blood volume ((Figure 1)).  Their primary functions are to transport **oxygen** from the lungs to the tissues and to return carbon dioxide to the lungs for exhalation.  Measuring 6-8 µm in diameter, RBCs are uniquely biconcave in shape, increasing the surface area available for efficient gas exchange.  Gas exchange is facilitated by **hemoglobin**, an iron-containing protein that binds oxygen.  RBCs **lack a nucleus** and organelles, allowing more space for hemoglobin but limiting them to a **120-day lifespan** before they are recycled by the spleen and liver.  Erythropoiesis, the differentiation of RBCs from early progenitor cells, is stimulated primarily by erythropoietin produced by the kidneys.  RBC pathology includes: - Anemia:  Reduced RBC count or hemoglobin level decreases oxygen delivery. - Polycythemia:  Excessive RBC production increases blood viscosity, predisposing to thrombosis. - Sickle cell disease:  Abnormal hemoglobin distorts RBCs into a characteristic sickle shape, leading to vascular occlusion, hemolysis, and tissue damage. - Thalassemia:  Decreased hemoglobin alpha- or beta-chain production results in abnormal polymers that cause ineffective erythropoiesis and chronic hemolysis. # Granulocytes Granulocytes are a category of white blood cell (WBC) (leukocyte) characterized by cytoplasmic granules and a lobed nucleus that rapidly respond to injury or infection as a part of the **innate immune response**.  They include neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils, each containing specialized, preformed granules loaded with enzymes and inflammatory mediators for rapid defensive responses.  Their production and activation are tightly regulated by specific colony-stimulating factors (eg, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) and interleukins. ## Neutrophils Neutrophils (10-12 µm) are the most abundant granulocytes (comprising approximately 60% of WBCs) and contain **multilobed nuclei** (2-5 lobes) ((Figure 2)).  The nuclear segmentation increases as neutrophils mature, with young neutrophils having band-shaped (less segmented) nuclei.  This segmental nature of the nuclei is the reason that mature neutrophils are sometimes referred to as polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Neutrophils serve as first responders to **bacterial infections**, rapidly mobilizing to sites of invasion, where they phagocytize (ie, engulf) pathogens.  Their segmented nucleus allows neutrophils to squeeze through tight spaces in blood vessel walls (diapedesis) to reach infection sites without damaging their DNA ((Figure 3)).  This nuclear architecture also positions chromatin toward the cell periphery, maximizing central cytoplasmic space available for phagocytosis.  Their characteristic neutral-staining granules contain powerful destructive enzymes, including **myeloperoxidase** and lysozyme. For example, in a patient with pneumonia, neutrophils are recruited from the systemic circulation by chemokines and are subsequently activated by microbial molecules (eg, lipopolysaccharide, peptidoglycan, bacterial DNA) and opsonizing factors (eg, IgG, complement) to phagocytize and destroy the pathogenic bacteria.  Activated neutrophils also release cytotoxic granules (lysosomes) containing myeloperoxidase and other digestive enzymes that destroy extracellular bacteria and recruit additional immune components to the area.   However, these enzymes also cause significant damage to the pulmonary parenchyma and can result in liquefying necrosis of lung tissue and (potentially) lung abscess. Increased neutrophil counts (neutrophilia) are seen in infection or inflammation.  Decreased neutrophil counts (neutropenia) can occur due to various reasons—including chemotherapy, severe infections, and vitamin B12/folate deficiency—increasing susceptibility to infections. ## Eosinophils Eosinophils (12-17 µm) comprise approximately 2%-4% of WBCs and contain bilobed nuclei, resembling a pair of connected lobes ((Figure 4)).  This bilobed nuclear structure facilitates cellular mobility and flexibility, allowing eosinophils to migrate efficiently into inflamed tissues.  Their prominent eosinophilic (red-orange staining) granules contain cytotoxic molecules (eg, **major basic protein**, eosinophil peroxidase) optimized for combating **parasitic** infections by disrupting pathogen cell membranes.  Eosinophil proliferation and activation is stimulated by IL-5 produced by TH2 and mast cells (not to be confused with IL-4, which stimulates IgE production).  When a parasite invades the mucosa or enters the bloodstream, it is coated by IgG and IgA antibodies that bind the Fc receptors located on the eosinophil cell surface.  This triggers eosinophil degranulation and release of cytotoxic proteins and reactive oxygen intermediates, substances that damage and destroy antibody-bound parasites.  This mechanism is an example of antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity, which is also used by macrophages, neutrophils, and natural killer cells. Eosinophils also regulate **allergic** reactions by modulating inflammatory responses.  They synthesize prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and cytokines that contribute to the inflammation seen in late-phase type 1 hypersensitivity and chronic allergic reactions. Increased eosinophil counts (eosinophilia) suggest an allergic process (eg, asthma, hay fever), parasitic infection (eg, helminths such as *Ascaris* \[Loffler syndrome, intestinal obstruction\] and *Angiostrongylus* \[eosinophilic meningitis\]), drug reaction (eg, DRESS \[**D**rug **R**eaction with **E**osinophilia and **S**ystemic **S**ymptoms\]), or certain autoimmune disorders (eg, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis). ## Basophils Basophils (12-15 µm), the rarest granulocytes (comprising <1% of WBCs), have bilobed nuclei often obscured by dense, dark purple granules ((Figure 5)).  These large granules store **histamine** and heparin, critical mediators of allergic reactions and inflammation.  The basophil's granule-packed cytoplasm enables rapid, controlled release of histamine to induce **vasodilation** and enhance immune cell access to affected tissues, facilitating a prompt inflammatory response.  Increased basophil counts (basophilia) are rare but can be seen in certain types of malignancy (eg, chronic myeloid leukemia, myeloproliferative disorders). # Agranulocytes Agranulocytes, another category of WBCs, lack prominent cytoplasmic granules compared to granulocytes and are critical for **cell-mediated immunity** and antigen recognition.  They consist of lymphocytes and monocytes. ## Lymphocytes Lymphocytes (6-15 µm), constituting an estimated 20%-40% of WBCs, typically feature a large, round nucleus surrounded by a narrow rim of basophilic cytoplasm ((Figure 6)).  This **high nucleus/cytoplasm ratio** allows for the storage of a **large amount of genetic information** essential for generating **adaptive immunity** processes (eg, antigen recognition, immune memory).  Subtypes include **B cells** (producing specific antibodies through plasma cell differentiation), **T cells** (targeting infected or cancerous cells through cytotoxicity or helper functions), and **natural killer cells** (recognizing and eliminating virus-infected cells via perforin and granzyme release).  Lymphocyte differentiation is driven by antigen exposure and cytokines (eg, IL-2, IL-7) that stimulate maturation into effector or memory cells (with heightened response capabilities on reexposure). Lymphocytosis can be seen in viral infections and lymphoid malignancies (eg, chronic lymphocytic leukemia).  In contrast, lymphopenia is seen in immunodeficiencies and, occasionally, certain viral infections (eg, HIV, COVID-19). ## Monocytes Monocytes (12-20 µm), comprising approximately 3%-8% of WBCs, contain large, irregularly shaped, kidney-bean nuclei with **abundant gray-blue cytoplasm** ((Figure 7)).  Their expansive cytoplasmic volume facilitates **phagocytosis** of pathogens and debris.  On migration into tissues, monocytes differentiate into **macrophages and dendritic cells**—specialized antigen-presenting cells crucial for coordinating immune responses by processing and presenting antigens to T cells.  The differentiation of monocytes is promoted by macrophage colony-stimulating factor. Monocytosis can be seen in chronic infections (particularly bacterial infections \[eg, tuberculosis\]), chronic inflammatory conditions (eg, sarcoidosis), and certain malignancies (eg, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, acute monocytic leukemia).  In contrast, monocytopenia is less common but may occur in hairy cell leukemia and as an adverse effect of certain medications (eg, chemotherapy agents). # Platelets Platelets (thrombocytes) are the **smallest** blood cells (2-4 µm) and are irregularly shaped fragments derived from **megakaryocytes** in the bone marrow ((Figure 8)).  Their differentiation is regulated primarily by thrombopoietin produced by the liver.  The small size of platelets and the **lack of nuclei** optimize rapid circulation and facilitate quick adhesion to damaged vessel walls, forming initial **platelet plugs**.  Platelets contain numerous **granules filled with clotting factors** (eg, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor) and growth factors (eg, platelet-derived growth factor), enabling prompt secretion on activation to stabilize blood clots and promote tissue healing.  With a **7- to 10-day lifespan**, their production and function are tightly regulated to prevent excessive bleeding or clotting. Thrombocytopenia (low platelets) increases the risk for bleeding.  Thrombocytosis (high platelets) may lead to thrombosis.  Platelet dysfunction (eg, Bernard-Soulier syndrome, Glanzmann thrombasthenia) impairs clotting, even in the setting of normal counts, due to molecular defects in platelet adhesion or aggregation. # Summary Blood consists of 3 main cell types, each with specialized functions. Red blood cells (erythrocytes), the most abundant blood cells, are responsible for oxygen transport via hemoglobin.  Common disorders include anemia (low red blood cell count), polycythemia (excess red blood cells), and sickle cell disease (abnormal hemoglobin). White blood cells (leukocytes) are key to immunity and are divided into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes).  Neutrophils fight bacterial infections, eosinophils combat parasites and allergies, and basophils release histamine in allergic responses.  Lymphocytes (B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells) mediate adaptive immunity, whereas monocytes mature into macrophages and dendritic cells, aiding in pathogen clearance.  Abnormal white blood cell counts can indicate infections, inflammation, or malignancies. Platelets are small cell fragments essential for clotting; imbalances can lead to bleeding disorders (thrombocytopenia) or excessive clotting (thrombocytosis). ​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌

articles.title: Anatomy: Wrist
articles.markdown:
# Anatomy: Wrist # Introduction The wrist is the joint connecting the forearm and the hand.  It allows the transfer of forces across the joint while permitting a wide range of motion for the hand.  It is composed of a stable bony framework with ligaments, tendons, muscles, and nerves, whose organization influences how wrist conditions (eg, due to compression, degeneration, or trauma) present clinically. # Skeleton and joints The wrist skeleton consists of the distal radius and ulna (joined at the distal radioulnar joint \[DRUJ\]) proximally and the 8 carpal bones (arranged in proximal and distal rows) distally ((Figure 1)), ((Figure 2)). ## Distal radioulnar joint The DRUJ is an articulation between the distal radius and ulna, stabilized by the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC).  It allows pronation and supination of the forearm and is functionally distinct from the carpal joints.  It is critical for coordinated hand positioning and load transmission during grip and manipulation. ## Proximal carpal row The 4 proximal carpal row bones (laterally to medially) are the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform.  The **scaphoid** bridges both carpal rows, functioning as the link for force transmission between the forearm and the hand.  The **pisiform** is a unique sesamoid bone embedded in the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) tendon; it functions primarily as a mechanical pulley and ligament attachment site, contributing to the medial boundary of the Guyon canal. ## Distal carpal row The 4 distal carpal row bones (laterally to medially) are the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate.  The bones interlock tightly, forming a stable platform for the metacarpal bases. The midcarpal joint separates the 2 rows and contributes most to wrist flexion and extension.  Together, the carpal bones form an intercalated segment system with no direct muscular attachments; this arrangement allows complex, synchronized motion but makes the wrist uniquely susceptible to instability patterns. # Ligaments The wrist is stabilized by a network of intrinsic and extrinsic ligaments.  Intrinsic ligaments connect carpal bones to each other; extrinsic ligaments connect the radius or ulna to the carpal bones.  Certain ligaments are particularly important for maintaining carpal stability and proper wrist function. ## Extrinsic ligaments - **Volar radiocarpal ligaments** (especially the radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments):  These are the most important extrinsic stabilizers.  They connect the radius to the scaphoid, lunate, and capitate and are essential for guiding and constraining carpal motion. - **Dorsal radiocarpal ligaments**:  These ligaments coordinate coupled motion during flexion.  They also contribute to stability. - **Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments**:  These provide lateral stability by limiting radial and ulnar deviation, respectively. ## Intrinsic ligaments - **Scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL)**:  This is the most important intrinsic ligament.  It is the critical stabilizer of the scapholunate joint and maintains overall carpal stability. - **Lunotriquetral ligament**:  This important stabilizer of the proximal carpal row connects the lunate with the triquetrum. ## Triangular fibrocartilage complex The TFCC is a separate, specialized structure on the ulnar side of the wrist comprised of an articular disc, the palmar and dorsal radioulnar ligaments, the ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligaments, and the extensor carpi ulnaris subsheath.  It stabilizes the DRUJ and ulnar carpus, facilitates smooth pronation-supination, and absorbs ulnar-sided load.  Injury to TFCC ligaments disrupts carpal mechanics and can lead to instability and arthritis. # Muscles and tendons The muscles controlling the wrist are organized into flexor (volar) and extensor (dorsal) compartments.  They work together to produce wrist motion and maintain stability. ## Flexors (anterior compartment) - **Flexor carpi radialis (FCR)**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus; inserts at the base of the second metacarpal; flexes and radially deviates the wrist. - **FCU**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle of the humerus and olecranon; inserts on the pisiform, hook of hamate, and base of the fifth metacarpal; flexes and ulnarly deviates the wrist. - **Palmaris longus**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle; inserts into the palmar aponeurosis and flexor retinaculum; assists wrist flexion. - **Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS)**:  Originates from the medial epicondyle, radius, and ulna; inserts on the middle phalanges of fingers 2-5; contributes to wrist and finger flexion (proximal interphalangeal joint). - **Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP)**:  Originates from the proximal ulna and interosseous membrane; inserts on the distal phalanges of fingers 2-5; flexes the wrist and fingers (at the distal interphalangeal joint \[DIP\]) ((Figure 3)), ((Table 1)). ## Extensors (posterior compartment) - **Extensor carpi radialis longus**:  Originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus; inserts at the base of the second metacarpal; extends and radially deviates the wrist. - **Extensor carpi radialis brevis**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle; inserts at the base of the third metacarpal; extends the wrist and assists radial deviation. - **Extensor carpi ulnaris**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle and posterior ulna; inserts at the base of the fifth metacarpal; extends and ulnarly deviates the wrist. - **Extensor digitorum**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle; inserts on the extensor expansions of fingers 2-5; extends the wrist and fingers. - **Extensor indicis**:  Originates from the posterior ulna; inserts on the extensor expansion of the index finger; extends the index finger and assists wrist extension. - **Extensor digiti minimi**:  Originates from the lateral epicondyle; inserts on the extensor expansion of the little finger; extends the little finger and assists wrist extension ((Figure 4), ((Table 2)). Together, these flexor and extensor muscles coordinate wrist motion, stabilize the joint, and facilitate complex hand movements. # Fascial anatomy The wrist is enveloped by the superficial antebrachial fascia; 2 major stabilizing structures lie deep to it: the flexor retinaculum on the volar side and the extensor retinaculum on the dorsal side ((Figure 5)): - **Flexor retinaculum** (ie, transverse carpal ligament):  Forms the carpal tunnel, transmitting the median nerve and 9 flexor tendons.  Because it forms a rigid fibroosseous tunnel, swelling of the tendon sheaths or subsynovial connective tissue can increase pressure and produce median nerve compression. - **Extensor retinaculum**:  Anchors 6 dorsal tendon compartments, each containing specific extensor tendons with associated synovial sheaths.  These compartments prevent tendon bowstringing and form closed spaces where tenosynovitis or infection may localize. These retinacula serve as major anatomic boundaries that partition the wrist into discrete functional spaces. # Synovial compartments and deep spaces ## Flexor tendon sheaths Flexor tendons are invested in synovial sheaths that facilitate gliding.  The 2 largest—the radial bursa (flexor pollicis longus \[FPL\]) and ulnar bursa (FDS/FDP to the little finger)—may communicate in the palm.  This communication creates predictable pathways for infections (eg, flexor tenosynovitis), which can track into the radial or ulnar bursae or form a horseshoe abscess (infection in one finger leading to infection on the opposite side of the hand). ## Extensor compartments Each extensor compartment on the dorsum of the wrist possesses its own synovial sheath, which can become inflamed in overuse conditions (eg, de Quervain tenosynovitis). ## Joint spaces The radiocarpal, midcarpal, and carpometacarpal joints contain synovial cavities that may be involved in septic arthritis, inflammatory synovitis, or posttraumatic effusions.  Because they are bound by strong capsuloligamentous structures, infection and fluid spread are often contained and produce localized swelling. ## Vessels The wrist receives its blood supply from both the radial and the ulnar arteries, which form anastomotic networks around the carpal bones ((Figure 6)). ## Radial artery The radial artery courses laterally down the forearm and, at the wrist, divides into the following: - **Superficial palmar branch** (contributing to the superficial palmar arch). - **Deep palmar branch** (forming the deep palmar arch). - **Dorsal carpal branch** (forming the dorsal carpal arch). The deep palmar branch passes through the first dorsal interosseous space to join the deep branch of the ulnar artery, whereas the dorsal carpal branch anastomoses with the dorsal carpal branch of the ulnar artery to form the dorsal carpal arch. ## Ulnar artery The ulnar artery runs medially and divides into the following: - **Palmar carpal branch** (forming the palmar carpal arch with the radial palmar carpal branch). - **Superficial branch** (primarily forming the superficial palmar arch). - **Deep branch** (joining the deep palmar arch). The ulnar artery is typically the dominant contributor to the superficial palmar arch, whereas the deep palmar arch is most often completed by the radial artery. Venous drainage typically parallels arterial flow.  These anastomoses provide robust collateral circulation, which is clinically significant for maintaining hand perfusion even if a single artery is compromised. # Nerves The wrist is innervated by branches of the median, ulnar, and radial nerves. ## Median nerve - **Course**:  Passes through the carpal tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum, just radial to the midline of the wrist.  The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel (supplying sensation to the central palm); the main trunk continues into the hand ((Figure 7)). - **Motor**: - Supplies most volar forearm muscles that cross the wrist: - FCR:  Deviates wrist flexor and radial deviator (primary function). - Palmaris longus:  Assists wrist flexion. - FDS:  Contributes to wrist and finger flexion. - Supplies most thenar muscles and the lateral 2 lumbricals. - **Sensory**:  Supplies the palmar surface of the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger ((Figure 8)). ## Ulnar nerve - **Course**:  Passes superficially to the flexor retinaculum through the Guyon canal, ulnar to the carpal tunnel.  Divides at the wrist into the superficial and deep branches ((Figure 9)). - **Motor**: - FCU:  Wrist flexion and adduction. - FDP (ulnar half; digits 4-5):  Wrist flexion and DIP finger flexion. - Most intrinsic hand muscles (deep branch) (including hypothenar muscles, interossei, adductor pollicis, and medial lumbricals). - **Sensory**:  Dorsal and palmar superficial branches supply sensation to the ulnar side of the hand (including the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger) and wrist ((Figure 10)). ## Radial nerve - **Course**:  Bifurcates in the proximal forearm into: - **Superficial radial nerve (sensory)**:  Runs subcutaneously along the radial aspect of the forearm and crosses the wrist dorsolaterally, superficial to the wrist capsule. - **Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) (motor)**:  Enters the supinator and travels along the dorsal forearm.  The PIN divides into articular branches to the dorsal radiocarpal joint, the TFCC, and the DRUJ ((Figure 11)). - **Motor (via the PIN)**:  Supplies the major wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor carpi radialis longus \[before the bifurcation\]). - **Sensory (superficial radial nerve)**:  Provides cutaneous sensation to the dorsolateral hand, including the dorsal thumb, index finger, and middle finger ((Figure 12)). # Clinically significant tunnels and spaces ## Carpal tunnel The carpal tunnel is a narrow, osteofibrous canal at the volar aspect of the wrist ((Figure 13)). - **Boundaries** - Dorsally and laterally by the carpal bones, which form an arch. - Volarly by the flexor retinaculum (ie, transverse carpal ligament). - Located just distal to the distal wrist crease at the base of the palm. - **Contents** - **Median nerve**:  Passes through the carpal tunnel and lies superficial (volar) to the flexor tendons within the tunnel; it is most vulnerable to compression at this site. - **Flexor tendons** (9):  Four from FDS, 4 from FDP, and 1 from FPL. - **Clinical significance** - Compression of the median nerve leads to **carpal tunnel syndrome**, presenting with numbness, tingling, and burning in the radial 3½ digits.  Symptoms are typically worsened at night or with wrist flexion. - Chronic compression causes thenar muscle atrophy, weakness of thumb opposition, and impaired fine motor skills. ((Figure 14)), ((Figure 15)). ## Guyon canal This fibroosseous tunnel on the ulnar side of the volar wrist is positioned superficially and ulnarly to the carpal tunnel ((Figure 16)). - **Boundaries** - Ulnar side:  Pisiform. - Radial side:  Hook of the hamate. - Floor:  Transverse carpal ligament (flexor retinaculum). - Roof:  Volar carpal ligament and pisohamate ligament. - **Contents** - **Ulnar nerve**:  Divides within the canal into a superficial sensory branch and a deep motor branch. - **Ulnar artery**:  Runs alongside the nerve. - **Clinical significance** - Compression of the ulnar nerve in Guyon canal (ie, **Guyon canal syndrome**) causes sensory loss in the ulnar digits and/or intrinsic hand muscle weakness, depending on the compression zone. - Dorsal ulnar sensation remains intact because the dorsal cutaneous branch exits proximal to the canal. ## Anatomic snuffbox This shallow, triangular depression at the dorsoradial wrist is defined by the following borders.  It is an anatomic space, not a true compartment or tunnel ((Figure 17)). - **Boundaries** - Medial:  Tendon of the extensor pollicis longus. - Lateral:  Tendons of the abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB). - Proximal:  Styloid process of the radius. - Floor:  Scaphoid and trapezium bones. - **Contents** - **Radial artery**:  Main vascular structure crossing the floor. - **Superficial branch of the radial nerve**:  Courses superficially over the region. - **Cephalic vein**:  Runs subcutaneously across the roof. - **Clinical relevance** - Tenderness in the snuffbox is a sign of **scaphoid fracture** ((Figure 18)). - The main blood supply to the scaphoid is provided by the dorsal scaphoid branch of the radial artery; this branch enters near the bone's distal pole and then proceeds in a retrograde manner to provide blood supply to the proximal pole.  Because fracture of the scaphoid can easily interrupt this retrograde flow, the fractured scaphoid is at risk for avascular necrosis of the proximal pole and fracture nonunion ((Figure 19)). # Additional clinical correlations ## De Quervain tenosynovitis De Quervain tenosynovitis involves stenosing inflammation of the first dorsal compartment, which houses the APL and EPB tendons.  Thickening of the tendon sheath restricts normal gliding, producing pain over the radial styloid that worsens with thumb motion and ulnar deviation of the wrist.  Chronic inflammation can lead to persistent tendon entrapment and impaired thumb abduction and extension.  The condition is often confirmed with a Finkelstein or Eichhoff test, in which ulnar deviation of the wrist reproduces the patient's radial-sided pain.  The two tests are similar and often confused.  The Finkelstein test involves the examiner passively deviating the wrist ulnarly while the patient's thumb is held out.  The Eichhoff test places the thumb inside a closed fist before ulnar deviation, which increases strain on the APL and EPB.  The "Finkelstein test" is the term most commonly used in practice and is often used to describe both maneuvers ((Figure 20)), ((Video 1)). ## Lunate dislocation Lunate dislocation requires a high-energy force to disrupt the numerous ligaments (eg, scapholunate, capitolunate, lunotriquetral) that typically stabilize the lunate.  When severe ligamentous injury occurs, the lunate can dislocate volarly from its normal position, compressing and/or injuring the median nerve.  Prompt reduction of the dislocated lunate is required to prevent permanent damage to the median nerve ((Figure 21)), ((Figure 22)). ## Scapholunate ligament injury The SLIL stabilizes the scaphoid and lunate.  Disruption of this ligament causes the scaphoid to flex and the lunate to extend, widening the scapholunate gap and producing instability.  Chronic injury alters carpal mechanics and can progress to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC wrist) with degenerative arthritis. ## Triangular fibrocartilage complex injury The TFCC stabilizes the distal DRUJ and ulnar carpus.  Injury causes DRUJ instability and abnormal pronation-supination motion.  It presents with ulnar-sided wrist pain, clicking, or grip weakness.  Chronic disruption alters load transmission across the ulnocarpal joint and may contribute to degenerative changes. ​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌

articles.markdown:
# Anatomy: Vertebrae # Introduction The vertebral column (spinal column) consists of 33 vertebrae that are organized into 5 regions: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal.  It contains and protects the spinal cord (and associated vessels and nerves); it also provides axial support and transmits loads between the head and pelvis while permitting controlled, region-specific motion. Vertebrae differ by region; however, common anatomic features include intervertebral discs, ligaments, supporting muscles, and neural elements. # Skeleton and joints A typical vertebra consists of a vertebral body (anterior, primary weight-bearing portion), the vertebral arch (posterior), and bony processes (spinous, transverse, and articular) ((Figure 1)). - **Vertebral bodies**:  Form the anterior, weight-bearing column; adjacent bodies (from the second cervical vertebra to the last lumbar vertebra) are separated by intervertebral discs. - **Vertebral arch**:  Projects posteriorly from the vertebral body; it consists of bilateral pedicles, the pars interarticularis on each side, and the laminae that complete the arch in the midline. - **Bony processes**:  Arise from the arch; they include the paired transverse processes and articular processes (forming the facet joints) along with the midline spinous process where the laminae meet.  These points serve as posterior attachment points for axial musculature and ligaments. Together, the posterior surface of the vertebral body and the encircling vertebral arch form the **spinal canal**, through which the spinal cord passes. ## Cervical vertebrae (7 vertebrae, C1-C7) The cervical vertebrae ((Figure 2)) are the most mobile segments of the vertebral column, maintaining a characteristic lordotic curvature to support head positioning and shock absorption.  Vertebral bodies are small (reflecting relatively lower axial load).  Unique features include: - **Atlas (C1)**:  Ring-shaped vertebra with no vertebral body, spinous process, or intervertebral disc below.  Superior articular facets articulate with the occipital condyles (occipitoatlantal joint), which are responsible for nodding. - **Axis (C2)**:  Distinguished by the odontoid process (dens), a tooth-shaped superior projection representing the embryologically fused body of C1.  The dens projects into the ring of C1 and is secured by the transverse ligament of the atlas, forming the atlantoaxial joint, which is responsible for approximately 50% of total cervical rotation. - **Transverse foramina**:  From C1-C6, the foramina contain the vertebral arteries, accompanying veins, and sympathetic plexus. ## Thoracic vertebrae (12 vertebrae, T1-T12) The thoracic spine ((Figure 3)) is the least mobile segment for flexion, extension, and lateral flexion and is oriented primarily toward axial rotation.  The thoracic spine is directly tied to chest wall excursion and respiratory mechanics via its rib articulations, maintaining a kyphotic alignment to optimize load distribution.  Key features include: - **Spinous processes**:  Long and inferiorly sloping (eg, inferior tip of the spinous process lies at the level of the vertebral body 1-2 segments below). - **Costal facets**:  Posterolateral demifacets on the vertebral bodies of T1-T10 articulate with the heads of the ribs at the costovertebral joints; this articulation is crucial for thoracic cage stability and respiratory mechanics. ## Lumbar (5 vertebrae, L1-L5) The lumbar spine bears the majority of axial compressive load from the trunk.  Key features include: - **Vertebral bodies** ((Figure 4)):  Largest in the spinal column; kidney-shaped with greater width than depth; robust pedicles and laminae enable efficient load transfer. - **Spinous processes**:  Nearly horizontal, creating a clinically accessible interspinous space. The spinal cord terminates within the lumbar vertebral column at the **conus medullaris** (approximately L1-L2). ## Sacrum (5 fused vertebrae, S1-S5) and coccyx (3-5 fused vertebrae) The sacrum is a large, triangular bone of 5 fused vertebrae (fusion is typically complete by the mid-20s).  It forms the posterior wall of the bony pelvis ((Figure 5)) and articulates bilaterally with the iliac bones at the sacroiliac (SI) joints, providing the posterior pelvic stability essential for upright posture and locomotion.  Anterior and posterior sacral foramina convey the sacral nerve roots forming the sacral plexus, giving rise to the sciatic, pudendal, and gluteal nerves.  The sacral hiatus (opening at the inferior sacrum) serves as the landmark for caudal epidural injections. The coccyx, located at the inferior tip of the sacrum, represents the vestigial tail and serves as an attachment site for the coccygeal muscles, gluteus maximus, ligaments, and components of the pelvic floor. ## Joints Two joint systems connect adjacent vertebrae.  These include: - **Intervertebral symphyses (fibrocartilaginous joints)**:  Connect adjacent vertebral bodies.  Formed by intervertebral discs, which are composed of a gel-like nucleus pulposus surrounded by the fibrous annulus and function as shock absorbers, permitting multiplanar motion. - **Facet joints (synovial joint)** (paired synovial joints at each vertebral level):  Connect articular processes (ie, inferior articular process of the vertebra above to the superior articular process of the vertebra below), enclosed by a fibrous capsule lined with synovium.  The orientation of facet joints dictates the dominant plane of motion at each region: - **Cervical facets (oblique)**:  Permit flexion/extension, lateral bending, and rotation. - **Thoracic facets (coronal)**:  Favor rotation and limit flexion and extension due to rib cage constraint. - **Lumbar facets (sagittal)**:  Favor flexion/extension and resist rotation (acute, severe torsional forces can be a source of injury). Each spinal vertebra has 3 joints (2 facet joints and 1 intervertebral symphysis). Key ligaments stabilizing the vertebral column include: - **Anterior longitudinal ligament (ALL) → resists hyperextension/anterior disc herniation**:  Runs longitudinally along the anterior vertebral bodies for the length of the column. - **Posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL) → resists hyperflexion/posterior disc herniation**:  Runs longitudinally along posterior vertebral bodies within the spinal canal; it narrows laterally, especially at lumbar levels, leaving the posterolateral annulus poorly supported (eg, predisposing to posterolateral disc herniation). - **Ligamentum flavum**:  Runs posteriorly and segmentally connecting adjacent lamina one level at a time.  It forms part of the posterior wall of the vertebral canal; therefore, hypertrophy of this ligament can narrow the canal space.  The high elastin content (in contrast to ALL/PLL, which are mostly collagen) maintains resting tension, assists extension, and preserves canal patency. - **Interspinous and supraspinous ligaments**:  Connect the spinous processes of adjacent vertebrae; limit flexion and separation of spinous processes during flexion, especially in the thoracolumbar region. Each vertebra has anterior mobility facilitated by the discs and posterior mobility at a pair of facet joints.  Forward flexion of the spine stresses the vertebral bodies and discs; extension stresses the facet joints and posterior vertebral arch. # Muscles Back muscles ((Figure 6)) are organized into 2 functional categories: - **Intrinsic (deep) muscles**:  Act segmentally to stabilize and move the spine.  The intrinsic muscles are arranged in 3 layers of increasing depth, with fiber span inversely related to depth (the deepest muscles span the fewest segments and provide the finest segmental control). - **Extrinsic (superficial) muscles**:  Link axial posture to limb function (eg, trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids). Intrinsic muscles by layer include: - **Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis)**:  Form a long, superficial column extending from sacrum to skull.  They act as the primary extensors of the spine, producing lateral flexion and providing eccentric control during forward flexion (decelerating trunk flexion under load).  This eccentric role explains why erector spinae fatigue and strain are so common in lifting injuries. - **Transversospinalis (semispinalis - cervical spine, multifidus - lumbar spine, rotatores - thoracic)**:  Run deep to the erector spinae and obliquely from transverse processes to higher spinous processes; they are shorter-span fibers and produce rotation and fine segmental stabilization.  Multifidus is the most important lumbar stabilizer, reflecting load control. - **Segmental muscles (interspinales, intertransversarii)**:  Deepest layer; their primary function is proprioceptive, with a high density of muscle spindles providing continuous feedback about intervertebral position and movement to the CNS. Loss of deep stabilizers (eg, multifidus inhibition) shifts the load to the discs and facets, accelerating degeneration. # Vessels Segmental arterial supply enters at each level and reinforces longitudinal spinal arteries ((Figure 7)): - **Vertebral arteries**:  Ascend through transverse foramina of the cervical spine (typically C6 → C1), curve over the posterior arch of C1, and enter the foramen magnum ((Figure 8)); they are vulnerable to rotation/trauma. - **Posterior intercostal (thoracic) and lumbar arteries**:  Divide into spinal branches that enter via the intervertebral foramina, dividing into anterior and posterior radiculomedullary arteries. - **Artery of Adamkiewicz**:  Constitutes the dominant anterior radiculomedullary artery, usually from the left between T9-L2; it is critical for anterior spinal cord perfusion. Venous drainage occurs via the valveless internal vertebral (epidural) venous plexus.  The plexus is clinically significant due to the following: - **Bidirectional flow**:  Communicates with thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic veins. - **Lack of valves**:  Allows retrograde spread of infection, tumor emboli, or thrombus from the pelvis and abdomen directly to the spine and cranium (eg, enabling vertebral metastases from prostate, breast, and renal cancers). # Nerves Spinal nerve roots exit the vertebral canal through the **intervertebral foramina**, which are bounded by the pedicles (superior/inferior), vertebral body/disc (anterior), and facet joint (posterior).  Pathology at any of these sites (eg, disc desiccation, osteophyte, facet hypertrophy, ligamentum flavum thickening) can compress the exiting nerve root ((Figure 9)). Once outside the canal, each spinal nerve divides into **2 rami** with distinct territories: - **Dorsal ramus**: Supplies the intrinsic back muscles and overlying posterior skin. - **Ventral ramus**:  Forms the major peripheral nerves, including the intercostal nerves in the thorax and the brachial and lumbosacral plexuses in the limbs. ## Segmental logic for localization The level at which a spinal nerve exits depends on the region ((Figure 10)): - **Cervical**:  Nerves exit *above* their corresponding vertebra (eg, C1 nerve root above C1 vertebrae, C2 above C2, and so on through C7).  However, because there is no C8 vertebra, the C7 cervical nerve exits **below** C7 and above T1. - **Thoracic and lumbar regions**:  Nerves exit *below* their corresponding vertebrae (eg, T2 nerve root exits below T2 vertebrae; L5 nerve root exits below L5 vertebrae). Below the L1-L2 level (conus medullaris \[termination of the spinal cord\]), the lumbar and sacral roots travel as the **cauda equina** (Latin: "horse's tail") before exiting at their respective foramina.  Therefore, needles inserted below L3-L4 (eg, epidural, lumbar puncture) avoid cord injury because the needle passes between free-floating roots rather than piercing the cord itself. ## Sympathetic trunk The sympathetic trunk is a paired, bilateral structure running continuously from the skull base to the coccyx, anterolateral to the vertebral column ((Figure 11)).  In the neck, it runs posteromedially to the carotid sheath; in the thorax, it lies against the heads of the ribs/costovertebral joints, and, in the lumbar spine, it lies on the anterolateral surface of the vertebral bodies. # Meningeal compartments, paraspinal fascial planes, and pathways of spread Within the vertebral canal, the meninges partition the space into distinct compartments; whereas, outside the canal, paraspinal fascia organizes adjacent tissues into longitudinal planes.  This organization creates planes that facilitate predictable spread of infection, hemorrhage, and malignancy. The spinal meninges, including the dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater, are direct continuations of their cranial counterparts ((Figure 12)), forming a sealed, continuous system from the brain to the sacrum.  This relationship explains how pathology (infection, hemorrhage, raised pressure) can propagate between the cranial and spinal compartments.  Relevant meningeal compartments include the following: - **Epidural space**:  An anatomic space between the dura mater and the walls of the vertebral canal, containing epidural fat, lymphatics, and the internal vertebral venous plexus.  The epidural space extends from the foramen magnum to the sacral hiatus and is the target for epidural anesthesia and steroid injections. - **Subdural space**:  A potential space between the dura and arachnoid, normally containing only a thin film of fluid.  It becomes clinically relevant when bridging veins tear (in trauma or anticoagulation), allowing blood to accumulate. - **Subarachnoid space**:  Space that contains cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the neural elements (spinal cord, nerve roots, cauda equina).  It is directly continuous with the cranial subarachnoid space.  Therefore, lumbar puncture provides an indirect measure of intracranial pressure.  Lumbar puncture is contraindicated when intracranial pressure is elevated due to a mass lesion (because releasing CSF pressure inferiorly can precipitate tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum). The dural sac itself ends at S2, where the filum terminale externum (coccygeal ligament) anchors it to the coccyx. Paraspinal fascia partitions muscle groups into longitudinal compartments, guiding the spread of infection or hematoma along the column. # Histology Intervertebral discs are characterized by the following histologic features: - **Annulus fibrosus**:  Concentric collagen lamellae with alternating fiber orientation; it resists torsion and tensile forces. - **Nucleus pulposus**:  Proteoglycan-rich, highly hydrated core that behaves hydrostatically to distribute compressive loads. - **End plates**:  Hyaline cartilage that interfaces with vertebral bodies, permitting diffusion-based nutrition to the largely avascular disc. # Clinical correlations - **Disc herniation** ((Figure 13)):  Most commonly posterolateral due to annular weakness (eg, narrow PLL laterally).  Anatomically, a posterolateral herniation affects the **traversing root** (ie, root heading toward the foramen *1 level below)* rather than the exiting root at that level.  For example, a posterolateral herniation of the disc between L4 and L5 affects the L5 nerve root rather than the exiting L4 nerve root.  Herniations can also be central (affect multiple nerve roots) and far lateral (which *does* affect the exiting root) (eg, lateral disc herniation between L5 and S1 affects the exiting L5 nerve root). - **Radiculopathy**:  Possibly due to mechanical or nonmechanical causes and characterized by pain symptoms occurring along a particular dermatome, indicating nerve involvement (eg, nerve root compression).  It can result from lumbar ((Table 1)) or cervical ((Table 2)) disc herniation.  Sciatica is a common radiculopathy affecting the sciatic nerve ((Figure 14)). - **Spondylosis** (broad term encompassing age-related degenerative changes in the spine):  Can involve the discs (eg, disc degeneration/loss of disc height), facet joints (eg, arthritis with osteophyte formation, hypertrophy of facets, end plate sclerosis), or spinal ligaments (eg, thickening of the ligamentum flavum). - **Spondylolisthesis** ((Figure 15)):  Constitutes anterior displacement of a vertebral body relative to the one below, typically due to spondylolysis or degenerative laxity of the spinal ligaments. - **Spinal stenosis** ((Figure 16)):  Can be caused by advanced spondylosis and/or ligamentum flavum thickening, which reduces canal diameter, leading to neurogenic claudication (relieved by flexion \[(Figure 17)\], which increases canal area). - **Cauda equina syndrome (spinal cord compression)** ((Figure 18)) ((Table 3)):  Involves acute compression of nerve roots making up the cauda equina (eg, by large disc herniation, infection, malignancy) that presents with radiculopathy (unilateral or bilateral), possible bladder and rectal sphincter paralysis, and sensory loss (saddle anesthesia) affecting the dermatomes of the involved nerve roots.  It must be treated urgently to prevent permanent damage. - **Vertebral artery dissection**:  Occurs when a tear in the arterial wall, caused by neck trauma (eg, rapid rotational manipulation), allows blood to enter and separate the layers, forming an intramural hematoma that can narrow the vessel lumen or precipitate thrombus/embolus to the posterior circulation.  Symptoms include new-onset posterior headache, neck pain, or symptoms of vertebrobasilar ischemia (eg, vertigo, diplopia, dysphagia, ataxia). - **Vertebral compression fracture (VCF)** ((Image 1)):  When associated with pain, typically involves an acute presentation characterized by spinal tenderness in the setting of trauma (eg, lifting, twisting, ground-level fall).  The pain and spinal tenderness of VCF are classically localized to the midline, but referred or radicular pain in the flank or upper abdomen may also occur. - **Atlantoaxial instability**:  Failure of the transverse ligament of the atlas or dens pathology (eg, from trauma, rheumatoid arthritis), leading to excessive C1-C2 motion with risk of cord compression. - **Meningitis** (bacterial, viral, fungal):  Spreads freely through the subarachnoid space in both directions, leading to symptoms of nuchal rigidity, headache, and fever. ​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​

# Anatomy: Urinary System

# Introduction

The urinary system maintains homeostasis by regulating blood volume, pressure, and composition and by excreting metabolic waste.  It consists of the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra ((Figure 1)).  The kidneys perform filtration and selective reabsorption; the remaining structures act as conduits and reservoirs for urine.

# Kidneys

The kidneys are paired organs that regulate fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance; produce urine through filtration, reabsorption, and excretion; help control blood volume and blood pressure; and synthesize various hormones (eg, erythropoietin, renin, calcitriol).  The kidneys are located in the retroperitoneum between the T12 and L3 vertebral levels ((Figure 2)).  The right kidney is slightly lower than the left (due to the position of the liver) and is slightly smaller.

Multiple layers of tissue cover the kidneys.  At the deepest level is the renal capsule, which is a closely adherent fibrous connective tissue.  Superficial to the renal capsule is the perinephric (ie, perirenal) fat, which cushions and protects the kidney.  The renal fascia (Gerota fascia) lies above the perirenal fat and encloses the kidney and adrenal gland, anchoring them to the posterior abdominal wall.  The outermost layer is the paranephric (ie, pararenal) fat, which lies external to the fascia.

The kidney is organized into compartments:

-   **Hilum**:  A depression located at the medial aspect of each kidney that is the site of entry for the renal artery and exit for the renal vein and renal pelvis.
-   **Renal cortex**:  The outer layer of renal parenchyma, which lies deep to the renal capsule.  Portions of the cortex project inward to surround the renal medullary pyramids and are referred to as renal columns or cortical septa.
-   **Renal medulla**:  The inner layer of renal parenchyma, lying between the renal cortex and hilum, arranged into renal pyramids.  The apex of each renal pyramid (the papilla) empties into a minor calyx.  Each renal pyramid and its overlying renal cortex make up a renal lobe.
-   **Renal sinus**:  Fat-filled cavity within the kidney, located at the hilum, that contains the renal collecting system (eg, minor calyces → major calyces → renal pelvis).

**Blood supply**

Blood is supplied to the kidneys through the renal arteries, which receive about 20% of cardiac output.  These arteries originate from the abdominal aorta at L1-L2, and the right renal artery passes posterior to the inferior vena cava (IVC), making it longer than the left.  The renal artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions and into segmental arteries then into interlobar arteries then arcuate arteries then interlobular arteries then afferent arterioles then glomeruli then efferent arterioles and then peritubular capillaries.

Blood is removed from the kidneys through venules (which receive blood from peritubular capillaries), which drain into interlobular veins, then arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, and ultimately the renal veins, which drain into the IVC.

The left renal vein is longer than the right; it also passes through the angle formed by the aorta (posteriorly) and the superior mesenteric artery (anteriorly), making it more susceptible to compression.  The left renal vein often receives blood from the left ovarian vein (females) or left testicular vein (males), left suprarenal vein, and left inferior phrenic vein; the right-sided counterparts of these veins typically drain directly to the IVC ((Figure 3)).

**Innervation**

Nerves enter and exit the kidney along the renal vessels at the hilum.  The innervation of the kidney is mostly sympathetic input with a small contribution from the parasympathetic system.

-   **Sympathetic fibers (T8-L1)**:  Via the renal plexus with contributions from the celiac plexus, intermesenteric plexus, aorticorenal ganglia, and thoracic splanchnic nerves; the fibers are responsible for stimulating renin release, sodium retention, and renal vasoconstriction (raises blood pressure).
-   **Parasympathetic fibers**:  Via the vagus nerve (CN X); the fibers inhibit inflammation and cytokine release.

**Lymphatic drainage**

The kidneys drain lymph predominantly to the paraaortic lymph nodes.

**Histology**

The nephron is the fundamental functional unit of the kidney; it is responsible for transforming filtered blood (the filtrate) into urine ((Figure 4)).  Each kidney contains approximately 1 million nephrons, each of which consists of a renal corpuscle (site of filtrate formation) and a tubule (site of filtrate refinement).  The renal corpuscle is located within the renal cortex, whereas the renal tubule (consisting of the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule, and collecting duct) spans the renal cortex and medulla.

The renal corpuscle consists of:

-   Glomerulus:  This network of capillaries with a fenestrated endothelium receives blood from the afferent arteriole.  The remaining blood that is not filtered out at the glomerulus leaves through the efferent arteriole and supplies the renal tubules through the peritubular capillaries and eventually leaves the kidney at the renal vein.
-   Glomerular (Bowman) capsule:  The capsule surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtered fluid to the renal tubule.  The outer layer consists of simple squamous epithelium, and the inner layer consists of negatively charged epithelium lined by podocytes ((Figure 5)).

The renal tubule consists of:

-   Proximal tubule:  Includes the proximal convoluted tubule (in the cortex) and proximal straight tubule (descends into the medulla, beginning the loop of Henle).  It is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium with a brush border (microvilli).
-   Loop of Henle:  Includes the descending limb (lined by simple squamous epithelium) and the ascending limb, which includes the thin portion (lined by simple squamous epithelium) and the thick portion (lined by simple cuboidal epithelium).  The descending loop extends to various depths in the medulla depending on the type of nephron:  Cortical nephrons are superficial within the cortex (near the kidney capsule) and have short tubules that project into the upper medulla, whereas juxtamedullary nephrons are located deeper in the cortex and have long tubules that project deep into the medulla.
-   Distal convoluted tubule:  Located within the renal cortex and lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (without a brush border).
-   Collecting duct:  Typically considered the most distal portion of the nephron.

The collecting system is a series of converging ducts that convey filtrate from the nephrons to the ureter.  Filtrate is moved from the connecting tubule to the cortical collecting tubules to the cortical collecting duct to the medullary collecting duct to the papillary duct (at the apex of each renal pyramid) to the minor calyx to the major calyx and then to the renal pelvis.  Most of the collecting system is lined by simple cuboidal or columnar epithelium, which becomes urothelium at the minor calyx.  The renal pelvis contains specialized pacemaker cells, which initiate electrical signals to cause peristalsis of the ureters, which are modulated by sympathetic and parasympathetic input.

# Ureters

The ureters are bilateral retroperitoneal muscular tubes that join the renal pelvis at the ureteropelvic junction and transport urine from the renal pelvis to the trigone of the bladder.  They measure 20-30 cm in length and 3-6 mm in diameter.

**Anatomic course**

The ureters originate bilaterally at the renal pelvis and course inferiorly toward the bladder within the retroperitoneum, just anterior to the psoas muscles.  Midway from the kidney to the pelvic inlet, the ureters cross posterior to the gonadal artery and vein.  The ureters then gain access to the pelvis by crossing anterior to the external iliac artery at, or just after, the bifurcation of the common iliac artery.

-   Females:  Within the pelvis, the ureters lie medial to the ovarian vessels and anterior to the internal iliac artery.  They descend further into the pelvis, running along the broad ligament of the uterus.  The ureters then course along the uterosacral ligament and cross posterior to the uterine artery ("water under the bridge") at the level of the internal cervical os just before entering the bladder ((Figure 6)).
-   Males:  After crossing the pelvic brim, the ureters run posterolaterally along the sidewall of the lesser pelvis.  At the level of the ischial spine, the ureter makes a sharp turn forward and then courses behind the vas deferens and in front of the seminal vesicles to enter the bladder.  The ureters enter the posterior aspect of the bladder at the trigone, traveling through the muscular bladder wall obliquely, which helps prevent reflux of urine from the bladder to the ureters.

**Blood supply**

The blood supply to the proximal ureter comes from branches of the renal artery.  At the distal ureter, the arterial blood supply arises from the superior vesical artery.  In between, the arterial supply to the ureter is anastomotic and highly variable, with possible afferent branches from the gonadal arteries, common and internal iliac arteries, aorta, and uterine arteries ((Figure 7)).  The veins that remove blood from the ureters correspond to the arterial supply.

**Innervation**

The ureters are supplied by the ureteric plexus, which receives contributions directly from nerve roots (T9-T12, L1, S2-S4) and from the renal, aortic, superior hypogastric, and inferior hypogastric plexus.  Parasympathetic innervation arises from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) and promotes ureteral peristalsis.  In contrast, sympathetic fibers from T12-L1 generally inhibit peristalsis.  Afferent (sensory) fibers enter the spinal cord at T11-L1.  Ureteral pain is often felt in a dermatomal pattern corresponding to these spinal cord segments (eg, flank, lower abdomen, scrotum or labia majora).

**Lymphatic drainage**

Lymph from the ureters is drained segmentally:  The upper third drains to paraaortic nodes; the middle third drains to paraaortic nodes (left) or paracaval nodes (right); and the lower third drains to the common iliac, external iliac, or internal iliac nodes.

**Histology**

The mucosal layer of the ureter lines the lumen and is continuous with the lining of the bladder and renal pelvis.  The epithelium is composed of urothelium (a type of transitional epithelium) stratified with multiple cell types, including goblet cells that produce mucus, columnar to cuboidal cells at the base, and surface umbrella cells (or facet cells) that are dome shaped and flatten when the ureter is distended with urine.  Umbrella cells are connected by tight junctions, making the lining impermeable to urine.

Just beneath the mucosa is the lamina propria, which is composed of loose connective tissue, vessels, and lymphatics.  There is no submucosal layer.  The muscularis layer is composed of an inner longitudinal layer of smooth muscle and an outer layer of circular smooth muscle; there is an additional outer longitudinal layer in the lower third of the ureter.  The adventitia is composed of connective tissue with vessels, nerves of the ureteric plexus, and lymphatics.

# Urinary bladder

The bladder is a hollow, distensible organ that receives urine from the ureters and stores it until micturition (voiding).  The bladder sits low in the pelvis when empty and rises into the lower abdomen as it fills.  The superior portion of the bladder is covered by peritoneum, which forms a fold posteriorly (rectovesical pouch \[males\] or vesicouterine pouch \[females\]).  This allows the upper portion of the bladder to be flexible and change shape as it fills, whereas the lower aspect of the bladder is fixed in position and attached to the endopelvic fascia.

Anteriorly, the bladder is separated from the pubic bone by the fatty connective tissue of the retropubic space (ie, space of Retzius).  In males, the bladder abuts the distal portion of the vas deferens, seminal vesicles, and rectum.  In females, the bladder abuts the lower uterine segment, cervix, and vagina.

The bladder comprises 4 components ((Figure 8)):

-   **Dome**:  The superior aspect of the bladder.  This portion contains the apex, where the median umbilical ligament (remnant of the fetal urachus) attaches the bladder to the umbilicus.
-   **Base**:  The inferior aspect of the bladder.  This portion contains the trigone, which is a triangular area bordered anteriorly by the internal urethral orifice and posteriorly by the 2 ureteric orifices.
-   **Body**:  The area between the dome and base.
-   **Neck**:  The area surrounding the urethral orifice.  The pubovesical ligament connects the neck of the bladder to the pubic bone and tendinous arch of the pelvic fascia, anchoring the bladder in position and providing support.  In males, the puboprostatic ligament connects the anterior prostate to the pubic bone and further stabilizes the bladder neck.

**Blood supply**

Blood is supplied to the bladder from the superior and inferior vesical arteries, which are branches of the internal iliac artery.  In females, additional blood is supplied through the uterine and vaginal arteries.  Blood is removed from the bladder through the vesical venous plexus that drains into the internal iliac veins.

**Innervation**

Sympathetic fibers (T10-L2) via the hypogastric plexus inhibit detrusor contractions to allow bladder filling ((Figure 9)).  Parasympathetic fibers (S2-S4) via pelvic splanchnic nerves cause detrusor contractions and lead to bladder emptying ((Figure 10)).  Somatic (voluntary) innervation occurs through the pudendal nerve (S2-S4), which also innervates the external urethral sphincter.  Afferent (ie, sensory) information (eg, distension, inflammation) from the bladder is conveyed by parasympathetic and sympathetic fibers to the spinal cord and then to the brain via the dorsal columns.

**Continence and micturition**

Normal voiding physiology involves coordinated inhibition and activation of the bladder muscle (detrusor), pelvic floor, and urethral sphincter muscles that are mediated by the autonomic and somatic nervous systems.  Continence is maintained by the bladder (detrusor muscle), external urinary sphincter (EUS), and internal urinary sphincter (IUS).  The EUS is a skeletal muscle that receives somatic motor innervation (voluntary control) from the perineal branches of the pudendal nerve (S2-S4).  In contrast, the bladder and IUS receive autonomic innervation:  Sympathetic stimulation promotes urine storage and continence by increasing IUS tone and inhibiting detrusor contractions.  As volume rises, afferent input from the bladder to the spinal cord increases.  Cortical centers within the brain recognize when the bladder is full and trigger a transition from the storage phase to the emptying phase.  This releases the pontine micturition center in the brainstem from tonic inhibition, allowing the pons to coordinate detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation through parasympathetic activity ((Figure 11)).

**Lymphatic drainage**

The superolateral aspects of the bladder drain to the external iliac nodes, whereas the fundus and bladder neck drain to the internal iliac and common iliac nodes.

**Histology**

The bladder is composed of 4 layers.  The deepest layer is the mucosa, which is composed of stratified transitional epithelium (urothelium).  It contains surface umbrella cells that are large and round when empty and flatten as the bladder fills.  Similar to the ureter, the cells are linked by tight junctions, which provide a watertight barrier that prevents the passage of toxins and pathogens across the epithelium.  The mucosa forms folds (ie, rugae) when bladder volumes are low.  As the bladder expands, the rugae flatten, allowing an increase in volume.  The muscularis layer is composed of 3 layers of smooth muscle fibers with different orientations:  Inner longitudinal layer, middle circular layer, and outer longitudinal layer.  The adventitia is composed of connective tissue; on the dome of the bladder, serosa (ie, peritoneum) is present instead of adventitia.

# Urethra

The urethra transports urine from the bladder to the external urethral orifice to allow its elimination from the body.  In males, it also conveys ejaculate.  Two sphincters control the passage of urine from the bladder to the urethra ((Figure 12)):

-   **Internal urethral sphincter**:  In males, it is composed of circular smooth muscle under autonomic control and prevents the retrograde flow of ejaculate into the bladder.  In females, it is a "functional" sphincter created by the smooth muscle surrounding the bladder neck and the angle formed between the bladder neck and the urethra.
-   **External urethral sphincter**:  In both males and females, it is composed of skeletal muscle and is under somatic (voluntary) control via the pudendal nerve (S2-S4).

## Male urethra

The male urethra is 18-20 cm in length and is divided into posterior and anterior components ((Figure 13)).

**Posterior urethra**

The posterior urethra is relatively fixed to the pelvic bones by supportive structures (eg, sphincter and fascial layers of the urogenital diaphragm, puboprostatic ligament), making it largely immobile.  It has 2 main sections:

-   **Prostatic urethra**:  Begins at the bladder neck and traverses the prostate gland.  It receives seminal fluid from the ejaculatory ducts and secretions from the prostatic ducts.  It is lined by transitional (urothelial) epithelium, continuous with the bladder mucosa.
-   **Membranous urethra**:  Passes through the pelvic floor and into the deep perineal pouch.  It is lined by pseudostratified or stratified columnar epithelium and is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter.

**Anterior urethra**

The anterior urethra is mobile, running through the corpus spongiosum along the length of the penis.  It receives secretions from the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands (which produce a lubricating, alkaline preejaculatory fluid) and from the urethral glands (which secrete mucus that lubricates and protects the urethral lining).  It has 2 main sections:

-   **Bulbar urethra**:  Portion located at the proximal end of the penis and lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium.
-   **Penile urethra**:  The longest portion, extending to the external urethral orifice at the glans.  It is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium proximally and transitions to stratified squamous epithelium distally.

**Blood supply**

-   The posterior urethra is supplied by branches from the inferior vesical artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery.  The anterior urethra is supplied by the bulbourethral and urethral arteries, which are branches of the internal pudendal artery.
-   Venous drainage of the posterior and anterior urethra occurs via the prostatic venous plexus, which empties into the internal iliac vein.

**Innervation**

The posterior urethra receives sympathetic and parasympathetic inputs from the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus.  Sensory innervation of the anterior urethra is supplied by branches of the dorsal nerve of the penis (a branch of the pudendal nerve).

The external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle) receives somatic innervation from the pudendal nerve, whereas the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle at the bladder neck) is controlled by sympathetic fibers from the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus.

**Lymphatic drainage**

The posterior urethra drains to the internal and external iliac nodes.  The anterior urethra drains primarily to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

## Female urethra

The female urethra is approximately 4 cm in length and runs along the anterior vaginal wall, traversing the perineal membrane posterior to the pubic symphysis.  At its distal end, the urethra is related to the Skene glands (ie, paraurethral glands or lesser vestibular glands), and the ducts of these glands open laterally to the external urethral meatus.  The proximal urethra is lined by transitional epithelium, which transitions into pseudostratified columnar epithelium at the midpoint and to stratified squamous epithelium at the distal end.

**Blood supply**

The urethra is supplied by the internal pudendal, vaginal, and inferior vesical arteries.  Venous drainage occurs via the vesical venous plexus, which drains into the internal iliac vein.

**Innervation**

The female urethra receives sympathetic and parasympathetic input from the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus.  Sensory innervation of the urethra is provided by branches of the pudendal nerve, and afferent fibers contribute to the regulation of continence and micturition.

The external urethral sphincter (skeletal muscle) receives somatic innervation from the pudendal nerve, whereas the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle at the bladder neck) is controlled by sympathetic fibers from the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus.

**Lymphatic drainage**

The proximal urethra drains to the internal iliac nodes, and the distal urethra drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

# Summary

The urinary system maintains homeostasis by regulating blood volume, pressure, and composition and by excreting metabolic waste.  It consists of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.  The kidneys are retroperitoneal organs responsible for filtration, selective reabsorption, hormone production, and urine formation through highly organized vascular, tubular, and collecting systems.  Urine is transported via the ureters to the bladder, where it is stored until coordinated autonomic and somatic control allows micturition through the urethra.  The structural organization, blood supply, innervation, lymphatic drainage, and epithelial transitions throughout the urinary tract support efficient urine production, transport, storage, and elimination.

​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌
