articles.title: Anatomy: Thyroid And Parathyroid Glands
articles.markdown: # Anatomy: Thyroid And Parathyroid Glands # Introduction The thyroid and parathyroid glands are endocrine organs in the anterior neck that regulate metabolism and calcium homeostasis, respectively.  The thyroid influences basal metabolic rate through thyroid hormone production, whereas the parathyroid glands maintain serum calcium levels.  Their intimate anatomic relationship and shared vascular supply make their anatomy particularly relevant during neck surgery. # Thyroid gland ## Gross anatomy The thyroid ((Figure 1)) is a **butterfly-shaped gland** located in the midline of the lower neck, anterior to the trachea and inferior to the thyroid cartilage.  It typically spans vertebral levels C5 through T1 and is made up of the following segments: - **Right and left lobes**:  Located on either side of the trachea. - **Isthmus**:  Connects the lobes across the midline (usually over the second through fourth tracheal rings). - **Pyramidal lobe**:  An embryologic remnant of the thyroglossal duct, present in approximately 40%-75% of the population.  It most commonly arises from the isthmus or left lobe and extends superiorly toward the hyoid bone. The thyroid gland is enclosed by a fibrous capsule and an outer fascial layer that anchors it to surrounding structures.  Its attachment to the larynx and trachea via the pretracheal fascia and ligament of Berry (a posterior suspensory ligament) causes the gland elevates with swallowing. ## Histology The fundamental unit of the thyroid gland is the thyroid follicle ((Image 1)), a spherical structure composed of a central lumen filled with colloid and surrounded by a single layer of follicular epithelial cells.  Each follicle is encircled by a basement membrane and a capillary network that facilitates hormone release into the circulation. Follicles are organized into lobules, which form the functional parenchyma of each thyroid lobe.  These lobules are separated by septa derived from extensions of the surrounding fibrous capsule.  The septa also serve as conduits for blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic channels traversing the gland. **Thyroid follicle** Each thyroid follicle has 2 main components ((Figure 2)): - **Follicular epithelial cells (ie, thyrocytes)** form a single layer of simple cuboidal epithelium that surrounds the lumen.  Thyrocytes are functionally polarized: - The apical surface, facing the lumen, contains microvilli and enzymes essential for thyroid hormone synthesis (eg, thyroid peroxidase). - The basolateral surface, adjacent to capillaries, contains the sodium-iodide symporter for iodide uptake and receptors for thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). - Thyrocytes **synthesize and secrete thyroglobulin** into the lumen, where it serves as the scaffold for thyroid hormone production.  Follicular cell height varies with activity: flattened cells indicate low activity, whereas tall columnar cells reflect TSH stimulation. - **Colloid** is a gel-like substance within the follicular lumen composed primarily of thyroglobulin.  At the apical surface of the follicular cells, thyroglobulin undergoes iodination and coupling reactions to form thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3), which remain bound within the thyroglobulin molecule. The colloid functions as a **hormone reservoir**.  Unlike most endocrine glands, the thyroid stores weeks to months of hormone.  Upon TSH stimulation, follicular cells endocytose colloid, degrade thyroglobulin, and release free T4 and T3 into the bloodstream. T4 is converted peripherally to T3, the biologically active form that regulates basal metabolic rate. Clinical correlation:  Excess thyroid hormone produces a hypermetabolic state (eg, upregulation of mitochondrial activity and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase expression) characterized by weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, tachycardia, and increased cardiac output (heightened beta-adrenergic sensitivity).  Deficiency leads to the opposite phenotype, with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and bradycardia.  Thyroid hormones are also required for normal linear growth in children and for fetal and early childhood brain development; untreated deficiency can cause irreversible neurocognitive impairment. **Interfollicular tissue** The connective tissue between thyroid follicles is highly vascular with a dense network of capillaries that supports the thyroid gland's metabolic activity.  This space also contains **parafollicular C cells**, which secrete **calcitonin** directly into the circulation.  Calcitonin lowers serum calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity and increasing renal calcium excretion, although it plays a relatively minor role in calcium homeostasis. Clinical correlation:  Medullary thyroid cancer is a neuroendocrine malignancy arising from the parafollicular C cells.  Serum calcitonin levels correlate with the risk of metastasis and are measured at the time of diagnosis; they also correlate with risk of recurrence and are therefore measured serially following surgery. ## Arterial supply Arterial supply to the thyroid is provided primarily by the following: - **Right and left superior thyroid arteries** (branches of the external carotid artery), which supply the superior poles of the thyroid lobes. - **Right and left inferior thyroid arteries** (branches of the thyrocervical trunk, arising from the subclavian artery), which supply the inferior and posterior portions of the gland and provide most of its blood supply. -   **Thyroid ima artery** (variable, uncommon) may arise from the brachiocephalic trunk or aortic arch to supply the isthmus. Clinical correlation:  The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs near the inferior thyroid artery and the ligament of Berry.  Injury to this nerve can result in vocal cord paralysis. Clinical correlation:  The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs near the superior thyroid artery and the superior pole of the thyroid and provides motor innervation to the cricothyroid muscle.  Injury can result in cricothyroid muscle paralysis, leading to vocal changes such as difficulty projecting or the inability to produce high-pitched sounds. ## Venous drainage Venous drainage occurs via 3 sets of thyroid veins: - **Superior thyroid veins** drain the upper poles and empty into the internal jugular veins. - **Middle thyroid veins** drain the lateral aspects of the gland and empty into the internal jugular veins. - **Inferior thyroid veins** drain the lower poles and isthmus.  They arise from a pretracheal venous plexus and typically drain into the brachiocephalic veins. Clinical correlation:  The pretracheal venous plexus lies anterior to the trachea and represents a major source of bleeding during emergency tracheostomy. ## Innervation **Sensory** (pain) fibers from the thyroid travel via the vagus nerve (jugular and nodose ganglia) and cervical spinal nerves (C2 through C5) via the cervical plexus. Clinical correlation:  Thyroid pain, as seen in subacute thyroiditis, presents with anterior neck pain that can radiate to the jaw or ear due to the shared sensory pathways involving the vagus nerve and cervical plexus. **Autonomic** input primarily regulates vascular tone and blood flow rather than hormone secretion: - Sympathetic innervation:  Arises from the superior and middle cervical ganglia. - Parasympathetic innervation:  Provided by branches of the vagus nerve (CN X). Clinical correlation:  Autonomic innervation has minimal direct effect on thyroid hormone secretion.  The primary regulator of hormone production is TSH from the anterior pituitary. ## Lymphatic drainage The thyroid drains into the prelaryngeal, pretracheal, and paratracheal lymph nodes, which then drain into the deep cervical lymph nodes. # Parathyroid glands ## Gross anatomy The parathyroid glands ((Figure 3)) are 4 small, ovoid endocrine glands located on the posterior surface of the thyroid gland.  They are usually embedded within or attached to the thyroid capsule. The glands are divided into the following categories: - **Superior parathyroid glands**:  More constant in position, typically located at the level of the **cricothyroid junction or the upper two-thirds of the posterior thyroid lobe**, posterior to the recurrent laryngeal nerve. - **Inferior parathyroid glands**:  More variable in location and may descend inferiorly with the thymus during development. Despite their small size, the parathyroid glands function as the primary regulators of serum calcium levels. ## Histology The parathyroid glands are composed of densely packed endocrine cells arranged in cords and clusters, supported by a rich capillary network that facilitates rapid hormone release into the circulation.  The glands contain 2 main cell types: - **Chief cells (predominant)**:  Small cells responsible for the **synthesis and secretion** of **parathyroid hormone** (PTH).  PTH **increases serum calcium** by acting directly on bone and the kidneys and indirectly on the intestine ((Figure 4)). - **Oxyphil cells**:  Larger cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm due to a high mitochondrial content.  Their function is not fully understood, but they are thought to represent inactive or less active forms of chief cells. Clinical correlation:  Hyperparathyroidism results in hypercalcemia, which can cause renal stones, osteoporosis, abdominal pain, and neuropsychiatric symptoms (eg, fatigue, depression, confusion) (ie, "stones, bones, groans, and psychiatric overtones").  Hypoparathyroidism results in hypocalcemia, which can lead to tetany, paresthesia, and neuromuscular irritability (eg, Chvostek and Trousseau signs). ## Arterial supply The parathyroid glands are primarily supplied by: - **Branches of the inferior thyroid arteries**, which provide the main vascular supply. - Variable contributions from the superior thyroid arteries. Clinical correlation:  Because their blood supply is closely associated with the thyroid gland, the parathyroid glands are at risk of devascularization during thyroidectomy, which can result in hypocalcemia. ## Venous drainage Venous drainage of the parathyroid glands parallels that of the thyroid: - Venous blood drains into the **thyroid venous plexus**. - From there, it empties into: - The superior and middle thyroid veins, then into the internal jugular veins. - The inferior thyroid veins, then into the brachiocephalic veins. ## Innervation The parathyroid glands receive **sympathetic innervation from the cervical ganglia**, which primarily regulate vascular tone and blood flow.  There is minimal to no significant parasympathetic influence on the parathyroid glands. Hormone secretion is not under significant neural control and is instead regulated directly by serum calcium levels via calcium-sensing receptors (CaSR) on chief cells. ## Lymphatic drainage The parathyroid glands drain into the deep cervical and paratracheal lymph nodes. # Summary The thyroid and parathyroid glands are anatomically related endocrine organs with distinct functions.  The thyroid regulates metabolism through the secretion of triiodothyronine and thyroxine by follicular cells and contributes modestly to calcium regulation via calcitonin secretion from parafollicular C cells.  In contrast, the parathyroid glands maintain calcium homeostasis primarily through parathyroid hormone secretion by chief cells. ​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌

articles.title: Anatomy: Thorax And Thoracic Cavity
articles.markdown: # Anatomy: Thorax And Thoracic Cavity # Introduction The thorax contains the lungs and heart and enables the mechanical processes required for breathing and circulation.  Its anatomy allows it to protect vital organs while accommodating continuous changes in volume and pressure.  This article covers the structural organization of the thoracic wall (bones, joints, muscles), pleural spaces, diaphragm, mediastinum, and associated neurovascular structures. # Skeleton and joints The bony thoracic wall is composed of the sternum, 12 pairs of ribs, 12 thoracic vertebrae, and the involved joints ((Figure 1)). ## Sternum The sternum has 3 components:  the manubrium superiorly, the body (or corpus sterni), and the xiphoid process inferiorly. ## Ribs The ribs are classified based on the anterior attachments: - **True ribs** (1-7) articulate directly with the sternum. - **False ribs** (8-10) articulate indirectly through costal cartilage. - **Floating ribs** (11-12) terminate in the abdominal wall, creating regional differences in stability and injury patterns. ## Thoracic vertebrae (T1-T12) The thoracic vertebrae form the posterior component of the thoracic cage. ## Joints - **Posterior joints**:  Ribs 1-10 articulate with the thoracic vertebrae through costovertebral joints (rib head to vertebral bodies) and costotransverse joints (rib tubercle to transverse processes).  These synovial joints provide stability while allowing the rib movements needed for breathing. - **Anterior joints**:  Sternocostal (costochondral) joints connect ribs 1-7 to the sternum.  Interchondral joints between adjacent costal cartilages (most commonly between ribs 6-8) help distribute forces and increase rib cage flexibility. - **Sternoclavicular joints**:  Sternoclavicular joints connect the clavicles to the manubrium and link upper limb motion to the thoracic cage. These structures form thoracic landmarks ((Figure 2)) and allow rib motion that expands the chest in multiple dimensions during breathing. # Muscles of the thoracic wall The thoracic wall muscles are organized into 3 distinct layers of intercostal muscles, plus additional accessory muscles that contribute to respiration and chest wall stability. ## Intercostal muscles The intercostal muscles occupy the spaces between adjacent ribs and are arranged in 3 layers ((Figure 3)): - **External intercostals**:  Fibers run downward and forward from the rib above to the rib below; the external intercostals elevate ribs and stiffen intercostal spaces during inspiration, preventing inward collapse as intrathoracic pressure falls ((Figure 4)). - **Internal intercostals**:  Fibers run downward and backward, perpendicular to the external layer; the interosseous portion contributes to forced expiration by depressing the ribs, whereas the interchondral (parasternal) portion assists inspiration ((Figure 5)). - **Innermost intercostals**:  The deepest layer is separated from the internal intercostals by the intercostal neurovascular bundles; these muscles function similarly to the internal intercostals. ## Accessory muscles - **Anterior thoracic muscles**:  Transversus thoracis extends from the posterior surface of the sternum to the costal cartilages of ribs 2-6 and assists with expiration by depressing the ribs. - **Posterior accessory muscles**:  The levatores costarum elevate the ribs.  The serratus posterior superior and inferior may assist respiration; their exact role remains uncertain. - **Cervical accessory muscles**:  Scalene muscles (anterior, middle, posterior) originate from the cervical vertebrae and insert on the first two ribs; they play an important role in elevating the upper ribs during inspiration. Coordinated action across intercostal spaces converts segmental muscle contraction into uniform cage expansion.  Disruption of this muscle action produces paradoxical motion (eg, flail chest). # Pleural cavities The **pleurae** are paired serous membranes within the thoracic cavity that surround each lung and separate it from the chest wall.  They fold back on themselves to form 2 smooth layers, creating a thin potential space known as the **pleural cavity**, which normally contains a small amount of lubricating fluid ((Figure 6)). ## Visceral pleura Visceral pleura covers the lung surface and extends into the lung fissures, contributing to the formation of the lung lobes. ## Parietal pleura Parietal pleura lines the chest wall, diaphragm, and mediastinum. At the lung root, the visceral and parietal pleura are continuous, forming the **hilum**.  Areas where the lungs do not fully occupy the pleural cavity form **pleural recesses** (costomediastinal recess, costodiaphragmatic recess), which allow lung expansion during deep inspiration.  The costodiaphragmatic recess is the largest recess and is where pleural fluid accumulates most commonly. The pleural cavity maintains a **negative pressure** that changes with respiration.  During inspiration, expansion of the thoracic cavity lowers intrapleural pressure, allowing the lungs to expand and draw in air.  During expiration, pressure increases as lung recoil occurs.  This negative pressure mechanism helps keep the lungs inflated; disruption of the pleural seal can lead to pneumothorax. # Mediastinum and compartments The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thorax located between the 2 pleural cavities, extending from the thoracic inlet superiorly to the diaphragm inferiorly and from the sternum anteriorly to the vertebral column posteriorly.  It is divided into superior and inferior compartments.  The inferior mediastinum is further subdivided into 3 compartments ((Figure 7)).  More detailed information regarding the anatomy and clinical relevance of the mediastinum can be found in the article on the anatomy of the mediastinum. ## Superior mediastinum The superior mediastinum contains the great vessels, trachea, and esophagus, whose fixed spatial relationships are essential for interpreting mediastinal widening on imaging. ## Inferior mediastinum - **Anterior (prevascular) mediastinum** - **Location**:  Between the sternum and pericardium; extends from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragm. - **Contents**:  Thymus, ectopic thyroid tissue, lymph nodes, internal mammary vessels. - **Middle (visceral) mediastinum** - **Location**:  Between the pericardium and great vessels anteriorly and the anterior vertebral bodies posteriorly. - **Contents**:  Heart, great vessels, trachea, main bronchi, esophagus, lymph nodes. - **Posterior (paravertebral) mediastinum** - **Location**:  From the anterior vertebral bodies to the posterior chest wall. - **Contents**:  Sympathetic chain, peripheral nerves. The anterior/middle/posterior mediastinum is an anatomic classification, whereas the prevascular/visceral/paravertebral compartments are a radiologic (CT scan–based) system; both describe the same region from different perspectives. # Vessels The thorax contains major arterial and venous structures that supply the thoracic wall and support systemic and pulmonary circulation. ## Arteries that supply the thoracic wall - **Posterior intercostal arteries**:  The posterior intercostal arteries arise segmentally from the descending thoracic aorta and supply the lateral and posterior thoracic wall.  They course within the costal groove along the inferior border of each rib as part of the intercostal neurovascular bundle, which is arranged in the order **vein, artery, nerve** (mnemonic: VAN).  This predictable relationship is clinically important and guides safe needle and chest tube placement when accessing the pleural space (eg, the thoracentesis needle should be inserted above the rib to avoid vessel or nerve injury ((Figure 8))). - **Internal thoracic arteries**:  The internal thoracic arteries arise from the subclavian arteries and descend along the posterior surface of the anterior chest wall, just lateral to the sternum.  They give rise to **anterior intercostal**, perforating, and sternal branches, supplying the anterior thoracic wall and sternum. - **Lateral thoracic artery**:  This artery descends along the lateral chest wall and frequently anastomoses with intercostal branches, contributing to the vascular network supplying the lateral thoracic wall. ## Major mediastinal arteries - **Ascending aorta**:  Arises from the left ventricle and gives rise to the coronary arteries ((Figure 9)). - **Pulmonary trunk**:  Originates from the right ventricle and divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries. - **Aortic arch**:  Begins at T4-T5 and gives rise to the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid artery, and left subclavian artery. - **Descending thoracic aorta**:  Extends from T4-T5 to T12 and supplies the thoracic wall and viscera. ## Venous drainage of thorax Blood from the thoracic wall drains via the internal thoracic veins into the brachiocephalic veins and through the intercostal veins into the azygos venous system.  The **azygos vein** ascends along the right side of the posterior mediastinum and empties into the **superior vena cava**, whereas the **hemiazygos** and **accessory hemiazygos veins** ascend on the left and cross to join the azygos vein.  This system provides an important collateral pathway between the superior and inferior venae cavae and becomes especially prominent when caval obstruction is present.  Venous return from the lungs occurs separately through the **pulmonary veins**, which drain oxygenated blood into the left atrium ((Figure 10)). # Nerves - **Phrenic nerves** ((Figure 11)):  Originate from C3-C5 spinal nerve roots and descend through the superior and middle mediastinum along the sides of the fibrous pericardium, providing motor innervation to the diaphragm and sensory pain fibers to the pericardium, mediastinal pleura, and central diaphragmatic pleura/peritoneum. - **Vagus nerves (CN X)**:  Descend through the superior and posterior mediastinum, contributing to the cardiac, pulmonary, and esophageal plexuses.  They provide motor fibers to the pharynx, larynx, and soft palate; sensory fibers to portions of the ear, larynx, and thoracic/abdominal viscera; and parasympathetic fibers that decrease heart rate/contractility, cause bronchoconstriction, and stimulate peristalsis ((Figure 12)). - **Recurrent laryngeal nerve**:  Supplies motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid and provides sensory innervation below the vocal cords.  The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the subclavian artery.  The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (which branches from the left vagus nerve) loops under the aortic arch.  Aortic aneurysm or mediastinal lymphadenopathy may compress this nerve, leading to hoarseness.  The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is also at significant risk during thyroid surgery. -   **Intercostal nerves** (T1-T11):  Ventral rami of thoracic spinal nerves that run within the costal grooves between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles.  They provide motor innervation to intercostal muscles and sensory innervation to the thoracic wall, pleura, and peripheral diaphragm.  Each nerve supplies a predictable horizontal dermatome and the corresponding intercostal muscles, allowing sensory deficits or pain patterns to localize thoracic levels, facilitating nerve blocks ((Figure 13)). - **Long thoracic nerve** (C5-C7):  Arises from cervical nerve roots and descends along the lateral chest wall.  It supplies the **serratus anterior muscle**, which stabilizes the scapula against the thoracic wall.  Injury results in **winged scapula** and impaired arm elevation above 90 degrees ((Figure 14)), ((Figure 15)). - **Sympathetic trunks**:  Run vertically along the vertebral bodies, beginning in the superior mediastinum and into the posterior mediastinum.  They carry sympathetic (thoracolumbar) fibers that regulate involuntary smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glandular activity, producing increased heart rate and contractility, bronchodilation, and reduced glandular secretion ((Figure 16)). # Lymphatics The lymphatic system of the thorax provides drainage for the lungs, thoracic wall, and mediastinal structures and reflects patterns of disease spread and pleural pathology ((Figure 17)). - **Thoracic duct**:  Drains lymph from the majority of the body (exceptions are the right upper limb and the right side of the head and neck).  It ascends through the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and azygos vein and empties into the **left venous angle** (junction of the left internal jugular and subclavian veins) ((Figure 18)). - **Mediastinal lymph nodes**:  Organized by compartment and drainage territory. - **Superior mediastinum (paratracheal, pretracheal, brachiocephalic)**:  Drain the trachea, thyroid, and thymus.  Enlargement may compress the trachea or recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing dyspnea or hoarseness. - **Anterior mediastinum (parasternal, anterior mediastinal)**:  Drain the anterior thoracic wall, thymus, and pericardium.  Common sites of spread for breast cancer and anterior mediastinal tumors. - **Middle mediastinum (tracheobronchial, hilar, carinal)**:  Drain the lungs, bronchi, heart, and trachea.  Frequently involved in lung cancer and granulomatous diseases (eg, sarcoidosis), often detected on chest imaging. - **Posterior mediastinum (posterior mediastinal, retrocardiac)**:  Drain the esophagus, posterior pericardium, and diaphragm.  Esophageal malignancy may spread to these nodes. Lymph from the thoracic wall drains to parasternal, intercostal, and diaphragmatic nodes, whereas pulmonary lymph drains centrally to bronchopulmonary and tracheobronchial nodes.  These pathways converge toward the thoracic duct.  Injury or obstruction of the thoracic duct results in **chylothorax** (a milky pleural effusion due to lymphatic leakage). # Diaphragm The diaphragm is a dome-shaped fibromuscular structure forming the inferior boundary of the thoracic cavity.  Its domes project superiorly into the chest, with the highest point typically between T4 and T8.  Its contraction increases thoracic volume and lowers intrathoracic pressure during inspiration.  The diaphragm contains 3 major openings that allow structures to pass between the thorax and the abdomen: - **Caval opening (T8)**:  Transmits the inferior vena cava. - **Esophageal hiatus (T10)**:  Transmits the esophagus and vagal trunks. - **Aortic hiatus (T12)**:  Transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerves and intercostal nerves (as described earlier). # Clinical correlations Injury or disease affecting thoracic structures can significantly impair ventilation and circulation. - **Rib fracture**:  Disrupts the thoracic cage, which can interfere with normal rib excursion and intercostal muscle function.  The pain associated with rib fractures limits chest wall expansion, resulting in shallow ventilation and an increased risk of dependent atelectasis and pneumonia. - **Flail chest**:  Occurs when fracture of ≥3 adjacent ribs in ≥2 locations creates an isolated chest wall segment that moves paradoxically to the remaining rib cage during respiration.  The paradoxical motion impairs generation of negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration.  As a result, tidal volume decreases and work of breathing increases ((Figure 19)), ((Image 1)). - **Tension pneumothorax:**  Develops when accumulated air causes high intrathoracic pressure that compresses the vena cava and impedes cardiac venous return, resulting in decreased cardiac output and hypotension.  This occurs when a 1-way valve has formed, allowing air to flow into the pleural space during inspiration but trapping it during expiration ((Figure 20)), ((Image 2)). - **Pericardial tamponade**:  Occurs when rapid accumulation of fluid within the noncompliant fibrous pericardium raises intrapericardial pressure, restricting ventricular diastolic filling.  This limits stroke volume and cardiac output, resulting in hypotension and obstructive shock physiology ((Figure 21)), ((Image 3)). - **Intercostal nerve injury**:  Occurs when trauma, surgery, or rib fracture damages a thoracic spinal nerve as it courses along the costal groove, resulting in segmental sensory loss or neuropathic pain in the corresponding dermatome.  Motor involvement may impair intercostal muscle function, reducing localized chest wall expansion during respiration. - **Phrenic nerve palsy**:  Results from damage to the C3-C5 motor fibers supplying the diaphragm, leading to ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis ((Image 4)).  Loss of diaphragmatic descent during inspiration reduces lung expansion and tidal volume, producing elevation of the affected hemidiaphragm and exertional dyspnea. - **Diaphragmatic injury**:  Results from blunt or penetrating trauma that disrupts diaphragmatic contraction, impairing generation of negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration.  This reduces lung expansion and may permit herniation of abdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity, leading to respiratory compromise ((Figure 22)). Clinical correlations specific to the mediastinum can be found in the article on the anatomy of the mediastinum. # Summary The bones, muscles, nerves, vessels, and connective tissues of the thorax protect vital organs and support breathing and circulation.  Its structure allows the chest to maintain the pressure relationships required for normal lung and heart function.  Thoracic anatomy disruption can lead to clinically important conditions such as rib fractures and flail chest, pneumothorax or pleural effusion, pericardial tamponade, vascular compromise, and intercostal or phrenic nerve injury. ​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌

articles.title: Anatomy: Skull And Cranial Cavity
articles.markdown:
# Anatomy: Skull And Cranial Cavity # Introduction The skull (ie, cranium) is a complex osseous structure that forms the bony framework of the head and face.  It comprises 22 bones and is divided into 2 regions ((Figure 1)): the neurocranium, which surrounds the brain, and the viscerocranium, the bony scaffold of the face.  The cranial cavity is the space within the skull that contains the brain, meninges, ventricles, and associated neurovascular structures. # Neurocranium ## Function The neurocranium encloses and protects the brain and provides attachment sites for the muscles of mastication and head and neck musculature.  It also contains various important foramina that transmit cranial nerves and major blood vessels. ## Bony anatomy The neurocranium is formed by 8 bones (4 paired, 4 unpaired) joined by immovable fibrous joints (ie, sutures). - Parietal bones:  Paired bones that form the superior and lateral walls of the neurocranium. - Temporal bones:  Paired bones that form a significant portion of the lateral skull base.  The temporal bones are divided into 4 main parts: the petrous, squamous, tympanic, and mastoid portions. - Petrous:  Houses the middle and inner ear structures. - Squamous:  Forms part of the temporal fossa (attachment site for the temporalis muscle of mastication), contains the zygomatic process (part of zygomatic arch), and houses the mandibular fossa (part of the temporomandibular joint \[TMJ\]). - Tympanic:  A curved bony plate that forms the bony portion of the external auditory canal. - Mastoid:  Serves as an attachment site for the sternocleidomastoid, splenius capitis, and longissimus capitis muscles and contains mastoid air cells. - Frontal bone:  Forms the anterior forehead and the roof of the orbits (orbital plates). - Occipital bone:  Forms most of the posterior skull and contains the foramen magnum (which transmits brainstem structures). - Sphenoid bone:  Forms the central portion of the skull base and contains the sella turcica (which houses the pituitary gland) and multiple important foramina.  The sphenoid is divided into the body (median portion), 2 greater wings (lateral portions), 2 lesser wings (anterior portions), and pterygoid processes, which serve as attachment sites for the pterygoid muscles of mastication. - Ethmoid bone:  Composed of multiple components.  The cribriform plate forms the horizontal portion and contains the olfactory foramina for olfactory nerve fibers.  The perpendicular plate forms the superior portion of the nasal septum.  The ethmoidal labyrinths contain the superior and middle nasal conchae and numerous ethmoid air cells.  The lamina papyracea forms the medial wall of the orbit. ## Subdivisions The neurocranium is subdivided into 2 sections: the calvaria and the cranial (skull) base. - Calvaria:  The superior dome-shaped portion of the neurocranium that is primarily composed of the 2 parietal bones, the frontal bone, and the occipital bone ((Figure 2)).  The calvaria protects the cerebral cortex and cerebellum. - Cranial base:  The floor of the cranial cavity is formed from the sphenoid and ethmoid bones and the inferior portions of the frontal, temporal, and occipital bones ((Figure 3)). ## Cranial fossae and foramina The cranial base contains 3 depressions called cranial fossae (ie, anterior, middle, posterior) that accommodate different regions of the brain and contain various foramina that transmit multiple nerves and vessels ((Figure 4)), ((Figure 5)). **Anterior cranial fossa**:  Formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, and the lesser wings of the sphenoid. - Contents:  Frontal lobes of the cerebral cortex and olfactory bulbs and tracts. - Key foramina - Cribriform foramina:  Transmit olfactory nerve (CN I) fibers. **Middle cranial fossa**:  Formed by the body and greater wings of the sphenoid bone and the squamous and petrous portions of the temporal bone. - Contents:  Temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex and the pituitary gland (within the sella turcica). - Key foramina - Optic canal:  Transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery. - Superior orbital fissure ((Figure 6)):  Transmits the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve (CN V1), and the superior ophthalmic vein. - Foramen rotundum:  Transmits the maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve (CN V2). - Foramen ovale:  Transmits mandibular branch of trigeminal nerve (CN V3). - Foramen spinosum:  Transmits middle meningeal artery. - Carotid canal: Transmits internal carotid artery. **Posterior cranial fossa**:  Formed by the occipital bone, the petrous portion of the temporal bone, and the clivus (a bony surface formed by portions of the sphenoid and occipital bones). - Contents:  Cerebellum, pons, and medulla. - Key foramina - Foramen magnum:  Transmits the medulla oblongata, spinal roots of the accessory nerve (CN XI), vertebral arteries, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries. - Internal acoustic meatus:  Transmits the facial nerve (CN VII) and the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). - Jugular foramen:  Transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), vagus nerve (CN X), accessory nerve (CN XI), and internal jugular vein. - Hypoglossal canal: Transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). ## Sutures The major sutures of the neurocranium include the following: - Coronal suture:  Between the frontal and parietal bones. - Sagittal suture:  Between the 2 parietal bones. - Lambdoid suture:  Between the parietal and occipital bones. - Squamous suture:  Between the temporal and parietal bones. ## Fontanelles Infant skulls contain fontanelles ((Figure 7)), membranous gaps between cranial bones that allow for brain growth and skull deformation during birth. - Anterior fontanelle:  Located at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures and typically closes at age 18 months. - Posterior fontanelle:  Located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures and typically closes at age 2-3 months. ## Histology and neurovascular supply Skull bones consist of 2 dense layers of compact bone (the inner and outer tables) separated by a central layer of cancellous (spongy) bone called the diploë, which contains marrow and diploic vessels. The arterial supply to the neurocranium is derived from both the external and internal carotid artery systems, and includes the following: - Periosteal vessels:  Primarily branches of the external carotid artery (eg, superficial temporal, occipital), with contributions from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system).  These supply the outer surface of the skull and overlying scalp. - Diploic arteries:  Arise from penetrating branches of both the external and internal carotid systems and supply the diploë. - Meningeal arteries:  Supply the inner surface of the skull and dura mater, most notably the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery (the external carotid system). Venous drainage of the neurocranium occurs via diploic veins, which communicate with the dural venous sinuses and ultimately drain into the internal jugular veins. The periosteum of the skull bones is pain-sensitive and receives sensory innervation from branches of the trigeminal nerve anteriorly and the upper cervical spinal nerves (C2-C3) posteriorly. # Viscerocranium ## Function The viscerocranium forms the structural framework of the face, supporting the orbit, nasal cavity, and oral cavity.  It also provides attachment sites for muscles of facial expression and mastication and houses the upper and lower teeth, thereby contributing to functions such as breathing, chewing, speech, and facial expression. ## Bony anatomy The viscerocranium comprises 14 bones (12 paired, 2 unpaired). - Maxillae:  Paired bones that form the upper jaw, orbital floor, lateral walls of nasal cavity, and anterior hard palate. - Zygomatic bones:  Paired bones that form cheek prominences and lateral orbital walls. - Nasal bones:  Paired bones that form the bridge of the nose. - Lacrimal bones:  Paired bones that contribute to the medial orbital wall and contain the lacrimal groove for the lacrimal sac. - Palatine bones:  Paired bones that form the posterior hard palate and part of the orbital floor and lateral wall of nasal cavity. - Inferior nasal conchae:  Paired bones that comprise the lateral nasal wall. - Vomer:  Forms the posteroinferior nasal septum. - Mandible:  Forms the lower jaw and articulates with the temporal bone at the TMJ. ## Subdivisions Unlike the neurocranium, the viscerocranium lacks formal subdivisions but can be functionally organized into the upper face, midface, and lower face based on the major anatomic structures within each region. **Upper face** - The orbit is a pyramidal structure composed of portions of the frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxilla, palatine, lacrimal, and ethmoid bones ((Figure 8)).  It houses and protects the globe, extraocular muscles, and ocular nerves and vessels. - The nasal skeleton is formed by contributions from the nasal bones, maxillae, ethmoid bone, vomer, inferior nasal conchae, and palatine bones.  These structures form the nasal septum and lateral nasal walls. **Midface** - The midface (maxillary complex) is centered around the maxillae, which articulate with multiple surrounding bones (zygoma, nasal, frontal, palatine, and ethmoid).  The maxillae house the upper teeth, form the orbital floor, and contribute to the inferior nasal cavity and hard palate. **Lower face** - The lower face is composed of the mandible, which houses the lower teeth and is essential for mastication and speech.  It is the only movable bone in the skull. ## Foramina Several branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) are transmitted via viscerocranial foramina.  These foramina and their corresponding nerves serve as targets for regional nerve blocks. - Infraorbital foramen:  Transmits the infraorbital nerve (branch of CN V2), which provides sensation to the lower eyelid, upper lip, and lateral nose. - Mental foramen:  Transmits the mental vessels and mental nerve (branch of CN V3), which provides sensation to the lower lip and chin. - Mandibular foramen:  Transmits the inferior alveolar vessels and inferior alveolar nerve (branch of CN V3), which provides sensation to the lower teeth. The infraorbital, mental, and inferior alveolar vessels also travel through their respective foramina. ## Sutures Most clinically significant sutures are in the neurocranium.  Viscerocranial sutures (eg, intermaxillary suture, frontozygomatic suture) are typically only relevant in specific contexts (eg, trauma, surgical reconstruction). ## Histology and neurovascular supply The bones of the viscerocranium are structurally similar to those of the neurocranium; however, the diploë is generally less well developed than in the calvaria. The arterial supply to the viscerocranium is derived primarily from branches of the external carotid artery, particularly the facial and maxillary arteries, with contributions from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system).  Key branches include the infraorbital, superior and inferior alveolar, and mental arteries, which supply the maxilla, mandible, and associated structures. Venous drainage occurs mainly via the facial and maxillary venous systems, which communicate with the dural venous sinuses via the ophthalmic veins and cavernous sinus. Sensory innervation to the viscerocranium is provided by the 3 branches of the trigeminal nerve (V1-V3). # Cranial cavity The cranial cavity is the internal space within the neurocranium that contains the brain and its associated structures, including the meninges, dural venous sinuses, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the ventricular system, and intracranial arteries. ## Meninges The meninges are 3 connective tissue layers that surround the brain (and spinal cord) and provide mechanical protection, support blood vessels, and contain CSF ((Figure 9)). - **Dura mater**:  The outermost and strongest meningeal layer.  In the cranial cavity, it consists of 2 layers: the periosteal layer, which adheres to the inner surface of the skull, and the meningeal layer, which forms inward folds (dural reflections) that partition and stabilize the brain.  These 2 layers are normally fused but separate at certain points to form the dural venous sinuses.  The dura mater is supplied primarily by the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery.  The dura is highly pain-sensitive and receives sensory innervation mainly from the trigeminal nerve and the upper cervical nerves (C2-C3). - **Arachnoid mater**:  The middle meningeal layer, located between the dura mater and pia mater.  It is a thin membrane that loosely covers the brain without following the contours of the gyri and sulci.  Beneath it lies the subarachnoid space, which contains CSF, cerebral arteries and veins, and cranial nerve roots.  The arachnoid mater also forms arachnoid granulations, which allow reabsorption of CSF into the venous circulation.  It is avascular and has minimal to no sensory innervation. - **Pia mater**:  The innermost meningeal layer; a delicate, highly vascular membrane that closely adheres to the surface of the brain and spinal cord.  Unlike the arachnoid mater, it follows the contours of the brain, extending into the gyri and sulci.  The pia mater contributes to the formation of the choroid plexus, which produces CSF.  It is supplied by small branches of the cerebral and cerebellar arteries, which arise from the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems.  The pia lacks sensory innervation. ## Dural reflections Dural reflections are folds in the meninges that stabilize the brain within the skull.  They include: - Falx cerebri:  Separates the right and left hemispheres. - Tentorium cerebelli:  Separates the cerebrum and cerebellum. - Falx cerebelli:  Separates the cerebellar hemispheres. - Diaphragma sellae:  Covers the pituitary gland within the sella turcica. ## Dural venous sinuses The dural venous sinuses are venous channels located between the 2 layers of the dura mater that drain blood from the brain (ie, cerebral veins) into the internal jugular veins ((Figure 10)).  These can be conceptually organized into midline and lateral drainage pathways. - Midline:  Cerebral veins drain into the superior and inferior sagittal and straight sinus, into the confluence of sinuses, the transverse sinuses, the sigmoid sinuses, and the internal jugular veins. - Lateral:  The orbit, face, and brain drain into the cavernous sinus ((Figure 11)), a paired sinus located lateral to the sella turcica.  The cavernous sinus empties into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, then into the transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and the internal jugular vein.  Important structures within or adjacent to the cavernous sinus include the internal carotid artery and CN VI within the sinus, and CN III, CN IV, CN V1, and CN V2 within its lateral wall. ## Ventricular system CSF is continually produced by the choroid plexus via active secretion ((Figure 12)).  It then passes through a series of interconnected cavities (ie, ventricles), traveling from the lateral ventricles to the foramina of Monro, the third ventricle, the aqueduct of Sylvius, and the fourth ventricle.  CSF exits the fourth ventricle through either of the paired lateral foramina of Luschka or the medial foramen of Magendie to reach the subarachnoid space.  CSF then flows to the arachnoid granulations, where it is reabsorbed (down a pressure gradient) into the venous sinuses, which empty into the jugular veins. ## Arterial supply The intracranial structures are provided by the internal carotid (anterior circulation) and vertebrobasilar (posterior circulation) systems, which together form the circle of Willis ((Figure 13)). # Clinical correlations ## Skull fractures Skull fractures occur when traumatic forces exceed the structural strength of the cranial bones.  They may be classified based on the pattern and location of the fracture. - Linear fractures (most common):  Appear as a thin break in the bone without displacement.  They are often associated with blunt trauma and may be clinically silent unless underlying structures such as blood vessels or brain tissue are injured. - Depressed fractures:  Occur when a portion of the fractured skull is displaced inward toward the brain, often due to high-energy trauma from objects with a small surface area (eg, hammer).  These fractures may compress or lacerate the underlying brain tissue and frequently require surgical elevation of the depressed bone fragments. - Basilar skull fractures:  Involve the base of the skull and may affect the temporal, sphenoid, occipital, or ethmoid bones.  These fractures are often associated with characteristic clinical findings ((Figure 14)), including: - Periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon eyes") ((Image 1)). - Postauricular ecchymosis (Battle sign). - Hemotympanum. - CSF leakage from the nose (CSF rhinorrhea) or ear (CSF otorrhea).  Inspection of fluid on a gauze dressing shows a halo sign ((Figure 15)). - Cranial nerve palsies (eg, anosmia, vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss). ## Intracranial hemorrhages Intracranial hemorrhages can occur in the epidural, subdural, or subarachnoid spaces ((Table 1)): - Epidural hematoma:  Hemorrhage between the skull and the dura mater, most commonly due to middle meningeal artery injury ((Figure 16)). - Fracture of the pterion (ie, junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones), which overlies the middle meningeal artery, can lead to epidural hematoma. - Subdural hematoma:  Hemorrhage between the dura and arachnoid mater, most often bridging cortical vein injury (eg, elderly falls). - Subarachnoid hemorrhage:  Hemorrhage between the arachnoid and pia mater ((Figure 17)).  This type of hemorrhage is most often due to rupture of saccular (berry) aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation. # Summary The skull is a complex bony structure that houses and protects the brain and supports the structures of the face.  The intracranial cavity is a space within the skull that contains the brain, meninges, ventricles, and important vascular structures. ​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​

›Introduction

The skull (ie, cranium) is a complex osseous structure that forms the bony framework of the head and face.  It comprises 22 bones and is divided into 2 regions : the neurocranium, which surrounds the brain, and the viscerocranium, the bony scaffold of the face.  The cranial cavity is the space within the skull that contains the brain, meninges, ventricles, and associated neurovascular structures.

›Neurocranium

Function

The neurocranium encloses and protects the brain and provides attachment sites for the muscles of mastication and head and neck musculature.  It also contains various important foramina that transmit cranial nerves and major blood vessels.

Bony anatomy

The neurocranium is formed by 8 bones (4 paired, 4 unpaired) joined by immovable fibrous joints (ie, sutures).

  • Parietal bones:  Paired bones that form the superior and lateral walls of the neurocranium.
  • Temporal bones:  Paired bones that form a significant portion of the lateral skull base.  The temporal bones are divided into 4 main parts: the petrous, squamous, tympanic, and mastoid portions.
    • Petrous:  Houses the middle and inner ear structures.
    • Squamous:  Forms part of the temporal fossa (attachment site for the temporalis muscle of mastication), contains the zygomatic process (part of zygomatic arch), and houses the mandibular fossa (part of the temporomandibular joint [TMJ]).
    • Tympanic:  A curved bony plate that forms the bony portion of the external auditory canal.
    • Mastoid:  Serves as an attachment site for the sternocleidomastoid, splenius capitis, and longissimus capitis muscles and contains mastoid air cells.
  • Frontal bone:  Forms the anterior forehead and the roof of the orbits (orbital plates).
  • Occipital bone:  Forms most of the posterior skull and contains the foramen magnum (which transmits brainstem structures).
  • Sphenoid bone:  Forms the central portion of the skull base and contains the sella turcica (which houses the pituitary gland) and multiple important foramina.  The sphenoid is divided into the body (median portion), 2 greater wings (lateral portions), 2 lesser wings (anterior portions), and pterygoid processes, which serve as attachment sites for the pterygoid muscles of mastication.
  • Ethmoid bone:  Composed of multiple components.  The cribriform plate forms the horizontal portion and contains the olfactory foramina for olfactory nerve fibers.  The perpendicular plate forms the superior portion of the nasal septum.  The ethmoidal labyrinths contain the superior and middle nasal conchae and numerous ethmoid air cells.  The lamina papyracea forms the medial wall of the orbit.

Subdivisions

The neurocranium is subdivided into 2 sections: the calvaria and the cranial (skull) base.

  • Calvaria:  The superior dome-shaped portion of the neurocranium that is primarily composed of the 2 parietal bones, the frontal bone, and the occipital bone .  The calvaria protects the cerebral cortex and cerebellum.
  • Cranial base:  The floor of the cranial cavity is formed from the sphenoid and ethmoid bones and the inferior portions of the frontal, temporal, and occipital bones .

Cranial fossae and foramina

The cranial base contains 3 depressions called cranial fossae (ie, anterior, middle, posterior) that accommodate different regions of the brain and contain various foramina that transmit multiple nerves and vessels , .

Anterior cranial fossa:  Formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, and the lesser wings of the sphenoid.

  • Contents:  Frontal lobes of the cerebral cortex and olfactory bulbs and tracts.
  • Key foramina
    • Cribriform foramina:  Transmit olfactory nerve (CN I) fibers.

Middle cranial fossa:  Formed by the body and greater wings of the sphenoid bone and the squamous and petrous portions of the temporal bone.

  • Contents:  Temporal lobes of the cerebral cortex and the pituitary gland (within the sella turcica).
  • Key foramina
    • Optic canal:  Transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery.
    • Superior orbital fissure :  Transmits the oculomotor nerve (CN III), trochlear nerve (CN IV), abducens nerve (CN VI), ophthalmic branch of trigeminal nerve (CN V1), and the superior ophthalmic vein.
    • Foramen rotundum:  Transmits the maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve (CN V2).
    • Foramen ovale:  Transmits mandibular branch of trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
    • Foramen spinosum:  Transmits middle meningeal artery.
    • Carotid canal: Transmits internal carotid artery.

Posterior cranial fossa:  Formed by the occipital bone, the petrous portion of the temporal bone, and the clivus (a bony surface formed by portions of the sphenoid and occipital bones).

  • Contents:  Cerebellum, pons, and medulla.
  • Key foramina
    • Foramen magnum:  Transmits the medulla oblongata, spinal roots of the accessory nerve (CN XI), vertebral arteries, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries.
    • Internal acoustic meatus:  Transmits the facial nerve (CN VII) and the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII).
    • Jugular foramen:  Transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), vagus nerve (CN X), accessory nerve (CN XI), and internal jugular vein.
    • Hypoglossal canal: Transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

Sutures

The major sutures of the neurocranium include the following:

  • Coronal suture:  Between the frontal and parietal bones.
  • Sagittal suture:  Between the 2 parietal bones.
  • Lambdoid suture:  Between the parietal and occipital bones.
  • Squamous suture:  Between the temporal and parietal bones.

Fontanelles

Infant skulls contain fontanelles , membranous gaps between cranial bones that allow for brain growth and skull deformation during birth.

  • Anterior fontanelle:  Located at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures and typically closes at age 18 months.
  • Posterior fontanelle:  Located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures and typically closes at age 2-3 months.

Histology and neurovascular supply

Skull bones consist of 2 dense layers of compact bone (the inner and outer tables) separated by a central layer of cancellous (spongy) bone called the diploë, which contains marrow and diploic vessels.

The arterial supply to the neurocranium is derived from both the external and internal carotid artery systems, and includes the following:

  • Periosteal vessels:  Primarily branches of the external carotid artery (eg, superficial temporal, occipital), with contributions from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system).  These supply the outer surface of the skull and overlying scalp.
  • Diploic arteries:  Arise from penetrating branches of both the external and internal carotid systems and supply the diploë.
  • Meningeal arteries:  Supply the inner surface of the skull and dura mater, most notably the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery (the external carotid system).

Venous drainage of the neurocranium occurs via diploic veins, which communicate with the dural venous sinuses and ultimately drain into the internal jugular veins.

The periosteum of the skull bones is pain-sensitive and receives sensory innervation from branches of the trigeminal nerve anteriorly and the upper cervical spinal nerves (C2-C3) posteriorly.

›Viscerocranium

Function

The viscerocranium forms the structural framework of the face, supporting the orbit, nasal cavity, and oral cavity.  It also provides attachment sites for muscles of facial expression and mastication and houses the upper and lower teeth, thereby contributing to functions such as breathing, chewing, speech, and facial expression.

Bony anatomy

The viscerocranium comprises 14 bones (12 paired, 2 unpaired).

  • Maxillae:  Paired bones that form the upper jaw, orbital floor, lateral walls of nasal cavity, and anterior hard palate.
  • Zygomatic bones:  Paired bones that form cheek prominences and lateral orbital walls.
  • Nasal bones:  Paired bones that form the bridge of the nose.
  • Lacrimal bones:  Paired bones that contribute to the medial orbital wall and contain the lacrimal groove for the lacrimal sac.
  • Palatine bones:  Paired bones that form the posterior hard palate and part of the orbital floor and lateral wall of nasal cavity.
  • Inferior nasal conchae:  Paired bones that comprise the lateral nasal wall.
  • Vomer:  Forms the posteroinferior nasal septum.
  • Mandible:  Forms the lower jaw and articulates with the temporal bone at the TMJ.

Subdivisions

Unlike the neurocranium, the viscerocranium lacks formal subdivisions but can be functionally organized into the upper face, midface, and lower face based on the major anatomic structures within each region.

Upper face

  • The orbit is a pyramidal structure composed of portions of the frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxilla, palatine, lacrimal, and ethmoid bones .  It houses and protects the globe, extraocular muscles, and ocular nerves and vessels.
  • The nasal skeleton is formed by contributions from the nasal bones, maxillae, ethmoid bone, vomer, inferior nasal conchae, and palatine bones.  These structures form the nasal septum and lateral nasal walls.

Midface

  • The midface (maxillary complex) is centered around the maxillae, which articulate with multiple surrounding bones (zygoma, nasal, frontal, palatine, and ethmoid).  The maxillae house the upper teeth, form the orbital floor, and contribute to the inferior nasal cavity and hard palate.

Lower face

  • The lower face is composed of the mandible, which houses the lower teeth and is essential for mastication and speech.  It is the only movable bone in the skull.

Foramina

Several branches of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) are transmitted via viscerocranial foramina.  These foramina and their corresponding nerves serve as targets for regional nerve blocks.

  • Infraorbital foramen:  Transmits the infraorbital nerve (branch of CN V2), which provides sensation to the lower eyelid, upper lip, and lateral nose.
  • Mental foramen:  Transmits the mental vessels and mental nerve (branch of CN V3), which provides sensation to the lower lip and chin.
  • Mandibular foramen:  Transmits the inferior alveolar vessels and inferior alveolar nerve (branch of CN V3), which provides sensation to the lower teeth.

The infraorbital, mental, and inferior alveolar vessels also travel through their respective foramina.

Sutures

Most clinically significant sutures are in the neurocranium.  Viscerocranial sutures (eg, intermaxillary suture, frontozygomatic suture) are typically only relevant in specific contexts (eg, trauma, surgical reconstruction).

Histology and neurovascular supply

The bones of the viscerocranium are structurally similar to those of the neurocranium; however, the diploë is generally less well developed than in the calvaria.

The arterial supply to the viscerocranium is derived primarily from branches of the external carotid artery, particularly the facial and maxillary arteries, with contributions from the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid system).  Key branches include the infraorbital, superior and inferior alveolar, and mental arteries, which supply the maxilla, mandible, and associated structures.

Venous drainage occurs mainly via the facial and maxillary venous systems, which communicate with the dural venous sinuses via the ophthalmic veins and cavernous sinus.

Sensory innervation to the viscerocranium is provided by the 3 branches of the trigeminal nerve (V1-V3).

›Cranial cavity

The cranial cavity is the internal space within the neurocranium that contains the brain and its associated structures, including the meninges, dural venous sinuses, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the ventricular system, and intracranial arteries.

Meninges

The meninges are 3 connective tissue layers that surround the brain (and spinal cord) and provide mechanical protection, support blood vessels, and contain CSF .

  • Dura mater:  The outermost and strongest meningeal layer.  In the cranial cavity, it consists of 2 layers: the periosteal layer, which adheres to the inner surface of the skull, and the meningeal layer, which forms inward folds (dural reflections) that partition and stabilize the brain.  These 2 layers are normally fused but separate at certain points to form the dural venous sinuses.  The dura mater is supplied primarily by the middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery.  The dura is highly pain-sensitive and receives sensory innervation mainly from the trigeminal nerve and the upper cervical nerves (C2-C3).
  • Arachnoid mater:  The middle meningeal layer, located between the dura mater and pia mater.  It is a thin membrane that loosely covers the brain without following the contours of the gyri and sulci.  Beneath it lies the subarachnoid space, which contains CSF, cerebral arteries and veins, and cranial nerve roots.  The arachnoid mater also forms arachnoid granulations, which allow reabsorption of CSF into the venous circulation.  It is avascular and has minimal to no sensory innervation.
  • Pia mater:  The innermost meningeal layer; a delicate, highly vascular membrane that closely adheres to the surface of the brain and spinal cord.  Unlike the arachnoid mater, it follows the contours of the brain, extending into the gyri and sulci.  The pia mater contributes to the formation of the choroid plexus, which produces CSF.  It is supplied by small branches of the cerebral and cerebellar arteries, which arise from the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems.  The pia lacks sensory innervation.

Dural reflections

Dural reflections are folds in the meninges that stabilize the brain within the skull.  They include:

  • Falx cerebri:  Separates the right and left hemispheres.
  • Tentorium cerebelli:  Separates the cerebrum and cerebellum.
  • Falx cerebelli:  Separates the cerebellar hemispheres.
  • Diaphragma sellae:  Covers the pituitary gland within the sella turcica.

Dural venous sinuses

The dural venous sinuses are venous channels located between the 2 layers of the dura mater that drain blood from the brain (ie, cerebral veins) into the internal jugular veins .  These can be conceptually organized into midline and lateral drainage pathways.

  • Midline:  Cerebral veins drain into the superior and inferior sagittal and straight sinus, into the confluence of sinuses, the transverse sinuses, the sigmoid sinuses, and the internal jugular veins.
  • Lateral:  The orbit, face, and brain drain into the cavernous sinus , a paired sinus located lateral to the sella turcica.  The cavernous sinus empties into the superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, then into the transverse and sigmoid sinuses, and the internal jugular vein.  Important structures within or adjacent to the cavernous sinus include the internal carotid artery and CN VI within the sinus, and CN III, CN IV, CN V1, and CN V2 within its lateral wall.

Ventricular system

CSF is continually produced by the choroid plexus via active secretion .  It then passes through a series of interconnected cavities (ie, ventricles), traveling from the lateral ventricles to the foramina of Monro, the third ventricle, the aqueduct of Sylvius, and the fourth ventricle.  CSF exits the fourth ventricle through either of the paired lateral foramina of Luschka or the medial foramen of Magendie to reach the subarachnoid space.  CSF then flows to the arachnoid granulations, where it is reabsorbed (down a pressure gradient) into the venous sinuses, which empty into the jugular veins.

Arterial supply

The intracranial structures are provided by the internal carotid (anterior circulation) and vertebrobasilar (posterior circulation) systems, which together form the circle of Willis .

›Clinical correlations

Skull fractures

Skull fractures occur when traumatic forces exceed the structural strength of the cranial bones.  They may be classified based on the pattern and location of the fracture.

  • Linear fractures (most common):  Appear as a thin break in the bone without displacement.  They are often associated with blunt trauma and may be clinically silent unless underlying structures such as blood vessels or brain tissue are injured.
  • Depressed fractures:  Occur when a portion of the fractured skull is displaced inward toward the brain, often due to high-energy trauma from objects with a small surface area (eg, hammer).  These fractures may compress or lacerate the underlying brain tissue and frequently require surgical elevation of the depressed bone fragments.
  • Basilar skull fractures:  Involve the base of the skull and may affect the temporal, sphenoid, occipital, or ethmoid bones.  These fractures are often associated with characteristic clinical findings , including:
    • Periorbital ecchymosis ("raccoon eyes") .
    • Postauricular ecchymosis (Battle sign).
    • Hemotympanum.
    • CSF leakage from the nose (CSF rhinorrhea) or ear (CSF otorrhea).  Inspection of fluid on a gauze dressing shows a halo sign .
    • Cranial nerve palsies (eg, anosmia, vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss).

Intracranial hemorrhages

Intracranial hemorrhages can occur in the epidural, subdural, or subarachnoid spaces :

  • Epidural hematoma:  Hemorrhage between the skull and the dura mater, most commonly due to middle meningeal artery injury .
    • Fracture of the pterion (ie, junction of the frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones), which overlies the middle meningeal artery, can lead to epidural hematoma.
  • Subdural hematoma:  Hemorrhage between the dura and arachnoid mater, most often bridging cortical vein injury (eg, elderly falls).
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage:  Hemorrhage between the arachnoid and pia mater .  This type of hemorrhage is most often due to rupture of saccular (berry) aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation.

›Summary

The skull is a complex bony structure that houses and protects the brain and supports the structures of the face.  The intracranial cavity is a space within the skull that contains the brain, meninges, ventricles, and important vascular structures.
