**Muscles**:  Many muscles of the back are supplied by multiple different arteries (eg, branches of the vertebral, occipital, deep cervical, transverse cervical, posterior intercostal, subcostal, lumbar, and lateral sacral arteries).  Other muscles have a dominant arterial supply and also receive supplemental flow from other vessels: - Intercostal muscles: intercostal arteries. - Rotator cuff muscles: suprascapular artery, circumflex scapular artery. - Trapezius: superficial cervical artery or superficial branch of transverse cervical artery, dorsal scapular artery (arises from subclavian artery or transverse cervical artery). - Latissimus dorsi: thoracodorsal artery (branch of subscapular artery) ((Figure 13)). - Levator scapulae: dorsal scapular artery. - Rhomboid major and minor: dorsal scapular artery. - **Thoracic region**:  Supplied by the paired left and right posterior intercostal arteries, which run along the bottom of each rib between the posterior intercostal vein and intercostal nerve.  The 1st and 2nd posterior intercostal arteries arise from the supreme intercostal artery (a branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), whereas the rest arise from the thoracic aorta.  The posterior intercostal arteries travel laterally to wrap around the trunk and form anastomoses with the anterior intercostal arteries (arise from the internal thoracic artery). - **Lumbar region**:  Supplied by 4 pairs of left and right lumbar arteries (arise from the abdominal aorta). - **Sacral region**:  Supplied by the lateral sacral arteries (arise from posterior division of the internal iliac artery). - **Vertebrae**:  Supplied by the vertebral arteries in the neck, posterior intercostal arteries in the thoracic region, subcostal and lumbar arteries in the abdomen, and the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and medial sacral arteries in the pelvis.  These vessels form smaller equatorial, periosteal, and spinal branches to supply the vertebrae and spinal cord. - **Spinal cord**:  Complex arterial supply, including the single anterior and paired posterior spinal arteries that run longitudinally along the spinal cord.  These arteries are supplemented at intervals by the segmental medullary arteries and radicular arteries (branches of the spinal arteries) ((Figure 14)).  The artery of Adamkiewicz (ie, great anterior segmental medullary artery) also supplies the anterior aspect of the spinal cord from the lower thoracic spinal cord to the conus medullaris.  This artery may be either left- or right-sided and arises from the aorta, a lumbar artery, or a posterior intercostal artery. # Venous drainage The venous drainage of the back begins with the posterior intercostal veins (in the thoracic region) and the lumbar veins (in the lumbar region).  These converge into various larger vessels depending on location, and significant anatomic variation may exist in venous drainage among individuals: - The posterior intercostal veins on the **right** side of the body generally drain into the **azygos vein** ((Figure 15)), which runs longitudinally along the right anterior aspect of the vertebral column and communicates with the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava. - The posterior intercostal veins on the **left** side of the body drain into the left brachiocephalic vein (1st to 4th posterior intercostal veins), **accessory hemiazygos vein** (5th to 8th posterior intercostal veins), or **hemiazygous vein** (9th to 12th posterior intercostal veins).  The accessory hemiazygos vein and hemiazygos vein cross the vertebral column approximately at the level of T8-T9 to join the azygous vein. - The lumbar veins drain into the inferior vena cava and are connected by the ascending lumbar veins, which run superiorly to connect with the azygos vein on the right or hemiazygous vein and left renal vein on the left. The vertebrae and spinal cord are drained by the internal vertebral veins (drain laterally to the segmental veins in the trunk or to the vertebral veins in the neck) and by the internal and external vertebral venous plexuses, which communicate with each other and with the systemic and portal venous systems. - **External vertebral venous plexus**:  Runs along the bodies and arches of the vertebrae and receives blood from the basivertebral veins; forms anastomoses with the occipital, vertebral, and deep cervical veins in the cervical region. - **Internal vertebral venous plexus**:  Lies within the vertebral canal surrounding the dura mater of the spinal cord.  This plexus receives blood flow from the spinal cord and basivertebral veins and communicates with the occipital and basilar sinuses superiorly.  The Batson venous plexus is a valveless system that connects the internal vertebral venous plexus with thoracic and pelvic veins. # Summary The back is a multilayered structure composed of skin, fascia, muscles, vertebrae, ligaments, nerves, and vessels.  Its extrinsic muscles connect to the upper limbs and ribs, whereas its intrinsic muscles maintain posture and move the vertebral column.  A rich network of nerves and vessels supply the structures of the back. ​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌

articles.title: Anatomy: Layers Of The Abdominal Wall
articles.markdown: # Anatomy: Layers Of The Abdominal Wall # Introduction The abdominal wall forms the boundary of the abdominal cavity, providing structural support, protecting the viscera, and maintaining intraabdominal pressure.  The muscles of the abdominal wall function in moving the trunk and aiding in respiration, urination, defecation, and childbirth.  The abdominal wall extends from the xiphoid process and costal margins to the superior aspects of the bones of the pelvis. # Skin The skin of the abdomen varies in thickness, depending on the region and fat distribution, to provide insulation, flexibility to allow movement, sensory input, and acts as a barrier to infection.  Langer lines, which run parallel to the orientation of collagen fibers in the dermis, run roughly transverse across the abdomen. # Superficial fascia The superficial fascia (ie, hypodermis) supports the nerves and blood vessels that supply the abdominal wall and provides insulation and cushioning against trauma.  It provides a flexible connection between the skin and the underlying muscle and fascial layers that facilitates movement.  The thickness of the superficial fascia varies by location and tends to be thicker in the lower abdomen. - Above the umbilicus:  A single fatty layer that is continuous with superficial fascia of the thorax. - Below the umbilicus:  2 distinct layers ((Figure 1)): - **Camper fascia**:  Thicker, superficial fatty layer.  Camper fascia is continuous with the superficial fascia (subcutaneous fat) of the thigh and the fatty superficial tissue of the labia majora and mons pubis. - **Scarpa fascia**:  Thinner and deeper, membranous layer of tissue.  It continues into the perineum as Colles fascia and into the scrotum/labia majora as dartos fascia and fuses with the fascia lata of the thigh. # Fascial and aponeurotic layers ## Rectus sheath The rectus sheath is formed by the aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles.  These aponeuroses all fuse at the midline forming the longitudinal **linea alba**, which runs from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis ((Figure 2)).  The composition of the rectus sheath changes at the level of the **arcuate line**, which runs transversely about 5 cm below the umbilicus, at the level of the anterior superior iliac spine ((Figure 3)). - Superior to the arcuate line:  The rectus abdominis muscle lies between the anterior and posterior rectus sheaths.  The anterior sheath is composed of the aponeurosis of the external oblique and the anterior lamina of the aponeurosis of the internal oblique.  The posterior sheath is composed of the posterior lamina of the aponeurosis of the internal oblique and the aponeurosis of the transversus abdominis. - Inferior to the arcuate line:  The rectus abdominis muscle lies below the sheath.  The aponeuroses of the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis fuse and all pass anterior to the muscle.  Only transversalis fascia and peritoneum remain posteriorly. ## Transversalis fascia The transversalis fascia is a thin, fibrous tissue layer that lies deep to the transversus abdominis that is continuous with the iliac, diaphragmatic, and pelvic fascia. ## Parietal peritoneum The parietal peritoneum is a thin serous membrane that lines the abdominal cavity ((Figure 4)).  The folds of the peritoneum along the lower anterior abdominal wall serve as surgical landmarks.  From lateral to medial these include: - **Lateral umbilical ligaments**:  Contain the inferior epigastric vessels. - **Medial umbilical ligaments**:  Contain the obliterated umbilical arteries. - **Middle (median) umbilical ligament**:  Contains the remnant of the urachus. # Muscular layers The rectus abdominis and pyramidalis muscles lie midline along the anterior abdominal wall, whereas the external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis muscles lie along the anterolateral aspects of the abdominal wall ((Figure 5)). ## Rectus abdominis The rectus abdominis is a long, paired vertical muscle that travels from the pubic crest to the costal cartilages of ribs 5-7 and the xiphoid process.  It is interrupted by tendinous intersections, giving the six-pack appearance of the abdomen.  The rectus abdominis is enclosed in rectus sheath and separated midline by the linea alba.  It functions for trunk flexion, stabilization, and compression of viscera. ## External oblique - Origin:  Lower 8 ribs (5-12). - Insertion:  Iliac crest, pubic tubercle, linea alba. The external oblique runs diagonally downward as it travels medially across the abdomen.  The aponeurosis of the inferior free edge forms the inguinal ligament.  It functions in contralateral trunk rotation, flexion, and compression of abdominal contents. ## Internal oblique - Origin:  Thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, inguinal ligament. - Insertion:  Ribs 10-12, linea alba, pubic crest via conjoint tendon. The interal oblique runs diagonally upward as it travels medially across the abdomen.  It functions in ipsilateral trunk rotation, flexion, and compression of abdominal contents. ## Transversus abdominis - Origin:  Thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, inguinal ligament, costal cartilages 7-12. - Insertion:  Linea alba, pubic symphysis, xiphoid process. The transversus abdominis runs horizontally across the abdomen and functions to compress the abdominal viscera and provide stability to the core, spine, and pelvis. ## Pyramidalis - Origin:  Pubic crest. - Insertion:  Linea alba. The pyramidalis is a small triangular muscle that functions to tense the linea alba (and is absent in ~20% of people). # Nerve supply The abdominal wall receives segmental innervation from spinal nerves, following a dermatomal pattern ((Figure 6)).  Dermatome landmarks include T7 (xiphoid), T10 (umbilicus), and L1 (inguinal ligament).  The nerves originate at the spinal cord and course along the ribs and then along the abdominal wall in a medial and slightly inferior direction. - **Thoracoabdominal nerves** (T7-T11):  Continuation of lower intercostal nerves, and run between the external and internal oblique muscles.  They supply the muscles and skin of the anterolateral abdominal wall, and the branches (eg, anterior cutaneous branch and lateral cutaneous branch) run more superficially. - **Subcostal nerve** (T12):  Courses along the lower aspect of the 12th rib and supplies the muscles of the lower abdominal wall and skin over the anterior superior iliac spine and hip. - **Iliohypogastric nerve** (L1):  Supplies the skin over the iliac crest, above the pubis, and the lateral gluteal region and muscles of the lower abdominal wall. - **Ilioinguinal nerve** (L1):  Supplies the skin over the medial thigh, mons pubis, and anterior scrotum/labia and muscles of the lower abdominal wall. # Arterial supply The major arteries of the abdominal wall primarily run in a longitudinal direction and provide collateral blood flow between the femoral artery and the subclavian artery due to the extensive anastomoses between the vessels.  The superficial vessels run along the subcutaneous tissues, and the deep vessels run in the muscle or fascia layers. ## Superficial arteries - **Superficial branches of intercostal and subcostal arteries**:  Supply the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the upper abdominal wall. - **Superficial epigastric artery** (branch of the femoral artery):  Runs superiorly and medially toward the umbilicus, and supplies the superficial lower abdominal wall. - **Superficial circumflex iliac artery** (branch of the iliac or femoral artery):  Runs laterally parallel to the inguinal ligament to supply the lateral abdominal wall. - **Superficial external pudendal artery** (branch of the femoral artery):  Travels medially to supply the lower abdominal wall, mons pubis and labia, or scrotum. ## Deep arteries - **Superior epigastric artery** (branch of the internal thoracic artery):  Supplies the upper rectus abdominis and travels inferiorly along the posterior aspect of the rectus abdominis and anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery.  In patients with aortic or iliac artery obstruction, the connections between the superior and inferior epigastric arteries provide a major collateral pathway that preserves blood supply to the lower extremities. - **Inferior epigastric artery** (branch of the external iliac artery):  Arises immediately proximal to the inguinal ligament before the external iliac artery becomes the common femoral artery.  Ascends from the inguinal ring in a superior and medial direction up the abdomen, forming the lateral border of Hesselbach triangle ((Figure 7)).  At the level of the arcuate line, the inferior epigastric artery enters the posterior rectus sheath where it travels superiorly to the anastomose with the superior epigastric artery.   - **Deep circumflex iliac artery** (branch of the external iliac artery):  Travels superiorly and laterally to supply the lower and lateral abdominal wall. - **Musculophrenic artery** (branch of the internal thoracic artery):  Runs laterally to supply the upper abdominal wall, diaphragm, pericardium, and intercostal muscles. - **Posterior intercostal arteries, subcostal artery, and lumbar arteries** (branches of the aorta):  Supply the posterior and lateral abdominal wall and muscles. # Venous and lymphatic drainage Although veins usually accompany their paired arteries, the venous supply of the abdominal wall may be more variable.  The upper abdominal wall veins eventually converge at the subclavian veins, and the inferior abdominal wall veins generally drain to the external iliac veins.  Venous dilation may be a sign of downstream obstruction (eg, pelvic tumor, caput medusae portal hypertension). Lymphatic vessels of the abdominal wall generally follow the course of veins.  The upper abdominal wall drains to the anterior axillary, internal mammary, and parasternal lymph nodes, whereas the lower abdomen drains to the inguinal and external iliac lymph nodes.  Periumbilical lymphatics may drain through the lymphatics of the falciform ligament toward the liver. # Clinical correlations ## Surgical incisions Abdominal surgical incisions take into account abdominal wall anatomy to preserve function, minimize tension, and optimize healing while providing adequate surgical exposure.  Commonly used incision types include: - **Midline incisions**:  These are longitudinal incisions that provide broad access to the abdominal cavity and viscera.  Midline incisions are made along the linea alba and, therefore, do not transect abdominal wall muscles.  Because most nerves or blood vessels of the abdominal wall terminate as they travel medially and approach the midline, midline incisions minimize the risk of nerve or vessel injury.  However, midline incisions tend to cause more postoperative pain, increased scarring, and a greater risk of wound dehiscence. - **Oblique incisions**:  These incisions divide the muscles of the abdominal wall and require isolation and ligation of the epigastric vessels to avoid bleeding (eg, McBurney incision, subcostal incision). - **Transverse incisions**:  These incisions are made along Langer lines and allow for healing with less tension, resulting in a narrower scar and improved cosmetic results.  Transverse incisions limit access to the upper abdomen and are typically used for pelvic surgery (eg, Pfannenstiel incision, Cherney incision, Maylard incision). - **Laparoscopic incisions**:  Initial entry is often made at the umbilicus, which lies at the midline and is devoid of muscle, blood vessels, nerves, and has minimal subcutaneous tissue.  Additional ports are usually needed for most procedures and are placed in locations that enable manipulation of the operative field while minimizing the risk of injury to the nerves and vessels that supply the abdominal wall. ## Hernias A hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through an abdominal wall defect when intraabdominal pressure exceeds the counterpressure exerted by the abdominal wall.  This may be due to a localized weakness from surgery or trauma.  Hernias typically cause a bulge along the abdominal wall that may be exacerbated by increases in intraabdominal pressure (eg, coughing).  Surgical techniques that may reduce the risk of developing a hernia include laparoscopic surgery and use of off-midline (rather than midline) incisions. ## Nerve injury Nerve transection, stretching, suture entrapment, or thermal injury can occur during surgical manipulation.  This may cause weakness of abdominal muscles (predisposing to incisional hernia) or sensory impairment medial and inferior to the injury (because the nerves along the anterior abdominal wall typically run in an inferomedial direction).  The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves may be affected in transverse incisions ((Figure 8)), particularly if dissection extends beyond the lateral borders of the rectus abdominis muscles.  This can lead to numbness, paresthesia, or chronic pain of the lower abdomen or groin. ## Diastasis recti Rectus abdominus diastasis (diastasis recti) is an abnormally wide distance between the medial borders of the abdominal rectus muscles that commonly develops due to laxity of the linea alba, increased abdominal girth, and increased intraabdominal pressure in pregnancy ((Figure 9)).  Diastasis may cause a midline longitudinal bulge, particularly with increases in intraabdominal pressure ((Figure 10)).  However, unlike a true hernia, there is no actual defect in the fascia, so there is no risk of bowel incarceration. # Summary The abdominal wall functions in movement, insulation, and protection of vital organs.  It is composed of skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, muscles and their aponeuroses, and peritoneum.  The exact composition varies according to the location along the abdominal wall.  The blood supply is rich and redundant, and its nerve supply follows a segmental distribution with clinically useful dermatomal landmarks. ​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​

articles.title: Anatomy: Knee
articles.markdown: # Anatomy: Knee The knee is a hinge joint that connects the thigh and leg.  It allows for flexion, extension, and limited rotation, and it supports body weight during stance and gait while providing mechanical leverage for propulsion.  Its stability reflects the interplay between bone shape, meniscal contour, ligament support, and coordinated muscle action. # Bone structures The knee joint is a synovial hinge joint located between the femur, tibia, and patella.  It functions as the principal articulation of the lower limb, enabling flexion, extension, and limited rotation.  Major structures of the anterior and posterior knee are presented in the following figures ((Figure 1), (Figure 2)). ## Femur The distal femur contains several important landmarks: - **Femoral condyles**:  Two rounded prominences (medial and lateral) at the distal femur that articulate with the tibial plateau to form the main weight-bearing surfaces of the knee. - **Intercondylar fossa (notch)**:  Deep space between the condyles that serves as the origin for the cruciate ligaments posteriorly and opens anteriorly onto the patellar surface, accommodating the patella during motion. - **Trochlear groove (patellar surface; femoral sulcus)**:  Depression on the anterior distal femur that articulates with the patella.  It is covered with thick hyaline cartilage and helps stabilize patellar motion (eg, preventing excessive lateral movement) during knee flexion and extension. ## Tibia Key landmarks of the proximal tibia include: - **Tibial plateau**:  Broad, flat surface that articulates with the femoral condyles. - **Intercondylar eminence**:  Central projection formed by the medial and lateral tubercles that serves as the insertion site for the cruciate ligaments and meniscal horns, helping stabilize and support the femoral condyles during flexion and extension and preventing excessive anteroposterior motion. - **Tibial tuberosity**:  Bony projection on the anterior surface of the tibia that serves as the insertion site for the patellar tendon. ## Patella The patella is a large sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps tendon.  It serves several functions: - **Mechanical advantage for knee extension**:  Upward glide of the patella into the trochlear groove during knee extension optimizes force transmission across the joint and improves leverage. - **Joint protection**:  Patellar position protects the joint from direct trauma and reduces friction between the quadriceps tendon and the femoral surface. - **Joint nourishment**:  Compressive forces during movement create pressure changes that circulate oxygen, glucose, and waste products around the femoral cartilage and distribute lubricating synovial fluid evenly throughout the joint. ## Fibula The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the leg; it connects proximally to the tibia at the tibiofibular joint and through its entire length via the interosseous membrane, with its head positioned just below and posterior to the lateral tibial condyle. The fibula does not articulate with the femur and is not directly involved in the knee joint.  It is relatively non–weight bearing.  However, it serves important roles in the following: - **Knee joint stability**:  Alignment of the tibia with the femur is maintained through the supportive role of the fibula. - **Attachment site**:  The fibular head provides insertion for both the lateral collateral ligament (LCL) and the biceps femoris tendon. # Joint structures ## Articular cartilage Avascular, slippery cartilaginous tissue covers the articulating surfaces of femoral condyles, tibial plateaus, and patellar facets.  Its specialized matrix and layered structure allow low-friction motion, shock absorption, and nutrient diffusion through synovial fluid.  Histologically, articular cartilage consists of hyaline cartilage organized into superficial, middle, and deep zones optimized for shear and compressive resistance. ## Menisci The medial meniscus is a "C"-shaped cartilage firmly attached to the tibial plateau and the medial collateral ligament (MCL).  The lateral meniscus is circular and more mobile, separated from the LCL by the popliteus tendon.  Both menisci deepen the articular surfaces, improve load distribution, and assist in joint lubrication and proprioception.  Histologically, the menisci are fibrocartilaginous, with peripheral vascularization and central avascularity, explaining the poor intrinsic healing of inner meniscal tears. # Ligaments ## Cruciate ligaments The cruciate ligaments ((Figure 3)) are strong, intracapsular but extrasynovial bands of tissue that cross each other in an "X" configuration within the intercondylar fossa of the femur (*cruciate* = cross). - **Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)**:  Arises from the posteromedial aspect of the lateral femoral condyle and inserts into the anterior tibial plateau.  It prevents anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur during flexion and hyperextension, and excessive internal rotation of the tibia during pivoting. - **Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)**:  Extends from the anterolateral surface of the medial femoral condyle to the posterior tibial plateau.  It prevents posterior displacement of the tibia during flexion and contributes to rotational stability. ## Collateral ligaments The collateral ligaments are extracapsular ligaments that enhance knee stability by resisting side-to-side angulation.  They are taut during extension and more relaxed during knee flexion. - **Medial (tibial) collateral ligament (MCL)**:  A broad, capsular ligament that extends from the medial femoral epicondyle to the medial tibial condyle, attaching to medial meniscus.  It resists valgus stress (force that abducts tibia relative to the femur; "knock kneed" position). - **Lateral (fibular) collateral ligament (LCL)**:  An extracapsular, cord-like band extending from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the fibular head.  It is separated from the lateral meniscus by the popliteus tendon.  It resists varus stress (force that adducts tibia relative to the femur; "bow legged" position). ## Posterior capsule and supporting ligaments The posterior capsule of the knee prevents hyperextension and posterior displacement of the tibia.  In addition to the PCL, it consists of the following: - **Oblique popliteal ligament**:  Originates from an expansion of the medial hamstring (semimembranosus tendon) at the **posteromedial** aspect of the knee, running superolaterally across the posterior knee and attaching at the lateral femoral condyle. - **Arcuate ligament complex**:  Stabilizes the **posterolateral** aspect of the knee; it consists of the arcuate ligament ("Y"-shaped band from the fibular head), popliteus tendon, and LCL.  The arcuate ligament arches superomedially over the popliteus tendon and blends in with the posterior capsule, stabilizing the posterolateral corner. # Vessels The popliteal artery supplies the knee through 5 **genicular branches** that form a circumferential anastomotic network around the patella and capsule.  This network provides collateral circulation during knee flexion.  Venous return parallels arterial pathways and converges into the popliteal vein. # Nerves The knee joint receives innervation from articular branches of the femoral, sciatic (via the terminal tibial and common fibular \[peroneal\] nerves), and obturator nerves.  These nerves form a complex plexus around the joint capsule, contributing to both sensory and proprioceptive input. - **Anterior capsule → femoral nerve**:  The femoral nerve supplies branches to the quadriceps muscles (particularly via the nerve to vastus medialis) and provides sensory fibers to the anterior and anteromedial aspects of the joint. - **Posterior capsule and popliteal fossa → tibial nerve**:  The tibial nerve is formed from a terminal branch of the sciatic nerve and innervates the posterior capsule and cruciate ligaments (especially the posterior cruciate ligament).  In addition, it contributes to sensation in the popliteal fossa, the superficial diamond-shaped passageway external to the posterior capsule behind the knee, where nerves and vessels pass posteriorly ((Figure 4)). - **Lateral capsule and meniscus → common fibular (peroneal nerve)**:  The peroneal nerve curves superficially around the neck of the fibula, where it is vulnerable to injury. - **Medial capsule → obturator nerve**:  The posterior division of the obturator nerve gives an articular branch that supplies the posteromedial aspect of the knee capsule.  This branch travels through the adductor canal and often accompanies the femoral artery and its descending genicular branches as it passes through the adductor hiatus to reach the knee.  Because this articular branch shares segmental origins with the hip joint branch of the obturator nerve, pain from hip pathology can be referred to the medial knee. The shared segmental innervation of the knee explains the frequent occurrence of referred or diffuse knee pain, such as discomfort from meniscal, cruciate, or capsular injury that may radiate beyond the joint itself. # Tendons and muscles ## Quadriceps tendon The quadriceps tendon represents the convergence of the 4 quadriceps muscles (*quad* = 4): rectus femoris, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius, and vastus lateralis ((Figure 5)).  The tendon inserts on the base of the patella at the superior pole. - **Functions**:  Enables knee extension and hip flexion (rectus femoris). - **Blood supply**:  Lateral femoral circumflex artery; deep femoral artery. - **Innervation**:  Femoral nerve (L2-L4) to all 4 heads. ## Patellar tendon (ligament) The patellar tendon represents the continuation of the quadriceps tendon distal to the patella, located from the apex of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. - **Functions**:  Transmits quadriceps force to the tibia for leg extension; serves as the primary extensor mechanism of the knee. - **Blood supply**:  Genicular branches of the popliteal artery (inferior medial, inferior lateral) and recurrent tibial branches of the anterior tibial artery. - **Innervation**:  No direct motor nerve function; patellar reflex (L3-L4) tests integrity of femoral nerve and quadriceps motor arc. ## Hamstrings and pes anserinus The hamstring consists of 3 muscles spanning the posterior thigh, including the long and short heads of the biceps femoris (inserting laterally on the fibular head), the semitendinosus and semimembranosus (both inserting at the medial tibia).  The semitendinosus also contributes to pes anserinus ("goose foot") insertion, located on the medial tibia ((Figure 6)) and along with the sartorius and gracilis tendons. - **Functions**:  Assist in knee flexion and hip extension.  During knee flexion, the biceps femoris also laterally rotates the tibia, whereas the semimembranosus and semitendinosus medially rotate the tibia.  The pes anserinus provides dynamic medial stabilization to the knee and aids in flexion and medial rotation of the tibia. - **Innervation**:  L5-S2; tibial division of the sciatic nerve for the semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of the biceps femoris, and the common fibular (peroneal) nerve for the short head of the biceps femoris. - **Blood supply**:  Deep femoral artery (perforating branches; all 3 muscles), inferior gluteal artery (biceps femoris), popliteal artery (semimembranosus).  The pes anserinus is supplied by the medial inferior genicular artery. ## Gastrocnemius and popliteus The gastrocnemius arises via 2 heads from the posterior surfaces of the lateral and medial femoral condyles and crosses the knee (and ankle) joints, joining the deeper soleus muscle. - **Function**:  Primarily plantarflexes the ankle and assists in knee flexion. - **Innervation**:  Tibial nerve (S1-S2). - **Blood supply**:  Sural branches of the popliteal artery. The popliteus is a small triangular muscle originating from the lateral femoral condyle and inserting on the posterior tibia. - **Function**:  Unlocks the knee by laterally rotating the femur on the fixed tibia during weight-bearing or medially rotating the tibia on the femur during non–weight-bearing flexion.  (During knee extension \[eg, standing upright\], the femur is internally rotated \["locked"\] on a fixed tibia.) - **Innervation**:  Tibial nerve (L4-S1). - **Blood supply**:  Medial inferior genicular and posterior tibial arteries. # Bursae Several bursae ((Figure 7)) reduce friction between skin, tendons, and bone: - **Prepatellar bursa**:  Between the patella and the skin; commonly inflamed in "housemaid's knee." - **Superficial and deep infrapatellar bursae**:  Over and beneath the patellar tendon. - **Pes anserine bursa**:  Between the pes anserinus tendons and the tibia. - **Popliteal (gastrocnemius-semimembranosus) bursa**:  In the popliteal fossa; may communicate with the joint cavity and form a **Baker cyst** when distended. # Clinical correlations ## Trauma to ligaments, tendons, and associated structures Damage to supporting structures of the knee can be acute or chronic.  In general, acute injury is more likely to present with visible deformity (eg, hemarthrosis, deformity) and may predispose to future osteoarthritis or instability of the joint.  In contrast, chronic damage is usually due to degenerative disease (eg, arthritis); it may be asymptomatic or present with more insidious pain or intermittent mechanical symptoms (eg, joint locking, catching). - **Anterior cruciate ligament tear** ((Figure 8)):  Acute injuries are caused by sudden changes in direction, excessive internal rotation, or valgus bending forces when landing from a jump. - **Posterior cruciate ligament injury** (Figure 9)):  Acute injuries are caused by acute excessive posterior force to the knee, as with sports injuries or motor vehicle accidents (eg, dashboard impact on knee). - **Collateral ligament injury** ((Figure 10)):  Acute MCL tears are more common (also associated with tears to other ligaments, such as the "**unhappy triad**" of combined ACL, MCL, and medial meniscal injury caused by a twisting force) and caused by a valgus stress to a partially flexed knee.  Acute LCL tears are much less common, occurring with a varus force to an extended knee and typically in conjunction with other ligamentous injuries (eg, ACL, PCL). - **Meniscal tears**:  Most commonly affect the medial meniscus (due its less mobile positioning and attachment to the MCL).  Acute medial meniscal tears usually occur in the context of twisting with a planted foot during sudden deceleration and direction change and frequently involve the MCL.  Chronic degenerative tears usually occur in older patients and may primarily cause dull pain or mechanical symptoms (eg, catching, locking). - **Common fibular (peroneal) nerve injury** ((Figure 11)):  Injury to this structure (commonly due to compression where it wraps around the fibular head) can potentially result in foot drop and impaired toe extension due to resulting weakness of ankle dorsiflexors and evertors. - **Tendon rupture (eg, quadriceps tendon, patellar tendon)** ((Figure 12), (Figure 13)):  Quadriceps tendon rupture causes a palpable defect superior to the patella and a low-riding patella, whereas patellar tendon rupture causes a palpable defect inferior to the patella and a high-riding patella. ## Chronic overuse injuries - **Patellofemoral pain syndrome** ((Figure 14)):  Known as "runner's knee," it is more common in women and presents with anterior knee pain.  Contributing factors include overuse, malalignment, or history of previous acute injury to the knee.  By convention, the pain is not due to intraarticular (eg, meniscus) or peripatellar (eg, patellar tendon/ligament) disorders. - **Iliotibial band syndrome** ((Figure 15)):  This overuse injury is frequently seen in runners and presents with poorly localized lateral knee pain radiating to the thigh. - **Tendinitis**:  Inflammation can affect any of the tendons surrounding the knee joint.  One example is patellar tendinitis ((Figure 16)), which is seen commonly with activities that require frequent jumping and deceleration, and presents with pain on the inferior pole of the patella during tendon loading (eg, jumping). - **Osteoarthritis** ((Figure 17)):  Osteoarthritis is caused by degeneration of articular cartilage and is characterized by joint pain, stiffness, periarticular bony enlargement, and decreased range of motion.  Pain is typically on the anterior or medial knee, aggravated by weight bearing, with stiffness following inactivity.  Joint swelling and crepitus may also be present. - **Bursitis**:  Overuse injury can occur due to inflammation of the bursae (eg, pes anserine bursitis) and typically presents with local pain, tenderness, and swelling over the affected bursa.  Prepatellar bursitis (eg, "housemaid's knee" or "carpenter's knee") causing pain on the anterior knee can occur with repetitive kneeling ((Figure 18)). - **Baker cyst**:  A Baker cyst is a fluid-filled sac in the popliteal fossa that forms when synovial fluid from the knee joint extrudes into the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa.  It typically arises due to inflammatory or degenerative joint conditions or knee injuries that increase synovial fluid production.  The cyst may rupture, causing swelling and tenderness mimicking a deep venous thrombosis ((Figure 19)). ​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​

articles.markdown:
# Anatomy: Hip # Introduction The hip is a synovial ball-and-socket joint that connects the lower limb to the axial skeleton, supporting the body during standing and motion and providing a balance between mobility and stability.  This article focuses on relevant anatomy, biomechanics, and clinical correlations. # Bone structures ## Pelvis The acetabulum is a hemispherical, socket-like cavity on the lateral pelvis, formed by fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis ((Figure 1)).  The acetabulum articulates with the femur, forming the **hip joint** ((Figure 2)).  The acetabular labrum is a ring of fibrocartilage attached to the rim of the acetabulum.  It deepens the socket, increases the surface area of contact with the femoral head, and enhances the stability of the hip joint by maintaining negative intraarticular pressure and distributing load more evenly across the joint. ## Femur Key landmarks of the proximal femur include ((Figure 3)): - **Femoral head**:  Forms two-thirds of a sphere; covered with cartilage except at the fovea capitis, where the ligamentum teres (described later) attaches, aiding blood supply. - **Femoral neck**:  Joins the femoral head to the femoral shaft at an angle of approximately 125 degrees, supporting weight-bearing. - **Greater and lesser trochanters**:  Provide bony projections for muscle attachments (eg, gluteal and iliopsoas muscles). - **Intertrochanteric area**:  Earmarks the area between the trochanters, marking the boundaries of the hip joint capsule. - **Subtrochanteric area**:  Lies below the lesser trochanter and is crucial for load-bearing, making it prone to fractures. The hip joint is enclosed by a **strong fibrous capsule** that attaches proximally to the acetabular rim and distally to the intertrochanteric line and neck of the femur.  The **synovial membrane** lines the inner surface of the capsule, extending from the acetabular rim to the proximal femoral neck, where the capsule attaches.  The synovial membrane also produces synovial fluid, a viscous, hyaluronic acid–rich lubricant that nourishes the avascular articular cartilage, reduces friction, and absorbs shock.  In pathologic states such as synovitis, excess fluid accumulation can lead to effusion and joint distension. # Ligaments The intrinsic ligaments spiral around the femoral neck and become taut in extension, reinforcing the joint capsule. - **Iliofemoral ligament**:  Extends from the anterior inferior iliac spine to the intertrochanteric line; Y-shaped, and one of the strongest ligaments in the body.  Resists hyperextension and maintains upright posture with minimal muscular effort. - **Pubofemoral ligament**:  Arises from the superior pubic ramus and obturator crest, blending with the capsule and iliofemoral ligament; limits excessive abduction and extension. - **Ischiofemoral ligament**:  Extends from the ischial portion of the acetabular rim to the greater trochanter; tightens during internal rotation and extension. - **Ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres)**:  Transmits a small artery (branch of the obturator artery) to the femoral head; a weak intraarticular band from the acetabular notch and transverse acetabular ligament to the fovea capitis. # Muscles This section reviews the muscles involved in hip movement, which primarily involve flexion/extension (transverse axis in the sagittal plane), abduction/adduction (anteroposterior axis in the frontal plane), and medial/lateral rotation (vertical axis in the transverse plane). ## Flexors - **Iliopsoas** (psoas major + iliacus) - Function:  Strongest hip flexor, inserting on the lesser trochanter. - Innervation:  Femoral nerve (L2-L4) for iliacus; anterior rami (L1-L3) for psoas major. - Blood supply:  Primarily from the iliolumbar and lumbar arteries. - **Rectus femoris** - Function:  Strong hip flexor; also extends the knee.   Originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine, joins the other portions of the quadriceps femoris in a common quadriceps tendon, and attaches to the lower leg via the patella and patellar tendon.   - Innervation:  Femoral nerve (L2-L4). - Blood supply:  Deep femoral artery. - **Sartorius** - Function:  Weak hip flexor; also assists in abduction and external rotation.   Originates from the anterior superior iliac spine and crosses the anterior thigh to insert with the pes anserinus (common tendon for the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosous muscles) onto the superomedial surface of the tibia. - Innervation:  Femoral nerve (L2-L3). - Blood supply:  Femoral artery branches. (Note: The rectus femoris and sartorius are, along with vastus lateralis and vastus intermedius, considered part of the quadriceps femoris muscle.) Hip flexors are shown in this figure ((Figure 4)). ## Extensors - **Gluteus maximus** - Function:  Main hip extensor, especially during rising from sitting or climbing; also assists in external rotation and abduction. - Innervation:  Inferior gluteal nerve (L5-S2). - Blood supply:  Inferior gluteal artery. - **Biceps femoris** - Function:  Assists with hip extension; also flexes the knee (long head externally rotates). - Innervation:  Sciatic nerve (long head: tibial portion L5-S2; short head: common peroneal L5-S1). - Blood supply:  Deep femoral artery perforators. - **Semitendinosus and semimembranosus** - Function:  Assist with hip extension; also flex and internally rotate the knee. - Innervation:  Tibial nerve (L5-S2). - Blood supply:  Deep femoral artery. (Note: The biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus are referred to as the hamstrings.) Hip extensors are shown in these figures ((Figure 5), (Figure 6)). ## Abductors - **Gluteus medius and minimus** - Function:  Abduct the hip and stabilize the pelvis during single-leg stance; also assist in medial rotation (anterior fibers) and lateral rotation (posterior fibers).  Originates from the ilium and inserts on the greater trochanter of the femur.  Weakness causes contralateral pelvic drop (Trendelenburg sign) ((Figure 7)). - Innervation: Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). - Blood supply: Superior gluteal artery. - **Tensor fasciae latae** - Function:  Assists in hip abduction and medial rotation; stabilizes the knee via the iliotibial band, which acts as a tension band transmitting forces to stabilize the lateral knee during movement ((Figure 8)). - Innervation:  Superior gluteal nerve (L4-S1). - Blood supply:  Ascending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery. ## Adductors - **Adductor longus and brevis** - Function:  Major hip adductors; also assist in flexion. - Innervation:  Obturator nerve (L2-L4). - Blood supply:  Obturator artery. - **Adductor magnus** - Function:  Major hip adductor; hamstring portion also contributes to hip extension. - Innervation:  Obturator nerve (anteriorly L2-L4); sciatic nerve (posteriorly L4-L5). - Blood supply:  Obturator and medial circumflex femoral arteries. - **Gracilis** - Function:  Assists in thigh adduction; also flexes the knee and assists in internal rotation. - Innervation:  Obturator nerve (L2-L4). - Blood supply:  Obturator artery. - **Pectineus** - Function:  Assists in thigh adduction; also a weak flexor of the hip. - Innervation:  Femoral nerve (L2-L3). - Blood supply:  Obturator and medial circumflex femoral arteries. Hip adductors are shown in these figures ((Figure 9), (Figure 10)). ## Lateral rotators - **Piriformis** - Function:  Primary lateral rotator; also assists in abduction when hip is flexed. - Innervation:  Nerve to piriformis (S1-S2). - Blood supply:  Superior gluteal artery. - **Obturator internus** - Function:  Primary lateral rotator; assists in dynamic joint stability. - Innervation:  Nerve to obturator internus (L5-S1). - Blood supply:  Obturator artery. - **Quadratus femoris** - Function:  Primary lateral rotator; assists in adduction. - Innervation:  Nerve to quadratus femoris (L4-L5). - Blood supply:  Medial circumflex femoral artery. - **Superior and inferior gemellus** - Function:  Secondary lateral rotator; assists obturator internus. - Innervation:  Nerve to obturator internus (L5-S1) (superior); nerve to quadratus femoris (L4-L5) (inferior). - Blood supply:  Primarily the inferior gluteal artery. - **Obturator externus** - Function:  Secondary lateral rotator; contributes to external rotation and dynamic joint stability. - Innervation:  Obturator nerve (L3-L4). - Blood supply:  Obturator artery. These deep gluteal muscles are shown in this figure ((Figure 11)). # Biomechanics Hip movement arises from the coordinated function of its bones, ligaments, and muscles.  The femoral head and acetabulum provide a stable bony framework, whereas the capsular ligaments restrict excessive motion and ensure joint stability.  Surrounding muscle groups serve as dynamic stabilizers, generating movement while balancing the large forces transmitted through the joint.  Together, these structures enable the hip to achieve remarkable strength and mobility.  Biomechanically, a normally functioning hip supports multiaxial movement: - Flexion:  120 degrees - Extension:  30 degrees - Abduction:  45-50 degrees - Adduction:  20-30 degrees - Internal rotation:  35 degrees - External rotation:  45 degrees These movements are limited by ligamentous tension, muscular control, and bony architecture and can vary with age, gender, or pathology (eg, reduced in osteoarthritis).  Forces across the joint can reach 3-5 times body weight during walking and up to 8 times during running, distributed via the articular surfaces to minimize wear. # Vessels The hip receives its arterial supply primarily from 2 branches of the **deep femoral artery** ((Figure 12)): - **Medial circumflex femoral artery**:  Major supply to the femoral head via retinacular branches ascending along the neck. - **Lateral circumflex femoral artery**:  Supplies the anterior capsule and greater trochanter. Venous drainage follows arterial routes to the femoral vein.  Lymphatic drainage parallels the vascular system, with vessels draining first to the inguinal lymph nodes, then to the external and internal iliac nodes.  This pathway is clinically relevant for the spread of infections (eg, septic arthritis) or malignancies (eg, metastatic prostate cancer to the hip) and may lead to lymphedema after surgery or trauma. # Nerves The hip joint receives articular innervation from multiple branches of the lumbar and sacral plexuses.  This overlapping supply provides both proprioceptive feedback and pain sensation, which helps explain the common occurrence of **referred pain** to nearby regions such as the groin, anterior thigh, or medial knee.  Primary articular branches include: - **Femoral nerve**:  Supplies the anterior capsule and contributes sensory fibers that relay pain to the anterior thigh. - **Obturator nerve**:  Innervates the inferomedial capsule; irritation may refer pain to the medial thigh or knee. - **Superior gluteal nerve**:  Supplies the superolateral aspect of the capsule; also innervates the gluteus medius and minimus, which stabilize the pelvis during gait. - **Nerve to quadratus femoris**:  Provides fibers to the posteroinferior capsule and nearby deep rotator muscles. The sciatic nerve itself does not directly innervate the joint, but its close proximity to the posterior capsule makes it vulnerable to posterior dislocations and posterior surgical approaches. # Bursae Several bursae reduce friction between tendons and bony prominences: - **Trochanteric bursa**:  Between the gluteus maximus tendon and the greater trochanter; inflammation causes lateral hip pain (ie, trochanteric bursitis). - **Iliopsoas bursa**:  Between the iliopsoas tendon and the anterior capsule; communicates with the joint in some individuals. - **Ischial bursa**:  Between the gluteus maximus and the ischial tuberosity; inflamed in prolonged sitting. # Clinical correlations ## Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis is characterized by progressive degeneration of the hyaline articular cartilage on the femoral head and acetabular lunate surface, leading to joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and synovial inflammation ((Image 1)).  Patients typically have **groin pain**, stiffness after inactivity, and reduced range of motion (particularly internal rotation). ## Femoral fractures Femoral fractures vary by location and mechanism ((Figure 13)). - **Femoral head**:  Usually accompanies posterior hip dislocation after high-energy trauma (eg, motor vehicle collision). - **Femoral neck and intertrochanteric**:  Common in older adults with osteoporosis and typically occur after minor trauma (eg, ground-level fall).  The affected leg usually appears shortened, abducted, and externally rotated ((Figure 14)) ((Figure 15)).  Disruption of the medial circumflex femoral artery predisposes to avascular necrosis of the femoral head. - **Subtrochanteric**:  Typically results from high-energy trauma but can also occur from prolonged bisphosphonate use (ie, atypical fracture). Surgical treatment options include internal fixation and hemiarthroplasty ((Figure 16)). ## Avascular necrosis Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) occurs when the blood supply to the femoral head is compromised, leading to bone ischemia and collapse ((Image 2)).  Presenting as chronic groin/hip pain worse with activity , it can follow traumatic injury (eg, disruption of the medial circumflex femoral artery in femoral neck fractures) or occur nontraumatically due to corticosteroid use (eg, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus), chronic heavy alcohol use, or sickle cell disease. ## Posterior hip dislocation Posterior hip dislocation (ie, femoral head displaced posteriorly from the acetabulum) can occur in motor vehicle collisions in which the knee strikes the dashboard or from falls in elderly patients ((Image 3)).  On examination, the leg appears shortened and internally rotated, with the hip held in flexion and adduction.  The sciatic nerve is vulnerable to injury in posterior hip dislocation ((Figure 17)). ## Labral tear Acetabular labrum damage can occur from repetitive microtrauma (eg, in athletes) or from structural abnormalities (eg, femoroacetabular impingement) that disrupt the suction seal.  This leads to mechanical symptoms (eg, clicking, locking), along with groin pain exacerbated by rotation or flexion ((Figure 18)). ## Greater trochanteric pain syndrome Greater trochanteric pain syndrome is characterized by lateral hip pain and tenderness over the greater trochanter.  The primary driver is gluteal tendinopathy.  Secondary trochanteric bursitis is often seen ((Figure 19)).  Iliotibial band pathology often contributes by causing compression and irritation of the underlying tendons and bursa.  Symptoms include lateral hip pain that is worsened by lying on the affected side, prolonged standing, walking, stair climbing, or sitting with the legs crossed. ## Superior gluteal nerve injury Superior gluteal nerve injury can occur from improperly placed intramuscular injections in the gluteal region.  This leads to weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus muscles with a positive Trendelenburg sign ((Figure 20)). ## Developmental dysplasia of the hip Developmental hip dysplasia is a congenital condition in which a shallow acetabulum reduces joint congruence, predisposing to subluxation or dislocation.  In infants, it presents with asymmetric gluteal folds, limited abduction, and positive Ortolani/Barlow maneuvers ((Figure 21)). ## Slipped capital femoral epiphysis Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is an adolescent condition in which the femoral head slips through the growth plate; it is often linked to obesity or endocrine disorders ((Image 4)) and presents with hip/knee pain, limping, and limited internal rotation. ## Total hip replacement Total hip replacement (arthroplasty) is a surgical procedure that replaces the damaged or arthritic components of the hip joint with artificial implants to relieve pain and restore function.  A metallic femoral stem inserted into the femoral canal supports a spherical head (metal or ceramic) that articulates with an acetabular cup lined with high-density polyethylene, metal, or ceramic ((Figure 22)).  It can be performed for end-stage arthritis, avascular necrosis, femoral neck fracture, or developmental dysplasia that causes disabling pain and limited motion.  Complications include dislocation (especially early in the postoperative period), infection, prosthetic loosening, and leg-length discrepancy.  When properly aligned and maintained, modern prostheses can last 15-25 years and provide near-normal gait mechanics and pain-free function. # Summary The hip is a strong, stable synovial ball-and-socket joint that connects the lower limb to the trunk, supporting body weight during standing, walking, and running.  Stability arises from the deep acetabulum, labrum, and robust capsular ligaments—the iliofemoral, pubofemoral, and ischiofemoral—which reinforce the joint while permitting wide motion in multiple planes.  The femoral head and acetabular lunate surface are covered with smooth hyaline cartilage that distributes load and reduces friction.  Surrounding muscles, including the gluteals, iliopsoas, adductors, and hamstrings, coordinate to maintain posture and enable flexion, extension, abduction, and rotation. Blood supply is primarily via the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, whereas articular innervation from the femoral, obturator, gluteal, and quadratus femoris nerves provides both sensory and proprioceptive input.  Clinically, the hip is susceptible to fractures, dislocations, bursitis, osteoarthritis, and avascular necrosis, conditions that can impair stability, motion, and weight-bearing.  A summary of major muscles responsible for hip motion, along with their innervations, is provided in this table ((Table 1)). ​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌
