articles.markdown:
# Anatomy: Elbow/Forearm

# Introduction

The elbow and forearm form a mechanically coupled unit that positions the hand in space and transmits load from the hand to the arm.  The elbow provides hinge and rotational stability, whereas the forearm's radius and ulna enable pronation and supination through a linked proximal and distal radioulnar articulation.  Bony architecture and ligamentous and muscular support (provided by the flexor, extensor, and rotator muscle groups) ensure joint stability and coordination through these complex movements.  Neurovascular structures pass in predictable planes that explain common entrapment and injury patterns.

# Skeleton and joints

## Bones of the elbow

The major bones of the elbow and forearm are the humerus, radius, and ulna ((Figure 1)).

-   **Humerus** ((Figure 2)):  Comprises (in its distal portion) the upper part of the elbow joint.  Key landmarks include the trochlea (medial), capitulum (lateral), and medial and lateral epicondyles, which serve as attachment sites for ligaments and forearm muscles.
-   **Radius**:  Represents the mobile bone of the forearm, enabling pronation and supination.  Landmarks include the disc-shaped proximal head (articulates with the humerus and ulna), tuberosity (proximal medial aspect), radial neck (slender narrowing just distal to the head), and distal styloid process (articulates with the carpal bones at the wrist).
-   **Ulna**:  Represents the stabilizing, relatively fixed bone of the forearm at the elbow.  Landmarks include the olecranon process (proximal end; forms the tip of the elbow), coronoid process (anterior; articulates with the humerus during elbow flexion, promoting stability), and radial notch (an articulating site for the radius).

The elbow complex consists of 3 articulations enclosed within a single joint capsule, each of which is supported by stabilizing ligaments.

## Humeroulnar joint

-   **Articulating site**:  Trochlea of the humerus and trochlear notch of the ulna.
-   **Motion**:  Primary hinge joint for flexion and extension (does not participate in rotation).
-   **Supporting ligaments**:  Medial (ulnar) collateral ligament complex (MCL/UCL), which consists of anterior, posterior, and transverse bundles, joining the medial epicondyle of the humerus to the ulna.

## Proximal radioulnar

-   **Articulating site**:  Radial notch of the ulna and the head of the radius.
-   **Motion**:  Primary rotational joint, enabling the rotational movement of the radius around the ulna.
-   **Supporting ligaments**:  Annular ligament, which encircles this joint and secures the radial head against the radial notch of the ulna.

## Humeroradial

-   **Articulating site**:  Capitulum of the humerus and the proximal head of the radius.
-   **Motion**:  Joint allowing the radius to spin during forearm rotation; also enables the radius to flex and extend with the humerus.
-   **Supporting ligaments**:  Lateral collateral ligament complex, including radial collateral ligament (RCL), lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL), and accessory ligaments.  The RCL joins the lateral epicondyle of the humerus to the annular ligament.  The LUCL joins the lateral epicondyle to the ulna.

The MCL and RCL play key roles in supporting the integrity of the elbow joint during valgus and varus stress ((Figure 3)):

-   **Varus stress (stabilized by RCL/LUCL)**:  Force moving the forearm medially in relation to the upper arm, such as carrying a heavy object with the arm extended.
-   **Valgus stress (stabilized by MCL/UCL)**:  Force moving the forearm laterally in relation to the upper arm, such as during an overhead throw.

By enabling rotation, the humeroradial and proximal radioulnar joints facilitate the unique actions of pronation and supination.  Recent anatomic and imaging studies suggest possible variations in how these motions are classically described.

-   **During supination** (ie, palm facing outward, as in holding a bowl of soup), the radial head (ie, proximal radius) spins posteriorly within the annular ligament against the radial notch of the ulna.  The distal radius swings posterolaterally around the relatively fixed ulnar head, bringing the palm anteriorly.
-   **During pronation** (ie, palm facing backward), the radial head spins anteriorly within the annular ligament, and the distal radius moves anteromedially across the ulna, causing the radius and ulna to cross.

# Fasciae and spaces

The fascia of the forearm forms a continuous, dense connective tissue sleeve that compartmentalizes muscles, vessels, and nerves while maintaining structural integrity and providing sites of muscular attachment.

## Antebrachial fascia

This strong fibrous membrane is a continuation of the brachial fascia above the elbow.  It sends intermuscular septa that anchor onto bone and superficially compartmentalize the muscles of the forearm into anterior and posterior groups, each with distinct functions and a neurovascular supply.

-   **Anterior compartment**:  Flexor/pronator muscles; median nerve (and branches).
-   **Posterior compartment**:  Extensor/supinator muscles; radial nerve (and branches).

The antebrachial compartment has distinct borders:

-   **Proximal**:  Humeral epicondyles, olecranon, and posterior border of the ulna.
-   **Lateral**:  Anterior border of the radius via intermuscular septa.
-   **Distal**:  Flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis anteriorly (forming fibrous tunnels for wrist tendons); extensor retinaculum and dorsal fascia of the hand posteriorly.

## Interosseous membrane

This tough fibrous syndesmosis joins the radius and ulna, maintaining alignment and serving as a site of muscle attachment.  It establishes a deep, partial barrier between the anterior and posterior compartments, with intercompartmental communication facilitated by small apertures in the membrane that allow the passage of vessels (eg, posterior interosseous vessels).

## Cubital tunnel

Located posteromedially at the elbow, the tunnel roof is formed by the cubital tunnel retinaculum (Osborne ligament), which bridges the space between the medial epicondyle and olecranon.  The MCL serves as its floor, and the ulnar nerve traverses this space (compression there leads to cubital tunnel syndrome).

## Cubital fossa

The cubital fossa ((Figure 4)) is a triangular anatomic space on the anterior aspect of the elbow; it is clinically important for venipuncture and arterial or nerve localization.

Its boundaries are as follows:

-   **Superior**:  Imaginary line between the humeral epicondyles.
-   **Medial**:  Pronator teres.
-   **Lateral**:  Brachioradialis.

The contents of the fossa (from lateral to medial) include the biceps brachii tendon, brachial artery (and its bifurcation into radial and ulnar arteries), and the median nerve.  The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle and is not within the fossa, whereas the radial nerve lies just lateral to it before dividing into superficial and deep branches.

# Nerves and vessels

The muscles and skin of the anterior and posterior compartments of the forearm are innervated by 4 major nerves derived from the brachial plexus ((Figure 5)): the musculocutaneous, median, ulnar, and radial nerves and their branches.  The following section focuses primarily on innervation as it pertains to the forearm and elbow (a complete discussion of innervation to the upper arm and hand is provided in separate articles).

## Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C7; mainly cutaneous in the forearm)

Emerges lateral to the biceps tendon near the cubital fossa (but not within it), piercing the deep fascia to become the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

-   **Relevant branch**:  Terminates as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm (after emerging from the biceps tendon).
-   **Motor**:  Has no significant motor innervation distal to the elbow.  Above the elbow, facilitates elbow flexion (via biceps brachii ((Figure 6)) and brachialis) and supination (via biceps) ((Figure 7)).
-   **Sensory**:  Innervates skin of the anterior and posterolateral forearm (via cutaneous nerve) ((Figure 8)).

## Median nerve (C5-T1; lateral anterior compartment → pronation, wrist and finger flexion)

Runs centrally, between and through most flexor and pronator muscles.

-   **Relevant branches**:  Anterior interosseous nerve (AIN).
-   **Motor** ((Figure 9)):  Forearm pronation (pronator teres; pronator quadratus via AIN) and forearm flexors enabling wrist/finger flexion (flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis; lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus via AIN).
-   **Sensory** ((Figure 10)):  Anterior capsule of elbow.  Minimal sensory innervation to the forearm; supplies the hand (eg, lateral palmar surface, first 3½ digits).

## Radial nerve (C5-T1; posterior compartment → extension, supination)

Runs mostly posteriorly and laterally along the extensor-supinator muscles.

-   **Relevant branches**:  Deep branch, posterior interosseous nerve (PIN), superficial branch (sensory), and posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
-   **Motor** ((Figure 11)): Forearm supination (supinator, via deep branch and PIN) and extensors for wrist (extensor carpi radialis longus, extensor carpi radialis brevis via deep branch, extensor carpi ulnaris via PIN) and fingers (via PIN; extensor digitorum, indicis, and digiti minimi, along with others).  Above the elbow, innervates elbow extensors (triceps brachii ((Figure 12)), anconeus).
-   **Sensory** ((Figure 13)): Cutaneous branches innervate the posterolateral elbow joint, posterior forearm, and dorsolateral hand.

## Ulnar nerve (C8-T1) (medial anterior compartment → ulnar deviation/finger flexion)

Runs along the medial border of the arm posterior to the medial epicondyle, then enters the anterior compartment of the forearm by passing between the humeral and ulnar heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris.

-   **Relevant branches**:  Articular branches to the elbow capsule; cutaneous branches innervate mainly the hand (dorsal, palmar cutaneous branches).
-   **Motor** ((Figure 14)):  Forearm muscles enabling wrist flexion/ulnar deviation (flexor carpi ulnaris) and flexion of the distal phalanges of the fourth and fifth fingers (medial half of flexor digitorum profundus).
-   **Sensory** (Figure 15)):  Posteromedial aspect of the elbow joint; no cutaneous innervation to the forearm (cutaneous branches innervate the hypothenar region and dorsal ulnar hand).

The **median antebrachial cutaneous nerve**, arising from a separate branch of the brachial plexus, provides sensory innervation to the anteromedial and posteromedial forearm.

Blood supply is provided primarily by the brachial artery and its radial and ulnar branches ((Figure 16)):

-   **Brachial artery**:  Bifurcates just distal to the elbow crease into the radial and ulnar arteries.
-   **Radial artery**:  Follows the lateral forearm, palpable throughout its course, and gives the recurrent radial branch to the lateral collateral circulation.
-   **Ulnar artery**:  Gives off the common interosseous artery, dividing into anterior and posterior interosseous branches that run along either face of the interosseous membrane.  Anastomotic arcs around the elbow maintain perfusion during flexion.

Superficial and deep venous systems (cephalic, basilic, paired deep veins) ((Figure 17)) communicate through the median cubital vein, the common site for venipuncture.

# Muscles

The muscles of the forearm and elbow are organized into compartments based on fascial compartmentalization and function.  This section discusses the important muscles within each compartment, referencing relevant elements of the neurovasculature previously discussed.

## Anterior compartment (flexion/pronation)

The anterior compartment of the forearm is divided into superficial, intermediate, and deep layers.  It contains forearm flexors that are innervated primarily by the median nerve (except the flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of the flexor digitorum profundus), as well as pronator muscles.  The AIN innervates the muscles in the deep layer.  Blood is supplied by the radial and ulnar arteries.

The **superficial layer** includes the pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus (variably present), and flexor carpi ulnaris.  These muscles arise from a common flexor tendon on the medial epicondyle of the humerus.

-   **Pronator teres** has a second origin on the coronoid process of the ulna, and it inserts on the lateral surface of the midradius.  It pronates the forearm and assists with elbow flexion.
-   **Flexor carpi ulnaris** has a second origin from the olecranon and posterior border of the ulna, and it inserts on the base of the carpal bones (pisiform, hook of hamate) and the fifth metacarpal base.  It flexes and *ad*ducts the wrist and is innervated by the *ulnar nerve*.
-   **Flexor carpi radialis** inserts on the base of the second and third metacarpal; flexes and *ab*ducts the wrist.
-   **Palmaris longus** inserts onto the palmar aponeurosis and flexor retinaculum; it is variably present.

The **intermediate layer** consists of the flexor digitorum superficialis.  Its origins include a humeroulnar and a radial head, between which the median nerve and ulnar artery pass, serving as a landmark and potential site of nerve entrapment.  It splits into 4 tendons and inserts on the sides of the middle phalanges of digits 2-5.  It flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints and metacarpophalangeal joints of these same digits.

The **deep** layer includes the flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus.  Innervation is primarily provided by the AIN.

-   **Flexor digitorum profundus** arises from the ulna and interosseous membrane and inserts onto the bases of the distal phalanges of digits 2-5, flexing these joints.  Its medial part (digits 4-5) is innervated by the *ulnar nerve* and its lateral part (digits 2 and 3) by the AIN.
-   **Flexor pollicis longus** arises from the anterior radius and interosseous membrane and inserts onto the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb, flexing the thumb's interphalangeal joint.
-   **Pronator quadratus** spans the distal radius and ulna, stabilizing the distal radioulnar joint.  It acts synergistically with the pronator teres, enabling the final degree of pronation of the distal forearm.

## Posterior and lateral compartment (extension/supination)

The posterior compartment of the forearm, divided into superficial and deep layers and a lateral functional group, contains muscles responsible for elbow stabilization and extension, as well as supination of the wrist and digits.  Innervation of the posterior compartment muscles is provided by the radial nerve and its PIN branch.  The blood supply is provided mainly by branches of the radial recurrent artery, posterior interosseous artery, and radial artery.

The **superficial layer** consists of 4 muscles arising from the lateral epicondyle of the humerus via a common extensor tendon.  All posterior compartment extensors are supplied by the radial nerve or its deep branch (PIN).

-   **Extensor digitorum** inserts into the extensor expansions of digits 2-5, extends the metacarpophalangeal joints, and assists with interphalangeal joint extension.
-   **Extensor digiti minimi** runs along the medial side of the extensor digitorum, joins its tendon to the fifth digit, and produces independent extension of the little finger.
-   **Extensor carpi ulnaris** originates also from the posterior border of the ulna and inserts on the base of the fifth metacarpal; it produces wrist extension and ulnar deviation.
-   **Anconeus**, a small triangular muscle at the posterolateral elbow, extends from the lateral epicondyle to the olecranon, assisting the triceps in elbow extension and stabilizing the elbow joint during pronation and supination.

The **deep layer** consists of 5 muscles innervated by the PIN.  Except for the supinator, they originate from the posterior radius, ulna, and interosseous membrane.  These muscles control thumb and first digit extension and assist with forearm supination.

-   **Supinator** originates from the lateral epicondyle, lateral collateral ligament and annular ligaments, and supinator crest of the ulna.  It wraps around the proximal radius and inserts on its lateral surface, producing forearm supination (especially when the elbow is extended).  The deep branch of the radial nerve becomes the PIN after passing through the supinator's fibers, making this muscle an important landmark.
-   **Abductor pollicis longus** arises from the posterior ulna and radius and inserts on the first metacarpal.  It abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint.
-   **Extensor pollicis brevis** arises from the posterior radius and inserts on the proximal phalanx of the thumb, extending the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint.
-   **Extensor pollicis longus** arises from the posterior ulna and inserts on the distal phalanx of the thumb, producing extension at both the interphalangeal and the metacarpophalangeal joints.
-   **Extensor indicis** arises from the posterior ulna and joins the extensor expansion of the index finger, allowing independent extension of the index digit.

Although not a separate anatomic compartment, 3 muscles on the lateral aspect of the posterior compartment are often grouped as the lateral compartment ("mobile wad") because they are easily palpable along the lateral forearm and move freely with wrist and elbow movement, in contrast to the fixed deep extensors.  These muscles arise along the lateral supracondylar ridge or lateral epicondyle of the humerus, acting collectively to flex the elbow and extend or abduct the wrist.

-   **Brachioradialis** inserts on the lateral surface of the distal radius.  It flexes the elbow, especially when the forearm is in the midpronated position, and serves as a clinical landmark for the course of the radial nerve near the lateral epicondyle.
-   **Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis** insert on the bases of the second and third metacarpals, respectively.  They extend and abduct the wrist (radial deviation).

# Clinical correlations

-   **Lateral collateral ligament injury**:  Occurs due to failure of varus or posterolateral rotational restraint at the elbow, most commonly from combined varus, supination, and axial compression, causing elbow dislocation.  Presents with lateral elbow pain and instability during varus or supination stress testing.
-   **Radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow)** ((Figure 18)):  Occurs when the annular ligament slips under the radial head, primarily seen in young children with axial traction on an extended forearm (eg, child pulled, swung by arm).  Patients typically hold the elbow extended with the forearm pronated.
-   **PIN palsy**:  Results in motor weakness or paralysis of extensor muscles of the wrist and fingers without sensory loss (because the PIN is purely a motor nerve).  Can be caused by compression within the supinator or other points within the forearm due to repetitive forearm supination/pronation (eg, playing tennis).  Motor findings depend on the site of compression and can include partial wrist and/or finger drop.  Forearm supination is usually preserved due to the biceps and the superficial part of the supinator, which receive fibers proximal to the lesion.
-   **Cubital tunnel syndrome**:  Caused by entrapment of the ulnar nerve within the cubital tunnel, leading to paresthesia in ulnar digits and weakness of interossei.
-   **Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)** ((Figure 19)):  Caused by injury (eg, repetitive stress) to the origin of extensor carpi radialis brevis at the lateral epicondyle, leading to pain on resisted wrist extension.
-   **Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow)**:  Characterized by overuse tendinopathy of the common flexor–pronator tendon origin at the medial epicondyle, causing pain and tenderness along the medial elbow, especially with wrist flexion or forearm pronation against resistance.
-   **Olecranon bursitis** ((Figure 20)):  Characterized by inflammation of the subcutaneous bursa overlying the olecranon process, usually caused by repetitive trauma, prolonged pressure, infection, or gout and resulting in a painful, fluctuant swelling at the posterior elbow that moves independently of the joint itself.
-   **Distal radius fracture (Colles fracture)** ((Figure 21)):  Results from a fall on an outstretched hand (eg, athlete with high-impact fall, elderly patient with osteoporosis and low-impact fall).  Characterized by pain, swelling, and a dinner-fork deformity of the wrist that can result in compression of the median nerve through the carpal tunnel.
-   **Cubital fossa injury**:  Can cause swelling/compression/hematoma affecting the median nerve, resulting in impairment of forearm pronation (pronator teres) and proximal interphalangeal joint flexion (flexor digitorum superficialis), along with sensory deficits in the median distribution (radial 3.5 digits).  It can also (rarely) result in injury to the brachial artery, causing bleeding.

​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​

articles.markdown: # Anatomy: Ear # Introduction The ear is a complex sensory organ responsible for hearing (audition) and balance (equilibrium).  These functions rely on the precise transmission and transformation of mechanical stimuli (ie, sound waves, head movements) into neural signals interpreted by the brain. Anatomically, the ear is divided into 3 regions: the external (outer) ear, middle ear, and inner ear ((Figure 1)).  These regions play distinct but integrated roles in detecting, amplifying, and transducing stimuli related to sound and motion. # External ear The external ear is the entry point for sound waves and localizes and amplifies sound.  It is composed of the **auricle** (or pinna) and the **external acoustic meatus**.  The tympanic membrane separates the external ear from the middle ear. # External ear: Auricle The auricle collects, filters, and amplifies sound before transmitting it to the external acoustic meatus. ## Gross anatomy - **Helix** - This thickened, rolled rim of elastic cartilage forms the outer rim of the ear.  It begins near the ear canal, arches superiorly and posteriorly, and then descends toward the lobule (earlobe) in a smooth curve. - Its convex outer edge allows for reflection and filtration of high-frequency sound waves that help with vertical and front-to-back sound localization. - **Antihelix** - The curved inner ridge of elastic cartilage runs parallel and anterior to the helix and bifurcates superiorly into 2 crura. - It forms the inner structural framework of the auricle and creates a reflective surface that helps with sound localization. - **Concha** - This deep, bowl-shaped region leads into the ear canal. - It funnels sound into the canal, increasing sound intensity before it reaches the tympanic membrane. - **Tragus** - The small cartilaginous projection lies anterior to the ear canal. - It protects the canal opening, helps modulate sound entering the canal, and contributes to front-to-back localization. - **Antitragus** - This area is opposite the tragus. - It plays a minor role in shaping sound entry. - **Lobule** - The soft, noncartilaginous earlobe is located at the base of the auricle. - It has a minimal role in audition but is a common site for ear piercing. ## Histology The **auricle** is composed primarily of **elastic cartilage**, which provides flexibility and resilience, allowing it to maintain its shape while deforming under pressure.  This cartilage is covered by **perichondrium**, a vascular connective tissue layer that supplies nutrients to the avascular cartilage.  The overlying skin is thin and tightly adherent to the perichondrium, with minimal subcutaneous tissue. - Clinical correlation:  Auricular hematoma (eg, due to ear trauma) ((Figure 2)) separates the perichondrium from the underlying cartilage, disrupting its blood supply and leading to ischemia, fibrosis, and cauliflower ear ((Figure 3)). The **lobule** is histologically distinct from the rest of the auricle in that it lacks cartilage and is composed of **adipose** tissue and **loose connective tissue**, making it highly flexible. ## Arterial supply The auricle is supplied by branches of the **external carotid artery**, which form an anastomotic network that provides a robust blood supply: - Anterior surface of the auricle:  **Superficial temporal artery**. - Posterior surface of the auricle:  **Posterior auricular artery**. - Contributions from the occipital artery may also be present. ## Venous drainage - The auricle drains via the superficial temporal and posterior auricular veins, ultimately emptying into the **external jugular vein**. ## Innervation The external ear has complex sensory innervation from multiple cranial and cervical nerves: - Anterior and superior auricle:  Auriculotemporal nerve, which is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). - Inferior and posterior auricle (including the lobule):  Great auricular nerve (C2-C3 spinal nerves). - Upper posterior auricle:  Lesser occipital nerve (C2 spinal nerve). - Parts of the concha and external acoustic meatus:  Auricular branch of the vagus nerve (CN X). # External ear: External acoustic meatus ## Gross anatomy The external acoustic meatus is an **S-shaped canal** that conducts sound to the tympanic membrane.  The canal is a resonance chamber, amplifying frequencies important for speech perception.  The tympanic membrane converts air vibrations into mechanical energy for transmission to the bony ossicles of the middle ear. ## Histology The external acoustic meatus is lined by **keratinized stratified squamous epithelium**.  It is divided into 2 structurally and functionally different portions. - **Cartilaginous segment (lateral one-third of canal):** - Formed by elastic cartilage and continuous with the auricle.  It is lined by epithelium containing hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and ceruminous glands (which produce cerumen).  Cerumen traps debris, repels water, and has antimicrobial properties. - *Clinical correlation:  Cerumen impaction can obstruct the canal and impair sound conduction, causing conductive hearing loss.* - **Bony segment (medial two-thirds of canal):** - Formed by the temporal bone and lined by thin epithelium directly over the periosteum, with no subcutaneous tissue or glands.  This portion is highly sensitive, and inflammation in this area causes severe pain. Clinical correlation:  Otitis externa is an infection of the external auditory canal, which causes canal debris, discharge, and severe pain (especially with tragus movement). The **tympanic membrane** forms the medial limit of the external ear and is a trilaminar structure composed of stratified squamous epithelium (outer layer), a fibrous middle layer for strength, and an inner mucosal layer of simple cuboidal to low columnar epithelium. ## Arterial supply The external acoustic meatus and tympanic membrane are supplied by branches of the **external carotid artery**, primarily the: - **Deep auricular artery** (from the maxillary artery) with contributions from the superficial temporal artery and the posterior auricular artery. ## Venous drainage - The external acoustic meatus and tympanic membrane drain via the superficial temporal vein and the posterior auricular vein into the **external jugular vein**. ## Innervation Sensory innervation - Anterior and superior portions of the canal:  Auriculotemporal nerve (CN V3). - Posterior and inferior portions of the canal:  Auricular branch of CN X. - External surface of the tympanic membrane:  CN V3 and auricular branch of CN X. - Internal surface of the tympanic membrane (facing the middle ear):  Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the tympanic nerve. Clinical correlation:  Pain may be referred to the ear (ie, referred otalgia) from the throat/tonsils (via CN IX), teeth/temporomandibular joint (via CN V), and the larynx (via CN X) ((Figure 4)). # Middle ear The middle ear is an air-filled cavity within the temporal bone containing various structures that **transmit and amplify sound vibrations** from the tympanic membrane to the inner ear and **equalize pressure across the tympanic membrane** via its connection to the nasopharynx. ## Gross anatomy **Sound transmission** The middle ear structures ((Figure 5)) involved in sound amplification and transmission include: - **Ossicles**:  3 small bones that function as a **lever system**, amplifying and transmitting sound vibrations. - **Malleus**:  Structure attached to the tympanic membrane; transmits vibrations to the incus. - **Incus**:  Intermediate bone connecting the malleus to the stapes. - **Stapes**:  Footplate that rests on the oval window, transmitting vibrations to the inner ear. - Clinical correlation:  Otosclerosis is a condition in which abnormal bone remodeling fixes the stapes at the oval window, thereby impairing sound transmission and resulting in progressive conductive hearing loss. - **Oval window**:  The most medial aspect of the middle ear that receives vibrations from the stapes. Sound waves travel easily in air (ie, external ear) but are partially reflected when they encounter the fluid-filled inner ear.  The ossicles overcome this mismatch by increasing pressure at the oval window through the lever action of the ossicles.  The surface area difference between the large tympanic membrane and the smaller oval window concentrates the force at the stapes, allowing sound energy to be transmitted efficiently into the inner ear. The middle ear contains 2 **muscles** that **attenuate sound** transmission (ie, acoustic reflex) to prevent injury from loud sounds: - **Tensor tympani**:  Dampens vibrations of the tympanic membrane. - **Stapedius**:  Stabilizes the stapes and reduces excessive movement. Clinical correlation:  Damage to the facial nerve (CN VII) (eg, Bell palsy) can impair stapedius muscle function, leading to hyperacusis (increased sensitivity to sound). **Pressure equalization** Middle ear structures involved in pressure equalization include: - **Eustachian (auditory) tube:**  Connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and: - Equalizes pressure across the tympanic membrane. - Drains secretions from the middle ear. - Helps prevent reflux of nasopharyngeal secretions. - **Eustachian tube muscles** ((Figure 6)) - Tensor veli palatini:  Primary muscle that opens the tube during swallowing and yawning. - Levator veli palatini:  Assists in opening the tube. Clinical correlation:  Dysfunction of the eustachian tube (eg, due to upper respiratory infection) can lead to otitis media due to impaired drainage and pressure equalization. ## Histology The middle ear cavity is lined by **simple cuboidal to low columnar epithelium**, which transitions to respiratory-type epithelium near the eustachian tube, where goblet cells and cilia facilitate mucus clearance. The ossicles are composed of compact bone and are covered by a thin mucosal layer. Clinical correlation:  Inflammation of the middle ear mucosa (eg, otitis media) can lead to fluid accumulation, impairing sound transmission and causing conductive hearing loss. ## Arterial supply The middle ear is supplied by branches of the **external carotid artery**: - **Anterior tympanic artery** (branch of the maxillary artery). - **Stylomastoid artery** (branch of the posterior auricular artery). - With additional contributions from the middle meningeal artery and ascending pharyngeal artery. ## Venous drainage Venous drainage of the middle ear parallels the arterial supply and drains as follows: - Small tympanic veins → pterygoid venous plexus → **external jugular vein**. - Posterior tympanic veins → superior petrosal sinus → **transverse/sigmoid sinuses**. Clinical correlation:  Venous connections between the middle ear and intracranial dural venous sinuses provide a potential route for infection to spread from the ear to the brain. ## Innervation **Sensory innervation** - Mucosa of the middle ear and eustachian tube:  CN IX via the tympanic nerve (Jacobson nerve). **Motor innervation** - Tensor tympani:  CN V3. - Stapedius:  CN VII. - Tensor veli palatini:  CN V3. - Levator veli palatini:  CN X. # Inner ear The inner ear is a complex system of fluid-filled structures within the temporal bone that functions in both **hearing (cochlea)** and **balance (vestibular apparatus)** by converting mechanical stimuli into neural signals. ## Gross anatomy The structures of the inner ear are organized within 2 interconnected systems ((Figure 7)): the bony labyrinth and the membranous labyrinth. - **Bony labyrinth**:  Provides the **structural framework** of the inner ear.  It consists of a series of cavities within the petrous temporal bone filled with **perilymph**, an extracellular fluid–like solution rich in sodium.  The bony labyrinth is divided into 3 compartments: - **Cochlea**. - **Vestibule**. - **Semicircular canals**. - **Membranous labyrinth**:  Serves as the **functional apparatus** of the inner ear.  It is suspended within the perilymph and mirrors the shape of the bony labyrinth; it contains sensory receptors (hair cells) and is filled with endolymph, a potassium-rich fluid that enables hair cell activation.  The membranous labyrinth contains: - **Cochlear duct** (within the cochlea). - **Utricle and saccule** (within the vestibule). - **Semicircular ducts** (within the semicircular canals). Together, the bony and membranous labyrinths form a nested system in which perilymph surrounds the endolymph-filled sensory structures. **Hearing (cochlea)** The cochlea is a spiral structure where sound vibrations are converted into neural signals.  It contains 3 chambers: the **scala vestibuli** and **scala tympani**, which contain perilymph, and the **scala media (cochlear duct)**, which contains endolymph ((Figure 8)). The scala media (cochlear duct) houses the **organ of Corti**, which rests on the **basilar membrane** and is overlain by the **tectorial membrane** ((Figure 9)).  The basilar membrane supports rows of **inner and outer hair cells**, whose stereocilia project toward the overlying tectorial membrane. When the stapes pushes on the oval window, pressure waves propagate through the perilymph, causing displacement of the basilar membrane.  This creates a shearing force between the basilar and the tectorial membranes, deflecting hair cell stereocilia and opening mechanically gated ion channels.  Potassium influx from endolymph depolarizes the hair cells, leading to neurotransmitter release and activation of the **vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)**.  The round window serves as a pressure-relief membrane, allowing displacement of cochlear fluids during this process. The cochlea exhibits tonotopic organization ((Figure 10)), in which different frequencies are encoded at specific locations. - **High-frequency sounds** peak at the **base.** - **Low-frequency sounds** peak at the **apex**. **Balance (vestibular apparatus)** The vestibular apparatus detects ((Figure 11)) head position and movement, contributing to balance, posture, and eye coordination.  It includes the **semicircular canals** and the **utricle and saccule (otolith organs)**. **Semicircular canals** ((Figure 12)) contain **semicircular ducts** that are filled with endolymph.  These ducts are oriented in orthogonal planes to detect angular acceleration of the head.  Each semicircular duct contains an **ampulla** at one end, which houses the **crista ampullaris**, a ridge of sensory epithelium embedded in a gelatinous structure known as the **cupula**.  Head rotation causes relative movement of endolymph within the duct due to inertia, deflecting the cupula and bending the hair cell stereocilia, generating neural signals transmitted via the vestibular division of CN VIII. **Utricle and saccule (otolith organs)** ((Figure 13)) detect linear acceleration and head tilt.  The utricle detects horizontal linear acceleration, and the saccule detects vertical linear acceleration.  Each otolith organ contains sensory regions called **maculae**, where hair cells are embedded in a gelatinous layer topped with calcium carbonate crystals **(otoconia)**.  Linear acceleration or changes in head position cause displacement of the otoconia, which shifts the gelatinous layer and bends the hair cell stereocilia, resulting in signal transduction. Vestibular apparatus input is integrated with visual and proprioceptive information in the brainstem and cerebellum, allowing for maintenance of posture and stabilization of gaze through the **vestibuloocular reflex** and the **vestibulospinal reflex**. Clinical correlation:  Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo results from dislodged otoconia entering a semicircular canal (usually posterior), causing abnormal hair cell stimulation and brief positional vertigo. ## Histology The **bony labyrinth** is composed of **endochondral bone** that is dense and compact.  The inner surface of the bony labyrinth is lined by a thin layer of periosteum, covered by simple squamous epithelium–like cells that are in contact with perilymph. The **membranous labyrinth** is lined by **specialized epithelium** and contains **sensory hair cells** that detect mechanical stimuli.  These hair cells possess **stereocilia** that bend in response to fluid movement, leading to depolarization.  Endolymph has a high potassium concentration, which is essential for this process, and supporting cells provide structural and metabolic support. Clinical correlation:  Damage to hair cells (eg, due to noise exposure, aging, or ototoxic medications) results in sensorineural hearing loss, which is typically irreversible. ## Arterial supply The inner ear is supplied by the **labyrinthine artery**, which most commonly arises from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and, less commonly, directly from the basilar artery.  The labyrinthine artery is an end artery (with minimal collateral circulation) and divides into two main branches: - **Common cochlear artery**, which supplies the cochlea. - **Anterior vestibular artery**, which supplies portions of the vestibular apparatus. Clinical correlation:  Because the labyrinthine artery has no significant collateral supply, occlusion can result in sudden sensorineural hearing loss and vertigo. ## Venous drainage - Venous drainage of the inner ear parallels arterial supply: - Cochlear veins (primarily inferior cochlear vein) → inferior petrosal sinus → internal jugular vein. - Vestibular veins (primarily vein of the vestibular aqueduct) → inferior petrosal sinus or sigmoid sinus. ## Innervation The inner ear is innervated by **CN VIII**: - Cochlear division → hearing. - Vestibular division → balance. # Summary The ear is a complex sensory organ responsible for hearing and balance, converting mechanical stimuli such as sound waves and head movements into neural signals interpreted by the brain.  Hearing involves a coordinated sequence of sound collection by the external ear, mechanical amplification by the middle ear, and neural transduction within the cochlea of the inner ear.  In parallel, balance is maintained by the vestibular apparatus, which detects angular acceleration through the semicircular ducts and linear acceleration and head position through the utricle and saccule. ​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​

# Adrenal Gland Anatomy And Physiology # Introduction The adrenal glands are small, triangle-shaped endocrine organs that are located on top of each kidney that play a crucial role in metabolism, fluid and electrolyte balance, and stress response modulation.  This article focuses on normal adrenal function.  Pathologic adrenal conditions are discussed in detail in separate articles. # Anatomy The adrenal glands are bilateral structures each weighing about 4-6 g in adults.  They are composed of 2 distinct regions:  the adrenal cortex and the adrenal medulla. ## Adrenal cortex The outer portion of the gland comprises about 80%-90% of its mass.  It is further divided into 3 zones: - Zona glomerulosa:  The outermost layer, responsible for mineralocorticoid production (primarily aldosterone) - Zona fasciculata:  The middle and largest layer, responsible for glucocorticoid production (primarily cortisol) - Zona reticularis:  The innermost layer, responsible for androgen production (primarily dehydroepiandrosterone \[DHEA\] and androstenedione) ## Adrenal medulla The inner portion of the gland, comprising about 10%-20% of its mass and is responsible for catecholamine production (primarily epinephrine and norepinephrine) by chromaffin cells. The adrenal glands are highly vascularized, receiving blood supply from the superior, middle, and inferior adrenal arteries.  Venous drainage occurs primarily through the central adrenal vein. # Physiology The adrenal glands produce several hormones essential for maintaining homeostasis: **Glucocorticoids (primarily cortisol)** - Regulate metabolism, immune function, and stress response - Increase blood glucose levels through gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis - Suppress inflammation and immune responses - Maintain vascular tone and cardiac contractility **Mineralocorticoids (primarily aldosterone)** - Regulate electrolyte balance and blood pressure - Promote sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion in the kidneys, by increasing the number of basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase pumps and apical sodium channels on principal cells in the collecting duct and stimulating potassium and hydrogen ion secretion from the principal and intercalated cells, respectively. - Increase blood volume and blood pressure **Adrenal androgens (DHEA, androstenedione)** - Contribute to sexual characteristics in women (in men, testosterone from testicular secretion is the main androgen) - Serve as precursors for other sex hormones **Catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)** - Mediate the "fight or flight" response - Increase heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rate - Promote glucose mobilization and lipolysis A summary of adrenal anatomy and physiology is shown ((figure 1)).  Pathologic adrenal conditions are discussed in detail in separate articles.  These include Cushing syndrome (excess cortisol), primary hyperaldosteronism (excess aldosterone), pheochromocytoma (excess catecholamines), and adrenal insufficiency (insufficient cortisol and/or aldosterone). # Adrenal regulation The production and secretion of adrenal hormones are tightly regulated by various mechanisms: ## Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis The HPA axis controls glucocorticoid production ((figure 2)). - Stress or circadian rhythms stimulate the hypothalamus to release corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). - CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). - ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol.  Steroidogenesis is described in more detail in the section below. - Cortisol exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary. ## Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) RAAS regulates mineralocorticoid production ((Figure 3)). - Decreased blood volume or pressure stimulates renin release from the kidneys. - Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II. - Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone production in the zona glomerulosa. ## Sympathetic nervous system The sympathetic nervous system controls catecholamine production by chromaffin cells in the adrenal medulla ((Figure 4)). - Sympathetic stimulation (acetylcholine relased by sympathetic preganglionic neurons) triggers the release of epinephrine and norepinephrine. # ACTH and steroidogenesis ## ACTH mechanism of action ACTH acts by binding to the melanocortin 2 receptor on adrenocortical cells, activating adenylyl cyclase.  This increases cyclic AMP, stimulating protein kinase A and phosphorylation of various proteins.  ACTH has both acute and chronic effects on steroidogenesis: - Acute effects (within minutes): - Increases cholesterol transport from the cytoplasm to the inner mitochondrial membrane - Stimulates the rate-limiting step in steroidogenesis through increased activity of steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) protein - Chronic effects (hours to days): - Increases synthesis of steroidogenic enzymes - Promotes general adrenocortical cell growth (hyperplasia) and RNA and protein synthesis ## Key steps in steroid hormone synthesis pathway In response to ACTH and/or angiotensin II, the adrenal cortex synthesizes various steroid hormones from cholesterol through a series of enzymatic reactions ((Figure 5)).  The process can be broken down into several key steps: - Cholesterol uptake and transport: - Cholesterol is obtained from circulation (primarily LDL and HDL) or synthesized de novo. - StAR protein mediates the rate-limiting step of transporting cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane. - Pregnenolone synthesis: - Cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme converts cholesterol to pregnenolone. - Zone-specific steroidogenesis: - Zona glomerulosa (aldosterone pathway): - Pregnenolone is converted to progesterone. - 21-hydroxylase converts progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone (a weak mineralocorticoid). - 11β-hydroxylase converts 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone (a weak glucocorticoid). - Corticosterone is converted into aldosterone. - Zona fasciculata (cortisol pathway): - 17α-hydroxylase converts pregnenolone to 17-hydroxypregnenolone and progesterone to 17α-hydroxyprogesterone. - 21-hydroxylase converts 17α-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol. - 11β-hydroxylase converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. - Zona reticularis (androgen pathway): - DHEA is converted into androstenedione. - Peripheral tissue enzymes convert androstenedione to small amounts of testosterone. Certain enzyme deficiencies, such as 21-hydroxylase deficiency ((Figure 6)) or 11β-hydroxylase deficiency ((Figure 7)), can lead to various forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia ((Table 1)) (discussed in a separate article). # Summary The adrenal glands contain an outer layer (cortex) that synthesizes glucocorticoids (cortisol), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), and some androgens (DHEA), and an inner layer (medulla) that secretes catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine).  The production and secretion of adrenal hormones are tightly regulated by various mechanisms.  The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis controls glucocorticoid production through a cascade of hormonal signals involving CRH, ACTH, and cortisol.  RAAS regulates mineralocorticoid production in response to changes in blood volume and pressure.  The sympathetic nervous system governs catecholamine release from the adrenal medulla. ​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌

articles.markdown:
# Tumor Suppressor Genes # Introduction Cancer is a heterogeneous disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells that have acquired the ability to evade the body's normal control mechanisms.  The progression from normal cells to this neoplastic state is a multistep process in which cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes, leading to the malignant phenotype. Two key genetic changes seen in almost all cancer cells include inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and activation of proto-oncogenes ((Figure 1)).  These changes contribute to the properties unique to cancer, including: - Loss of growth suppression and resistance to apoptosis via inactivation of tumor suppressor genes. - Sustained cell proliferative signaling and capacity for cell invasion via activation of proto-oncogenes. Identification of these mutations is important, as these alterations can inform cancer risk screening, provide prognostic indicators, and guide selection of specific targeted therapies. # Tumor suppressor genes Tumor suppressor genes protect cells from developing into cancer.  They perform key regulatory functions, such as inhibiting excessive cell division, promoting apoptosis, and repairing damaged DNA.  In most cases, the presence of just 1 active allele is sufficient to maintain these protective roles.  However, when both alleles are inactivated (eg, through genetic mutations), these normal safeguards are no longer present, allowing for uncontrolled cell growth and potential tumor formation (ie, Knudson "2-hit" hypothesis ((Figure 2))). ## *RB1* gene - **Function**:  The *RB1* gene encodes the Rb protein, which integrates signals from various extracellular and intracellular sources to determine whether a cell should proceed through the cell cycle (ie, G1/S checkpoint). - If signals indicate the cell cycle should not proceed (eg, terminally differentiated cell, damaged DNA), the Rb protein stays in its active (ie, dephosphorylated) form.  While active, Rb binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors.  Without E2F, the cell cycle pauses at the G1/S checkpoint, allowing for the cell to repair itself if necessary ((Figure 3)). - If signals indicate the cell cycle can proceed (eg, DNA has been successfully repaired), cyclin-dependent kinases phosphorylate Rb, inactivating it.  Inactivated Rb releases the bound E2F, allowing the cell to proceed through the G1/S checkpoint. - **Mutation**:  One copy of the *RB1* gene is located on each homolog of chromosome 13.  A single functional allele is sufficient to produce enough Rb protein to regulate the G1/S checkpoint.  However, biallelic loss of *RB1* (eg, nonsense mutations, deletions) eliminates this protective function and allows cells to progress through the cell cycle unchecked. - **Associated condition**:  **Retinoblastoma**.  Although the Rb protein serves a tumor suppressor role ubiquitously in all cells, the *RB1* mutation particularly affects the retina.  Because total loss of tumor suppressor function is needed for cancer to develop, retinoblastoma can present in 2 main forms, depending on whether the patient has a germline *RB1* mutation. - Hereditary retinoblastoma:  These patients are born with a germline defect in 1 of the *RB1* genes, meaning every cell in the body already carries the first "hit" needed for tumor development.  Because only 1 additional (somatic) mutation is required to inactivate the remaining normal *RB1* allele, this second "hit" can occur independently in multiple retinal cells.  As a result, an increased risk of bilateral disease exists. - Sporadic retinoblastoma:  These patients lack an underlying germline *RB1* mutation.  In this case, 2 independent somatic mutations must occur within the same retinal cell to inactivate *RB1* and initiate tumor formation.  Because this requires 2 rare, spontaneous mutations in a single cell, tumor development is typically limited to unilateral disease at a later age. ## *APC* gene - **Function**:  The *APC* gene encodes the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) protein, which normally binds and promotes the degradation of beta-catenin.  Beta-catenin is a key component of the Wnt signaling pathway, which regulates essential cell processes (eg, proliferation, differentiation), particularly in intestinal epithelial cell renewal. - **Mutation**:  Various mutations (eg, frameshift, deletion) can cause loss of APC function.  Without functional APC, beta-catenin is not adequately degraded and accumulates in the cell, where it activates transcription factors that promote cell proliferation.  This unchecked signaling drives excessive growth of intestinal crypt epithelial cells. - **Associated conditions**:  Sporadic mutations affecting both alleles can lead to early-onset colorectal cancer.  Patients with an underlying germline mutation in *APC* have **familial adenomatous polyposis**, in which thousands of colon polyps develop; in addition, these patients have early-onset colon carcinoma.  *APC* mutations are also associated with other gastrointestinal malignancies (eg, gastric, pancreatic) and medulloblastoma. ## *BRCA1/BRCA2* genes - **Function**:  The *BRCA1* and *BRCA2* (breast cancer type 1 and breast cancer type 2) genes maintain the integrity of the genome by producing proteins that repair double-stranded DNA breaks via homologous recombination. - **Mutation**:  Loss of function leads to accumulation of unrepaired genetic mutations, which dramatically increases the risk of oncogenesis. - **Associated conditions**:  **Breast, ovarian, and prostate cancer**.  Estrogen-responsive tissue (eg, breast, ovarian) appear to be particularly sensitive to *BRCA1/2* dysfunction, leading to a predominance of cancers in these organs ((Table 1)). ## *TP53* gene - **Function**:  The *TP53* gene, often referred to as the "guardian of the genome," plays a critical role in maintaining genetic integrity.  During the G1 phase of the cell cycle, *TP53* responds to signals of cellular stress and DNA damage.  In response to significant genomic injury, the p53 protein is activated and halts further cell cycle progression, providing time for DNA repair.  If the damage is successfully repaired, the cell may proceed to divide; if the damage is irreparable, p53 initiates apoptosis. - **Mutation**:  Loss of *TP53* function allows cells with damaged DNA to survive and proliferate, contributing to malignant transformation. - **Associated conditions**:  Dysfunctional *TP53* is associated with **Li-Fraumeni syndrome**, a cancer predisposition syndrome in which patients are at significantly increased risk for early-onset development of a wide variety of cancers, including carcinomas (eg, breast, adrenocortical), soft tissue and bone sarcomas, brain tumors, and leukemias. ## *PTEN* gene - **Function**:  The *PTEN* (phosphatase and tensin homolog) gene encodes a phosphatase that negatively regulates both the PI3K/AKT pathway and the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, which are key drivers of cell growth, proliferation, and survival. - **Mutation**:  The loss of *PTEN* function leads to unopposed growth and survival signaling. - **Associated conditions**:  Hamartomatous tumors and **Cowden syndrome**, which has an increased risk for breast, thyroid, endometrial, colorectal, and renal cancer. ## *WT1* gene - **Function**:  The *WT1* gene encodes the WT1 protein, a transcription factor involved in regulating growth and development of the kidneys and gonads.  It functions as a tumor suppressor by inhibiting the transcription of several growth factor–inducible genes, thereby limiting excessive cell proliferation. - **Mutation**:  The loss or inactivation of *WT1* leads to abnormal growth factor expression within renal tissue, driving proliferation. - **Associated condition**:  **Wilms tumor** (nephroblastoma) ((Figure 4)). ## *NF1* gene - **Function**:  The *NF1* gene encodes the protein neurofibromin, which negatively regulates the RAS/MAP kinase signaling pathway.  This pathway controls cell proliferation and differentiation. - **Mutation**:  A mutation in *NF1* results in loss of function in neurofibromin, which leads to increased cell proliferation. - **Associated condition**:  **Neurofibromatosis type 1**.  This condition is characterized by multiple benign neurofibromas, CNS tumors (eg, optic gliomas, pilocytic astrocytomas), soft tissue sarcomas, and neuroblastoma ((Table 2)). ## *NF2* gene - **Function**:  The *NF2* gene encodes the protein merlin, a tumor suppressor protein primarily expressed in neural tissue.  Merlin associates with the plasma membrane and mediates contact inhibition, regulating cell adhesion by stabilizing cell-cell junctions and suppressing proliferative signaling. - **Mutation**:  Loss of merlin function disrupts contact inhibition, leading to abnormal cell proliferation. - **Associated condition**:  ***NF2*\-related schwannomatosis**, which is classically associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas.  Additional features include intracranial meningiomas and ependymomas ((Table 3)). ## *VHL* gene - **Function**:  The *VHL* gene encodes a protein, von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) ubiquitin ligase, that polyubiquitinates hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs), targeting them for degradation.  HIFs play a key role in oxygen sensing and angiogenesis ((Figure 5)). - **Mutation**:  *VHL* mutations (eg, deletion, nonsense, frameshift) disrupt normal HIF degradation, leading to HIF accumulation.  This condition results in overexpression of angiogenic growth factors (eg, VEG-F, PDG-F) and erythropoietin, driving abnormal blood vessel proliferation that can lead to highly vascular tumors and cysts. - **Associated condition**:  VHL disease, which can cause CNS hemangioblastomas, retinal hemangioblastomas, renal clear cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic cysts, and endolymphatic sac tumors of the middle ear ((Table 4)). # Summary Cancer development involves a multistep progression in which cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes leading to the malignant phenotype.  Almost all cancer cells characteristically have 2 key genetic drivers: biallelic inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and/or gain-of-function of proto-oncogenes.  These changes contribute to the properties unique to cancer, such as the loss of growth suppression and resistance to apoptosis via inactivation of tumor suppressor genes, and sustained cell proliferative signaling and capacity for cell invasion via activation of proto-oncogenes. ​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌

articles.title: Protooncogenes
articles.markdown:
# Protooncogenes # Introduction Cancer is a heterogeneous disease characterized by the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells that have acquired the ability to evade the body's normal control mechanisms.  The progression from normal cells to this neoplastic state involves a multistep process in which cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes, leading to the malignant phenotype.  Two genetic changes seen in almost all cancer cells include the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and the activation of protooncogenes ((Figure 1)). Protooncogenes encode proteins that regulate cell growth and survival.  This process depends on a tightly coordinated series of molecular events, including: - Signal initiation:  A signaling molecule binds its receptor on the cell surface.  Major receptor types include ion channel, steroid hormone, enzyme-linked, and G-protein–linked.  When growth factor binds, these receptors change their configuration, triggering intracellular activation. - Signal transduction:  The activated receptor transmits the signal through intracellular signaling cascades, which relay the message to the nucleus.  Examples of these signal transduction systems include the mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinase, cyclic AMP, inositol triphosphate, and JAK/STAT pathways.  These regulate cell proliferation and survival. - Gene expression and cellular response:  Once the signal reaches the nucleus, it activates specific transcription factors that modify the expression of target genes (eg, genes encoding proteins such as cyclin D1 that drive cell cycle progression), driving cell growth and differentiation. - Programmed cell death:  During development and tissue maintenance, cells undergo apoptosis when they are no longer needed or are damaged. If a protooncogene undergoes a mutation that enhances its activity level and/or alters its resultant protein, it can become an oncogene and induce malignant transformation.  Unlike tumor suppressor genes, which require complete loss of function via biallelic mutations, oncogenes exhibit gain-of-function mutations (ie, alteration of only a single allele is sufficient to promote oncogenesis). Protooncogenes are categorized based on their role within cell growth and survival. # Growth factors Growth factor protooncogenes encode signaling proteins that bind cell surface receptors to stimulate cell proliferation. ## *PDGFB* gene - **Function**:  The *PDGFB* gene encodes for the platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) protein, which promotes cell growth. - **Mutation**:  Overexpression of the *PDGFB* gene results in excessive PDGF, resulting in autocrine stimulation.  As a result, the cell continually stimulates its own growth receptors, driving uncontrolled proliferation. - **Associated conditions**:  Astrocytoma, osteosarcoma. # Growth factor receptors These protooncogenes encode transmembrane receptor proteins that bind extracellular growth factors to stimulate cell proliferation. Each receptor typically consists of an extracellular region that can bind ligands, a hydrophobic transmembrane region, and an intracellular domain with inducible tyrosine kinase activity. When a ligand binds to the receptor, it triggers dimerization of 2 receptor subunits.  Each subunit phosphorylates the other, activating intracellular signaling cascades to promote cell proliferation. ## *RET* gene - **Function**:  The *RET* gene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cell growth. - **Mutation**:  Gain-of-function mutations lead to constitutive activation of the receptor, leading to unregulated cellular proliferation. - **Associated conditions**:  **Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2**, which can cause medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, and a marfanoid habitus ((Table 1)). ## *ALK* gene - **Function**:  The *ALK* (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) gene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cell growth. - **Mutation**:  Gene rearrangements can generate a constitutively active fusion protein, leading to continuous activation of growth signaling. - **Associated conditions**:  Non–small cell lung carcinoma, anaplastic large cell lymphoma ## *EGFR* gene - **Function**:  The *EGFR* (epidermal growth factor receptor) gene encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase that initiates cell proliferation. - **Mutation**:  Overexpression of the *EGFR* gene leads to excessive receptor production and activity. - **Associated conditions**:  Non–small cell lung cancers (eg, adenocarcinoma); colon, breast, and brain cancer. ## *HER2* gene - **Function**:  The *HER2* (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2) gene encodes for a receptor with tyrosine kinase activity that is involved in epithelial cell growth and differentiation. - **Mutation**:  Overexpression of *HER2* can occur due to gene amplification, causing increased proliferation and resistance to apoptosis. - **Associated conditions**: - Breast cancer (particularly estrogen receptor– and progesterone receptor–negative cancer). # Signal transducers These protooncogenes encode intracellular signaling proteins that relay messages from cell surface receptors to the nucleus, activating genes involved in cell growth and proliferation. ## *ABL1* gene - **Function**:  The *ABL1* gene encodes ABL, a nonreceptor tyrosine kinase located in the cytoplasm; it mediates cell proliferation. - **Mutation**:  A translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 leads to a *BCR::ABL1* fusion gene (Philadelphia chromosome).  That fusion results in constitutive ABL signal transduction, driving continuous cell proliferation. - **Associated conditions**:  **Chronic myeloid leukemia**, acute lymphoblastic leukemia. ## *BRAF* gene - **Function**:  The *BRAF* gene encodes a serine/threonine kinase that functions in the MAP-kinase signaling pathway, regulating cell growth. - **Mutation**:  Activating mutations in the *BRAF* gene lead to constitutive MAP-kinase pathway activation. - **Associated cancers**:  Malignant melanoma, hairy cell leukemia, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, papillary thyroid cancer. ## *RAS* gene (*KRAS, HRAS, NRAS*) - **Function**:  The *RAS* gene encodes Ras, a GTP-binding protein that mediates signal transduction in the MAP-kinase pathway ((Figure 2)).  Ras cycles between an active (GTP-bound) and an inactive (guanosine 5′-diphosphate–bound \[GDP-bound\]) state, with intrinsic GTPase activity allowing for self-inactivation. - **Mutation**:  Mutations that reduce GTPase activity prevent Ras from converting GTP to GDP, locking it in the active state.  Ras proteins persistently activate downstream proliferative pathways, leading to continuous cell division. - **Associated conditions**:  Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, colorectal carcinoma, non–small cell lung cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, renal cancer, bladder cancer. # Transcription factors These protooncogenes encode nuclear proteins that regulate the transcription of target genes involved in cell cycle progression. ## *MYC* gene - **Function**:  The *MYC* gene family encodes nuclear phosphoproteins (C-MYC, N-MYC, L-MYC) that function as transcription factors to upregulate genes involved in cell cycle progression. - **Mutation**:  *MYC* activation typically occurs through chromosomal translocation or gene amplification. - *C-MYC* gene on chromosome 8 can be translocated to an immunoglobulin gene locus on chromosome 14.  This places *C-MYC* under the control of a highly active immunoglobulin promoter, leading to overexpression in B cells and driving B-cell proliferation. - *N-MYC* can be amplified, in which repeated rounds of DNA replication within a particular gene region increase the number of copies of the gene within a cell. - **Associated conditions**:  **Burkitt lymphoma** (*C-MYC*), **neuroblastoma** (*N-MYC*), and small cell lung carcinoma (*L-MYC*). # Cell cycle regulators Cell cycle regulators normally function in various parts of the cell cycle to promote cell division. ## *CCND1* gene - **Function**:  The *CCND1* gene encodes cyclin D1, a key regulatory protein that promotes progression through the G1/S checkpoint.  Under normal conditions, cyclin D1 expression is induced by growth factor signaling, allowing controlled cell cycle progression only when appropriate. - **Mutation**:  Gene amplification or chromosomal translocation of *CCND1* leads to overexpression of cyclin D1, driving cell proliferation independent of growth factor stimulation. - **Associated conditions**:  **Mantle cell lymphoma**; breast, lung, and esophageal cancer # Cell survival regulators This protooncogene encodes proteins involved in preventing apoptosis. ## *BCL2* gene - **Function**:  The *BCL2* gene encodes B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2) protein, which functions as an inhibitor of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway ((Figure 3)).  Bcl-2 inhibits apoptosis by preventing cytochrome c release from the mitochondria, which is necessary for caspase activation and apoptotic cell death. - **Mutation**:  Bcl-2 can be overexpressed due to a chromosomal translocation (eg, when the *BCL2* gene is placed next to an immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer element) or loss of regulatory genes.  As a result, cells can evade apoptosis and survive longer. - **Associated conditions**:  **Follicular lymphoma**, **chronic lymphocytic leukemia**. # Summary Cancer development involves a multistep progression in which cells accumulate genetic and epigenetic changes leading to the malignant phenotype.  Almost all cancer cells characteristically have two key genetic drivers: biallelic inactivation of tumor suppressor genes and/or gain-of-function of protooncogenes.  These changes contribute to the properties unique to cancer, such as the loss of growth suppression and resistance to apoptosis via inactivation of tumor suppressor genes, as well as sustained cell proliferative signaling and capacity for cell invasion via the activation of protooncogenes. ​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2

Inheritance

  • Autosomal dominant
  • Germ-line activating mutations of RET protooncogene

Type 2A

  • Medullary thyroid cancer (>95%)
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Parathyroid hyperplasia

Type 2B

  • Medullary thyroid cancer (>95%)
  • Pheochromocytoma
  • Mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus
