# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Lumbar Spine # Introduction Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) may effectively address lumbar spine dysfunction, alleviating low back pain, enhancing mobility, and restoring biomechanical function.  This article discusses lumbar anatomy and biomechanics, somatic dysfunctions, and OMT techniques. # Lumbar spine biomechanics The lumbar spine consists of 5 vertebrae **(L1-L5)** that are characterized by superior facets oriented backward and medially ((Figure 1)).  This facet orientation primarily facilitates **flexion** and **extension** while allowing limited sidebending and minimal rotation. The lumbosacral (Ferguson) angle, typically ranging from 25 to 35 degrees relative to the horizontal plane, describes the inclination of the sacral base and significantly influences lumbar spine biomechanics.  Normal lumbar **lordosis**, the inward curvature of the lumbar spine, enhances shock absorption and load distribution during standing and movement.  It is maintained by the shape of the vertebral bodies, the intervertebral discs, and the tone of the supporting musculature. Stability of the lumbar spine is maintained through muscular support, intervertebral discs, and various ligamentous structures.  The **posterior longitudinal ligament** runs along the posterior aspect of the vertebral bodies but progressively **narrows** from L1 to L5, becoming approximately half its original width at the L4-L5 segment.  This narrowing increases vulnerability to **disc herniations** at the lower lumbar levels.  The iliolumbar ligament, connecting the transverse processes of L4 and L5 to the iliac crest, is commonly one of the first ligaments to become tender during lumbar dysfunction.  Additional ligamentous structures include the ligamentum flavum (paired ligaments connecting adjacent vertebral arches), supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligaments, and anterior longitudinal ligament ((Figure 2)). # Congenital anomalies ## Sacralization and lumbarization **Sacralization**, a congenital deformity, occurs when one or both transverse processes of the **L5 vertebra fuse with the sacrum**, effectively reducing the number of lumbar vertebrae from 5 to 4.  This results in decreased lumbar lordosis (flattened lumbar curve), premature disc degeneration, and chronic low back pain because the weakened iliolumbar ligaments cause hypermobility (excessive movement of L4 on L5), reduced L5-S1 disc space, and biomechanical asymmetries that stress the sacroiliac (SI) joints, particularly in unilateral cases. **Lumbarization** is also a congenital anomaly that alters the biomechanics of the lumbosacral region and leads to early degenerative changes.  It results from **failure of fusion of S1** with the rest of the sacrum, effectively increasing the number of lumbar vertebrae from 5 to 6 (ie, L6). Sacralization and lumbarization are both forms of lumbosacral transitional vertebrae and are sometimes referred to as Bertolotti syndrome when they become symptomatic and cause low back pain ((Figure 3)). ## Facet tropism Facet tropism is characterized by asymmetry in the left and right facet joint angles.  It can be seen in up to 30% of patients, potentially predisposing to degenerative changes and low back pain starting at a young age. ## Spina bifida occulta Spina bifida occulta is a congenital anomaly characterized by a failure of the lumbar vertebral lamina to close and is associated with a patch of hair overlying the defect.  Although it is generally asymptomatic, patients can sometimes develop back pain and/or neurologic symptoms.  Unlike in spina bifida meningocele, meningomyelocele, and myeloschisis, herniation is not seen in spina bifida occulta ((Figure 4)). # Lumbar spine disorders ## Disc herniation and radiculopathy Lumbar disc herniation, typically affecting the L4-L5 or L5-S1 levels, is characterized by nucleus pulposus extrusion, with protrusion posterolaterally into the lower part of the intervertebral space.  Lumbar nerve roots exit the spinal canal through intervertebral foramina located inferior to their corresponding vertebrae.  Therefore, a herniation at the L4-L5 level typically compresses the L5 nerve root, whereas a herniation at the L5-S1 level typically compresses the S1 nerve root.  This compression results in sciatica with symptoms that include radiating pain, numbness, and weakness along the affected nerve distribution (dermatome) ((Table 1)). Diagnostic physical examination includes the straight-leg raising test (positive when pain occurs with leg elevation between 30 and 70 degrees), the crossed straight-leg raising test (positive when pain appears in the affected leg when the opposite leg is raised), and the neural slump test (positive when pain is reproduced with spinal flexion and leg extension while seated). ## Psoas syndrome Psoas syndrome is characterized by flexion contraction of the psoas muscle (or collectively, the iliopsoas) ((Figure 5)).  The psoas major originates on the anterolateral aspect of the lumbar vertebrae and inserts onto the lesser trochanter of the femur, allowing it to flex the hip; therefore, a shortened/hypertonic psoas either pulls the lumbar vertebrae anteriorly (ie, increased lumbar lordosis) or pulls the hip into flexion. Psoas syndrome is commonly seen in athletes and runners but can also be caused by repetitive truncal flexion or visceral irritation (eg, appendicitis, ureteral calculi, diverticulosis).  Patients typically experience low back pain and stiffness that is worsened by standing or walking.  Because of the attachment of the psoas to the lumbar spine, pelvis, and femur, psoas contracture causes the following examination findings: - **Positive** Thomas test:  Flexing the hip and knee on the unaffected side in the supine position causes the opposite leg (with the hypertonic psoas) to elevate off the table ((Figure 6)). - **Pelvic shift to the opposite side**:  The lumbar spine is pulled toward the affected side, inducing a pelvic shift to the opposite side. - **Nonneutral lumbar dysfunction** on the affected side:  Flexion and extension lumbar vertebral somatic dysfunctions are common. Treatment includes gentle stretching for the muscle spasm, addressing lumbar spine dysfunctions, and counterstrain for any associated tender points. ## Spondylolisthesis Spondylolisthesis (from *spondylos* = vertebra and *olisthesis* = slipping) is characterized by **anterior displacement** of a vertebral body in relation to the one below it.  Spondylolisthesis often occurs at L4 or L5 due to an instability of the articular processes and intervertebral joints caused by a **pars interarticularis fracture** (ie, "spondylolysis" from *spondylos* = vertebra and *lysis* = loosening/dissolution) ((Figure 7)).  The terms "spondylolisthesis" and "spondylolysis" should not be confused with "spondylosis" (from *spondylos* = vertebra, -*osis* = degeneration), which describes spinal degenerative changes (eg, osteophytes, narrowed disc space) ((Figure 8)).  Grading uses the percentage of displacement of L5 relative to the sacrum: - Grade I:  0%-25%. - Grade II:  25%-50%. - Grade III:  50%-75%. - Grade IV:  >75%. Patients typically have achy low back, buttock, and thigh pain.  These symptoms are reproduced with extension of the spine, which compresses the nerve roots and can trigger radicular pain.  Other common examination findings include tight hamstrings, a waddling gait, and a **positive vertebral step-off sign** (palpable forward displacement of the spinous process above the affected vertebra). Treatment is typically conservative and focuses on managing pain, reducing lumbar lordosis, and addressing associated somatic dysfunctions. ## Spinal stenosis Spinal stenosis is an abnormal **narrowing** of the spinal canal and/or intervertebral foramen.  In spinal stenosis, there is formation of facet joint osteophytes and hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, which can compress spinal nerve roots ((figure 7)).  Patients have **chronic** back pain radiating down the lower extremities, numbness/paresthesia, and occasionally weakness.  Symptoms are **worsened** with **lumbar extension**, which further narrows the spinal canal, and are relieved with lumbar flexion (eg, leaning on a stroller/shopping cart) ((figure 8)). Spinal stenosis typically affects the nerve root of the corresponding vertebral level as it exits the intervertebral foramen.  Treatment consists of physical therapy and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs/muscle relaxants.  Surgical laminectomy may be helpful in refractory cases. Lumbar somatic dysfunctions are commonly seen in patients with spinal stenosis (due to compensatory changes).  Because lumbar extension exacerbates pain, patients naturally spend more time with the lumbar spine flexed, which can cause flexion dysfunctions.  OMT can help improve overall function and mobility, although it does not address the underlying degenerative changes. ## Facet joint syndrome Lumbar facet joints become symptomatic from stress, arthritis, or trauma, presenting with localized pain aggravated by extension and rotation.  Examination shows restricted joint motion and facet joint tenderness. ## SI dysfunction SI dysfunction causes unilateral low back pain, buttock discomfort, and hip motion restrictions, often related to trauma, pregnancy, or repetitive strain.  FABER (**F**lexion, **AB**duction, **E**xternal **R**otation) and standing flexion tests aid in the diagnosis of SI dysfunction. # Somatic dysfunctions ## Vertebral somatic dysfunction Lumbar vertebral somatic dysfunctions commonly accompany the lumbar abnormalities discussed in this article.  These dysfunctions involve vertebrae becoming "stuck" in dysfunctional positions.  Treatment involves placing the vertebrae against the restrictive barrier and pushing through it with various techniques (eg, high-velocity low-amplitude \[HVLA\] thrust; direct muscle energy). For example, if diagnostic palpation of the L4 vertebra demonstrates that it is **rotated right** (ie, right transverse process more posterior) and stuck in the **flexed** position (ie, improves during flexion), the second law of spinal motion (Fryette law) indicates that L4 is **sidebent right** (ie, rotation and sidebending occur in the same direction for flexion/extension dysfunctions) ((Figure 11)). To perform HVLA treatment of this dysfunction **(L4 FR****R****S****R****)**, the patient is typically positioned on the side that the dysfunctional vertebra is rotated toward **(right lateral recumbent position)**.  The **arm on the same side** (against the table) is then pulled either cephalad (toward the head) or caudad (toward the feet), depending on the dysfunction, to induce lumbar sidebending toward the restrictive barrier: - If L4 is **sidebent right** (toward the table), the **right arm is pulled cephalad**, which **induces left sidebending** (away from the table). - If L4 is sidebent left (away from the table), the right arm is pulled caudad, which induces right sidebending (toward the table). Once the restrictive barrier to sidebending is reached, the barriers to extension and rotation are engaged by straightening the patient's inferior leg and rotating the pelvis forward (toward the table) before delivering a thrust (ie, lumbar roll HVLA) ((Figure 12)). To perform direct muscle energy for this dysfunction **(L4 FR****R****S****R****)**, the restrictive barrier is engaged by positioning the torso into flexion, left rotation, and left sidebending.  By using postisometric relaxation, the subsequent motions are aimed at progressively relaxing the shortened/spasmed muscles (that facilitate the dysfunction) to allow the physician to move the joint through the restrictive barrier: - Isometric contraction:  The physician applies a counterforce (directed against/toward the restrictive barrier) of equal value for 3-5 seconds as the patient attempts to move the joint in the opposite direction (ie, back toward the position of dysfunction). - Postisometric relaxation:  The resultant muscle relaxation allows the physician to move the joint through the restrictive barrier until a new barrier is reached. This process is repeated until the normal range of motion is restored. ## Tender points Tender points are tender nodules, generally 1-2 cm in diameter, that occur due to inappropriate neuromuscular reflexes following injury, strain, or chronic dysfunction.  Treatment involves counterstrain to interrupt these reflexive cycles by positioning the patient to relax the affected tissues, diminishing neuromuscular strain and pain. Anterior and posterior lumbar tender points, in addition to treatment positions involving moving the leg and hip, are summarized in the table ((Table 2)).  Tender points and counterstrain are discussed in more detail in a separate article. ## Myofascial restrictions Myofascial restrictions in the lumbar spine frequently develop secondary to trauma, surgery, inflammation, or chronic postural strain.  These restrictions disrupt normal myofascial glide and cause chronic pain, limited mobility, and altered biomechanics.  Techniques such as myofascial release and balanced ligamentous tension address these restrictions by gently releasing myofascial tension, restoring tissue mobility, and enhancing overall lumbar spine function. ## Viscerosomatic reflexes Viscerosomatic reflexes manifest as somatic dysfunctions in response to internal visceral pathology.  For instance, gastrointestinal, renal, or reproductive system disorders can cause reflexive muscular hypertonicity and segmental dysfunction within the lumbar region.  In addition to medical treatment of the underlying visceral disorders, OMT can be beneficial.  Viscerosomatic reflexes and autonomic levels associated with various organs are discussed in a separate article. ## Somatosomatic reflexes Somatosomatic reflexes occur when chronic sensory input from somatic dysfunction or injury results in hyperactive spinal reflexes.  This hyperactivity manifests as persistent muscular hypertonicity, tenderness, and restricted vertebral mobility at affected spinal segments.  Treatment involves techniques such as direct inhibitory pressure, counterstrain, and facilitated positional release, aiming to interrupt dysfunctional reflex loops, normalize segmental facilitation, and restore spinal segment mobility. # Summary Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) effectively addresses lumbar spine dysfunction by alleviating pain, restoring biomechanical balance, and improving mobility.  Understanding the biomechanics, anatomy, and common disorders of the lumbar spine, including disc herniation, congenital anomalies, psoas syndrome, spinal stenosis, and spondylolisthesis, is essential for effective treatment.  Lumbar somatic dysfunctions often accompany these conditions, presenting as restricted vertebral movements, myofascial tension, tender points, and reflexive muscular hypertonicity.  OMT techniques—including high-velocity, low-amplitude thrust; muscle energy; counterstrain; myofascial release; facilitated positional release; and balanced ligamentous tension—provide targeted and individualized management to enhance lumbar function and reduce symptoms. ​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌

articles.title: Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Lower Extremities
articles.markdown:
# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Lower Extremities # Introduction Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) of the extremities can restore optimal function, alleviate pain, and enhance overall mobility.  An understanding of the mechanics of extremity movements, associated somatic dysfunctions, and relevant anatomic landmarks greatly enhances diagnostic accuracy and treatment effectiveness.  This article reviews these elements and discusses targeted osteopathic treatments for common lower extremity somatic dysfunctions. # Piriformis syndrome Piriformis syndrome is thought to involve irritation or compression of the **sciatic nerve** by a hypertonic piriformis muscle because these structures travel in close proximity through the greater sciatic foramen ((Figure 1)).  This results in sciatica-like hip/buttock pain, tingling, and numbness that radiate down the leg and are exacerbated by direct pressure (eg, sitting on a wallet) or microtrauma (ie, overuse).  These symptoms are often associated with a tenderpoint, located 7 cm medial to and slightly above the greater trochanter ((Table 1)) Counterstrain can be used to relax the piriformis muscle by **flexing**, **abducting**, and **internally rotating** the thigh ((Video 1)).  Occasionally, the tenderpoint does not respond to internal rotation, so fine-tuning with external rotation should be performed instead.  Additional treatments such as myofascial release and muscle energy techniques may be applied to address associated sacral and pelvic somatic dysfunctions, further alleviating symptoms. # Patellofemoral pain syndrome Patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS) classically presents with **anterior knee pain** that worsens while walking up or down stairs and squatting (ie, isometric quadriceps contraction against resistance).  The etiology of PFPS is multifactorial (eg, trauma, structural abnormalities, excessive quadriceps activation while running) and involves **patellar malalignment** associated with loss of quadriceps strength (ie, quadriceps atrophy).  The result is asymmetric sliding along the femoral groove and wear and tear of the articular surface of the knee (causing pain without significant tenderness to palpation). In addition to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, management of PFPS includes **strengthening** exercises for the **quadriceps** and **hip** muscles and minimization of repetitive knee trauma/quadriceps overuse.  These exercises help **restore symmetry in patellar glide**, thereby improving knee mechanics and decreasing both pain and articular wear and tear. # Fibular head dysfunction During foot supination and pronation, movement of the distal fibula at the ankle and the proximal fibula (ie, fibular head) at the knee occurs in opposite directions (ie, **reciprocal motion**) ((Figure 2)): - Foot supination (ie, plantarflexion and inversion/internal rotation) pulls the distal fibula anteriorly.  Because the distal fibula is linked to the fibular head (ie, proximal fibula) via the interosseous membrane, this results in posterior glide of the fibular head (ie, proximal fibula). - Foot pronation (ie, dorsiflexion and eversion/external rotation) pushes the distal fibula posteriorly, resulting in anterior glide of the fibular head. **Anterior fibular head dysfunction** is characterized by restriction in foot supination (plantarflexion and inversion), indicating that the foot is "stuck" in the pronated (dorsiflexed and everted) position with the distal fibula displaced posteriorly and the fibular head "stuck" anteriorly.  Muscle energy (direct) restores normal motion by moving the stuck fibula through the restrictive barrier into posterior glide.  To perform muscle energy for anterior fibular head dysfunction, the physician positions the fibular head against the restrictive barrier by pushing posteriorly on the fibular head and inverting/internally rotating the foot.  The patient then attempts to evert/externally rotate the foot against resistance ((Figure 3)). In **posterior fibular head dysfunction**, the opposite applies in regard to diagnostic findings and treatment. # Chronic exertional compartment syndrome Chronic exertional compartment syndrome (CECS) is characterized by periodically **increased compartmental pressure** within a confined fascial space due to the expansion of muscle volume **during exercise**.  The anterior compartment of the lower leg is most commonly affected and results in tenderness to palpation and pain on plantarflexion (from stretching the irritated anterior compartment muscles). Unlike acute compartment syndrome, which occurs after trauma (eg, leg fracture), the swelling and increased pressure in CECS are usually transient and mild.  Management is typically conservative and includes reducing exercise intensity, using a heating pad prior to running (to loosen fascia), and icing the legs when symptoms occur (to reduce edema).  In addition, **myofascial release** relieves pain/edema by loosening the fascia and relaxing the underlying muscle, which **improves venous and lymphatic flow**.  Refractory cases can be treated with surgical fasciotomy. # Tarsal bone dysfunctions The foot has 2 longitudinal arches (medial and lateral) and 1 transverse arch, which act like elastic "springs" that assist with weight bearing and shock absorption.  These arches are formed from the tarsal and metatarsal bones and are reinforced by the ligaments and tendons of the foot ((Figure 4)). - Lateral longitudinal arch:  Calcaneus, cuboid, talus, and fourth and fifth metatarsal bones. - Medial longitudinal arch:  Calcaneus, navicular, talus, cuneiform bones and first to third metatarsal bones. - Transverse tarsal arch:  Cuboid, navicular, and cuneiform bones. Runners are prone to **somatic dysfunctions** and stress fractures of the **navicular bone** due to repetitive impact, which causes downward displacement of the bone toward the plantar surface, resulting in **collapse of the medial longitudinal and transverse tarsal arches**.  Foot pain in these patients typically progresses gradually over weeks and limits daily activities, particularly running.  In addition to rest and analgesics, patients may benefit from orthotics/braces for arch support and OMT (eg, Hiss plantar whip) to restore normal tarsal bone position. # Summary Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) of the lower extremities applies anatomic and biomechanical understanding to restore motion, alleviate pain, and support systemic function.  In the lower extremities, conditions such as fibular head dysfunction are treated with direct muscle energy to restore reciprocal fibular motion.  Piriformis syndrome, which causes sciatic nerve irritation, is treated with counterstrain and myofascial release.  Patellofemoral pain syndrome results from patellar maltracking and responds to quadriceps strengthening and biomechanical correction.  Chronic exertional compartment syndrome involves transient fascial pressure increases, managed conservatively with myofascial techniques and symptom control. ​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​

# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Innominates

# Introduction

Innominate somatic dysfunctions are characterized by altered biomechanics and restricted mobility of one or both innominate bones.  These dysfunctions can significantly impact pelvic stability, leading to cascading effects on posture, gait mechanics, and overall musculoskeletal health.  This article discusses the functional anatomy and mechanics of innominate motion, diagnostic techniques for identifying specific dysfunctions, and osteopathic manipulative treatment options.

# Anatomy

## Innominate bone and joints

The innominate bone (ie, the hip) is a large, paired bone that forms the lateral and anterior bony pelvis.  Each innominate is the result of the embryonic fusion of 3 bones: the ilium, the ischium, and the pubis ((Figure 1)).  These bones meet and fuse at the acetabulum, the cup-shaped socket on the lateral aspect of the innominate that articulates with the femoral head ((Figure 2)).

The innominate bones articulate at 3 key locations:

-   Sacroiliac (SI) joint:  A complex joint formed between the auricular surface of the ilium and the corresponding auricular surface of the sacrum.  This joint is responsible for transferring loads between the axial skeleton and the lower extremities.
-   Pubic symphysis:  A cartilaginous joint connecting the 2 pubic bones anteriorly.  It allows for slight movement, particularly during childbirth.
-   Hip joint (coxofemoral joint):  A synovial ball-and-socket joint between the acetabulum of the innominate and the head of the femur.  Although technically a lower extremity joint, its mechanics are intimately tied to innominate position.

Sacral anatomy, including supporting ligaments, is discussed in a separate article.

## Anatomic landmarks

Key palpable bony landmarks that are important for the diagnosis of innominate somatic dysfunctions include:

-   Iliac crests:  The palpable superior borders of the ilia.  Their relative positions can help identify upward and downward innominate movement in somatic dysfunctions.  In addition, the iliac crests align with the level of the L4-L5 intervertebral disc (useful landmarks when performing a lumbar puncture).
-   Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS):  Located at the anterior termination of the iliac crest, its relative position is a primary indicator of innominate rotation.
-   Posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS):  Found at the posterior termination of the iliac crest, overlying the sacroiliac joint.  Its position relative to the sacrum and the contralateral PSIS is used during the standing flexion test to identify innominate dysfunction.
-   Pubic ramus:  Palpable bony landmark located superiorly and laterally to the pubic symphysis.  Its relative superior or inferior position helps diagnose pubic shear dysfunctions, indicating vertical displacement at the pubic symphysis.

## Muscles influencing innominate motion

Several powerful muscles attach to the innominate bones, and their tone and action directly influence innominate position and mobility.  Imbalances in these muscles are frequent contributors to somatic dysfunctions, which are named here and discussed in further detail later in the article.

-   Hip flexors:  The iliopsoas, rectus femoris, and sartorius are primary anterior rotators of the innominate ((Figure 3)).  Hypertonicity can lead to an anterior innominate rotation dysfunction.
-   Hip extensors:  The gluteus maximus and hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris) are primary posterior rotators of the innominate ((Figure 4)), ((Figure 5)).  Hypertonicity can lead to posterior innominate rotation.  The gluteus maximus also acts as an external rotator of the hip.
-   Hip abductors:  The gluteus medius and minimus, in addition to the tensor fasciae latae, act to abduct the hip ((Figure 6)), ((Figure 7)).  Hypertonicity can lead to innominate outflares.
-   Hip adductors:  The adductor longus, brevis, and magnus adduct the hip.  Hypertonicity, especially if unilateral, can contribute to innominate inflares ((Figure 8)).
-   Abdominal muscles:  The rectus abdominis (attaching to the pubic symphysis and crest) can cause bilateral posterior innominate rotation or contribute to pubic shears if asymmetric ((Figure 9)).

# Biomechanics

## Innominate movement patterns

The innominate bones move in complex, 3-dimensional patterns primarily at the sacroiliac joints and, to a lesser extent, at the pubic symphysis.  These movements are typically described in relation to the sacrum.

-   Anterior rotation:  The ilium moves anteriorly and inferiorly.  This results in the ASIS moving inferiorly while the PSIS moves superiorly.  The ischial tuberosity moves superiorly.
-   Posterior rotation:  The ilium moves posteriorly and superiorly.  This causes the ASIS to move superiorly and the PSIS to move inferiorly.  The ischial tuberosity moves inferiorly.
-   Inflare:  The innominate rotates medially around a roughly vertical axis, bringing the ASIS closer to the midline and the ischial tuberosity further from the midline.
-   Outflare:  The innominate rotates laterally around a roughly vertical axis, moving the ASIS further from the midline and the ischial tuberosity closer to the midline.
-   Superior shear (upslip):  The entire innominate bone translates superiorly relative to the sacrum.
-   Inferior shear (downslip):  The entire innominate bone translates inferiorly relative to the sacrum (rare).

These movements are essential for normal shock absorption, load transfer, and facilitating lower limb and spinal motion.  During gait, the innominates undergo reciprocal anterior and posterior rotation.  As one leg moves into swing phase (hip flexion), that innominate rotates posteriorly.  Simultaneously, the stance leg moves into hip extension, and that innominate rotates anteriorly.

## Relationship to lumbar and sacral motion

The pelvis acts as a functional unit with the lumbar spine and sacrum.  Therefore, innominate motion is inherently linked to the mechanics of these adjacent structures.  For example, an anteriorly rotated innominate on one side can create a functional leg length discrepancy by effectively lengthening the leg (discussed in a separate article); this can lead to a compensatory sacral torsion and lumbar sidebending.  Conversely, primary lumbar or sacral dysfunctions can impose stresses on the SI joints, leading to secondary innominate dysfunctions.  For instance, lumbar scoliosis will invariably alter pelvic alignment.

# Diagnostic tests for innominate dysfunctions

Diagnosis of innominate dysfunction largely depends on a series of palpatory and motion tests.  The goal is to identify asymmetries in landmark position and restrictions in motion.

## Standing flexion test

The standing flexion test (StFT) is a key screening test for assessing iliosacral somatic dysfunction (motion of the ilium on the sacrum).

-   Procedure:  The patient stands with feet shoulder-width apart.  The physician sits or kneels behind the patient and places their thumbs inferior to and slightly medial to the PSIS bilaterally, ensuring symmetric contact.  The patient is instructed to bend forward slowly at the waist as if trying to touch their toes, keeping their knees straight.
-   Interpretation:  The physician observes the relative movement of the PSISs.  Normally, superior motion of the PSIS is minimal and symmetric.  If one PSIS moves further cranially (superiorly) than the other at the end range of forward flexion, the test is considered positive on that side.  A positive standing FT indicates excessive superior PSIS motion on one side due to an innominate dysfunction on the same side.  This restricted motion means the ilium is not moving as freely with the sacrum as it should during trunk flexion.

Positive StFTs on the right and left are demonstrated in the following images ((Figure 10)), ((Figure 11)).  The StFT should not be confused with the seated flexion test, which is abnormal in sacral (not innominate) dysfunctions.

## ASIS compression test

The ASIS compression test evaluates the integrity and springiness of the SI joints and can help identify general hypomobility or hypermobility.

-   Procedure:  The patient is supine.  The physician places the heels of the hands on the patient's ASISs, with fingers pointing cephalad or laterally.  A gentle downward (posterior) and slightly medial pressure is applied, first to one ASIS, then the other, and then both simultaneously.
-   Interpretation:  The physician assesses the amount of "spring."  Normally, spring is present and equal on both sides.  A positive test (ie, decreased spring on one side or decreased spring over the ASIS) indicates that there is an innominate dysfunction (ie, abnormal innominate position) on the same side as the positive test.  A "hard end feel," or lack of movement, suggests restriction or fixation on that side (hypomobility).  Excessive movement might suggest hypermobility or instability.  For example, a positive ASIS compression test on the left reveals a left-sided innominate dysfunction.

The ASIS compression test is shown in the following image ((Figure 12)).

## Palpation of bony landmarks for asymmetry

Careful palpation and comparison of bony landmarks bilaterally in various positions (standing, supine, and prone) are key for diagnosing innominate dysfunctions.  Once the side of innominate dysfunction is determined (eg, by a positive ASIS compression test or standing flexion test), the type of dysfunction is determined by assessing the position of the ASIS, PSIS, and pubic bones.

-   ASIS position:  The ASIS is assessed in the supine position for relative height (superior/inferior).  An ASIS that is more inferior on one side compared to the other suggests an anterior innominate rotation on that side.  Conversely, an ASIS that is more superior suggests a posterior innominate rotation.
-   ASIS-to-umbilicus distance:  Asymmetry in the distance between the ASIS and the midline (ie, umbilicus) indicates an innominate flare, in which the anterior portion of the innominate is "stuck" either in the medial (inflare) or lateral (outflare) position.  If the ASIS-to-umbilicus distance is greater on the side with a positive ASIS compression test, the diagnosis is an innominate outflare.  In contrast, if the ASIS on the side of the positive compression test is more medial (ie, the ASIS-to-umbilicus distance is shorter), the diagnosis is an innominate inflare.
-   PSIS position:  The PSIS is assessed in prone or standing position for relative height.  An inferior PSIS (with a superior ASIS) indicates a posterior innominate rotation.  Conversely, a superior PSIS (with an inferior ASIS) indicates an anterior innominate rotation.
-   Iliac crest height:  The iliac crest height is assessed with the patient standing.  Significant asymmetry can indicate a superior or inferior innominate shear (upslip/downslip) (or, as discussed in a separate article, leg length discrepancy).
-   Pubic symphysis alignment:  Pubic symphysis alignment is assessed with the patient supine.  The physician gently palpates the superior aspect of both pubic rami just lateral to the symphysis.  A difference in height suggests a superior or inferior pubic shear.

# Innominate dysfunctions

Integrating StFT, ASIS compression tests, and palpation of ASIS, PSIS, and pubic rami positions helps identify specific innominate dysfunctions: innominate rotation ((Figure 13)), innominate shear ((Figure 14)), innominate flare ((figure 12)), and pubic shear ((Figure 16)).  Associated findings and muscle energy/high-velocity low-amplitude (HVLA) techniques are discussed in the following sections.

Understanding muscle roles is essential for muscle energy treatments ((Figure 17)).  Hip flexors anteriorly rotate the innominate, increasing lumbar lordosis.  Hip extensors posteriorly rotate the innominate, reducing lordosis.  Muscle energy techniques involve postisometric relaxation, in which joints are positioned at restrictive barriers and the patient contracts against resistance.  HVLA positions joints at restrictive barriers, delivering rapid, controlled thrusts to restore alignment and mobility.

## Anterior innominate rotation

An anterior innominate rotation involves the ilium being rotated anteriorly in relation to the sacrum.

-   Etiology:  Often caused by hypertonicity of hip flexors or by activities involving forceful hip extension.
-   Test results:
    -   Standing flexion test:  Positive on the side of dysfunction.
    -   ASIS compression test:  May show increased resistance on the affected side.
-   Palpatory findings:
    -   ASIS:  Inferior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   PSIS:  Superior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Ischial tuberosity:  Relatively superior.
    -   Pubic ramus:  May be slightly inferior on the affected side.
-   Muscle energy technique ((Figure 18)):
    -   Positioning:  With the patient supine, the physician flexes the patient's hip and knee on the affected side to approximately 90 degrees.  The physician then further flexes the hip, effectively using the patient's femur as a lever to engage the posterior rotation barrier of the innominate.
    -   Activation:  The patient is instructed to gently extend the hip (push the thigh/knee towards the table or into the physician's stabilizing hand/shoulder) against the physician's isometric counterforce for 3-5 seconds.
    -   Correction:  After relaxation, the physician gently moves the innominate further into posterior rotation by increasing hip flexion, taking up the slack to the new barrier.  This is repeated 3-5 times.

## Posterior innominate rotation

A posterior innominate rotation occurs when the ilium rotates posteriorly.

-   Etiology:  Often associated with hypertonicity of hip extensors or with activities involving sudden hip flexion or lifting with knees straight.
-   Test results:
    -   Standing flexion test:  Positive on the side of dysfunction.
    -   ASIS compression test:  May show increased resistance on the affected side.
-   Palpatory findings:
    -   ASIS:  Superior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   PSIS:  Inferior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Ischial tuberosity:  Relatively inferior and potentially more prominent.
    -   Pubic ramus:  May be slightly superior on the affected side.
-   Muscle energy technique ((Figure 19)):
    -   Positioning:  With the patient lying supine and the affected leg hanging off the side of the table in extension to engage the anterior rotation barrier, the contralateral hip and knee are flexed and held by the patient to stabilize the lumbar spine and contralateral pelvis.
    -   Activation:  The patient is instructed to gently flex the hip (lift the straight leg towards the ceiling) against the physician's isometric counterforce applied to the anterior thigh for 3-5 seconds.
    -   Correction:  After relaxation, the physician gently encourages further hip extension, moving the innominate further into anterior rotation.

## Superior innominate shear

A superior innominate shear (upslip) involves superior displacement of the entire innominate relative to the sacrum.

-   Etiology:  Typically traumatic, such as a fall onto an ischial tuberosity, landing hard on one leg, or a sudden upward thrust through the leg.
-   Test results:
    -   Standing flexion test:  Positive on the side of dysfunction.
    -   ASIS compression test:  Often markedly restricted.
-   Palpatory findings:
    -   ASIS:  Superior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   PSIS:  Superior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Iliac crest:  Superior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Ischial tuberosity:  Superior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Pubic ramus:  Superior on the side of dysfunction.
-   HVLA technique ((Figure 20)):
    -   The physician flexes the patient's leg at the hip/knee before applying caudad traction to the ankle for 3-5 breaths.  Then, a rapid, short pulling force is applied at the end of exhalation.

## Inferior innominate shear

An inferior innominate shear involves inferior displacement of the entire innominate relative to the sacrum.  It is much less common than an upslip.

-   Etiology:  May result from a strong traction force on the leg in which the leg is pulled downwards, such as stepping into a hole unexpectedly.
-   Test results:
    -   Standing flexion test:  Positive on the side of dysfunction.
    -   ASIS compression test:  Often markedly restricted.
-   Palpatory findings:
    -   ASIS:  Inferior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   PSIS:  Inferior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Iliac crest:  Inferior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Ischial tuberosity:  Inferior on the side of dysfunction.
    -   Pubic ramus:  Inferior on the side of dysfunction.
-   HVLA technique:
    -   With the patient positioned laterally or supine, the physician grasps the affected leg above the ankle.  After abducting the leg slightly, a rapid, superiorly directed thrust is applied through the leg at the end of exhalation to reduce the inferior displacement.

## Innominate inflare

An inflare describes a medial rotation of the innominate in the transverse plane around a vertical axis, where the ASIS moves medially.

-   Etiology:  Often associated with muscle imbalances, such as hypertonic hip adductors or internal rotators, or occurs as compensation for lower extremity issues.
-   Test results:  Positive StFT on the affected side and positive ASIS compression test.
-   Palpatory findings:
    -   ASIS:  More medial (closer to the umbilicus) on the affected side.
    -   PSIS and ischial tuberosity:  More lateral.
-   Muscle energy technique ((Figure 21)):
    -   Positioning:  With the patient lying supine and the hip and knee on the affected side flexed to 90 degrees, the physician abducts the hip to engage the inflare barrier (resistance to further outflare).
    -   Activation:  The patient is instructed to gently adduct the hip (bring the knee toward the midline) against the physician's isometric counterforce for 3-5 seconds.
    -   Correction:  After relaxation, the physician gently moves the hip further into abduction, correcting the inflare.

## Innominate outflare

An outflare describes a lateral rotation of the innominate in the transverse plane, where the ASIS moves laterally.

-   Etiology:  Often results from hypertonic hip abductors (like gluteus medius/minimus) or external rotators, or occurs as compensation for lower extremity mechanics (eg, genu valgum).
-   Test results:  Positive StFT on the affected side and positive ASIS compression test.
-   Palpatory findings:
    -   ASIS:  More lateral (further from the umbilicus) on the affected side.
    -   PSIS and ischial tuberosity:  More medial.
-   Muscle energy technique ((Figure 22)):
    -   Positioning:  With the patient lying supine and the hip and knee on the affected side flexed to 90 degrees, the physician adducts the hip to engage the outflare barrier (resistance to further inflare).
    -   Activation:  The patient is instructed to gently abduct the hip (bring the knee away from the midline) against the physician's isometric counterforce for 3-5 seconds.
    -   Correction:  After relaxation, the physician gently moves the hip further into adduction, correcting the outflare.

## Pubic shears

Pubic shear dysfunctions involve vertical displacement (superior or inferior) of one pubic ramus relative to the other at the pubic symphysis.  Compression or gapping can also occur but are not commonly described as primary shears.

-   Etiology:  Can result from muscle imbalances (eg, rectus abdominis, adductors), trauma, or childbirth.  Often associated with other innominate dysfunctions like upslips or rotations.
-   Test results:  Direct palpation is the primary diagnostic method.  StFT may be positive if it is linked to a larger innominate dysfunction.
-   Palpatory findings:
    -   Superior pubic shear:  The superior aspect of one pubic ramus, just lateral to the symphysis, is palpated superiorly to the contralateral side.
    -   Inferior pubic shear:  One pubic ramus is palpated inferiorly.
-   Muscle energy techniques:
    -   Superior pubic shear:  While lying supine with the affected hip flexed, the patient is instructed to gently extend the hip (push the thigh towards the table) against the physician's isometric counterforce for 3-5 seconds.  After relaxation, the physician gently moves the innominate further into posterior rotation by increasing hip flexion (which also encourages inferior movement of the pubis).
    -   Inferior pubic shear:  While lying supine with the affected hip extended off the table, the patient is instructed to gently flex the hip (lift the leg towards the ceiling) against the physician's isometric counterforce for 3-5 seconds.  After relaxation, the physician gently moves the hip further into extension, which encourages anterior innominate rotation and can help draw the inferior pubis superiorly.

# Summary

Innominate somatic dysfunctions affect the alignment and mobility of the ilium, ischium, and pubis.  A detailed understanding of pelvic landmarks, such as the anterior superior iliac spine, posterior superior iliac spine, iliac crests, and pubic symphysis, is important for accurate diagnosis.  The biomechanics of innominate motion—including anterior/posterior rotations, inflares/outflares, and superior/inferior shears—are intricately linked to sacral and lumbar mechanics, influencing gait and posture.  Diagnosis is achieved through a combination of the standing flexion test and anterior superior iliac spine compression test, in addition to precise palpation of bony asymmetries.  Diagnostic algorithms for innominate rotations/shears and innominate flares/pubic shears are provided in the following flowcharts for reference ((Figure 23)), ((Figure 24)).

Common dysfunctions include anterior and posterior innominate rotations, superior shears (upslips), inflares, outflares, and pubic shears, each with characteristic palpatory findings and clinical presentations.  Osteopathic manipulative treatment involves muscle energy techniques and high-velocity low-amplitude thrusts to restore normal innominate biomechanics.

​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌

articles.markdown:
# Osteopathic Manipulative Treatment: Cervical Spine # Introduction Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) addresses cervical spine dysfunction by alleviating neck pain, improving mobility, and optimizing biomechanic function.  This article discusses cervical anatomy and biomechanics, cervical disorders, somatic dysfunctions, and various OMT techniques. # Cervical spine anatomy and biomechanics ## Cervical vertebrae The cervical spine is composed of 7 vertebrae **(C1-C7)** with distinctive anatomic features that collectively enable extensive rotation, flexion, extension, and sidebending.  A characteristic cervical **lordosis** (ie, a natural forward curve) provides shock absorption and supports head positioning.  This curvature is maintained by the interaction of vertebral shapes, intervertebral discs, muscular tone, and ligaments (eg, alar and transverse ligaments).  Ligamentous integrity is compromised in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome, increasing the risk for cervical instability and resulting neurologic consequences. Compared to vertebrae in other spinal regions, the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae are positioned more anteriorly, making them difficult to palpate directly.  As a result, osteopathic palpation is performed on the **articular pillars**, which include the articular processes and their connecting structures ((Figure 1)). The upper cervical spine includes 2 unique vertebrae: - **Atlas** (C1):  A ring-shaped vertebra that lacks a vertebral body and supports the skull.  It articulates superiorly with the occipital condyles of the skull at the occipitoatlantal (OA) joint and inferiorly with C2. - **Axis** (C2):  Distinguished by the odontoid process (dens), which projects upward and fits into the anterior arch of C1, forming the atlantoaxial (AA) joint. ## Cervical joint motion The joints of the cervical spine are listed below.  These joints follow distinct mechanical patterns ((Table 1)) that **do not obey the spinal laws of motion (Fryette)**, which apply to thoracic and lumbar spinal mechanics ((Figure 2)): - **OA joint**:  Formed between the occipital condyles and the superior articular facets of C1.  Primarily allows **flexion and extension** (nodding motion), accounting for half of the neck's flexion and extension.  **Sidebending and rotation occur in opposite directions** in both neutral and nonneutral (flexion and extension) dysfunctions (ie, **O**pposite **A**lways). - **AA joint**:  Formed between the dens of C2 and the anterior arch of C1, along with paired lateral facets.  Responsible for approximately **50% of total cervical rotation** (the remaining cervical rotation is spread throughout the lower vertebrae).  Sidebending, flexion, and extension are insignificant. - **C2-C7**:  Contain **facet joints** that are oriented **superiorly** and **posteriorly** at 45 degrees, allowing extensive **sidebending** and **rotation** in the **same direction** (in both neutral and nonneutral dysfunctions).  These vertebrae feature uncovertebral joints (Luschka joints), which are formed by the articulation of uncinate processes and provide additional stability and control of lateral movements. ## Muscular and neurologic structures The following muscles are major contributors to cervical motion and stability:: - **Scalenes (anterior, middle, and posterior)**:  These muscles originate from the cervical transverse processes and insert on the first two ribs.  They serve as accessory muscles of respiration and assist with neck flexion and sidebending. - **Sternocleidomastoid**:  This muscle originates from the sternum and clavicle and inserts on the mastoid process.  It flexes the neck when acting bilaterally and rotates the head to the opposite side when acting unilaterally. - **Suboccipital muscles**:  These deep muscles include the rectus capitis posterior major and minor and obliquus capitis superior and inferior, which fine-tune head positioning and proprioception. The cervical spine includes **8 cervical nerve roots**.  The upper 7 cervical nerves **exit superiorly to their corresponding vertebrae**, whereas the eighth cervical nerve root exits between the C7 and T1 vertebrae.  The cervical nerve roots C5-T1 contribute significantly to the brachial plexus, a complex network of nerves supplying the upper limb.  The cervical nerves are further discussed later. The **vagus nerve** (CN X) provides **parasympathetic** innervation originating from the medulla oblongata, descending through the **OA joint region to the C2** vertebral level.  This innervation regulates **visceral functions**, particularly involving the heart, lungs, and upper and middle gastrointestinal tract ((Table 2)).  Visceral autonomic innervation is discussed extensively in a separate article. # Cervical spine disorders ## Cervical disc herniation and radiculopathy Cervical disc herniation typically occurs at C5-C6 and C6-C7 levels, where disc protrusion compresses cervical nerve roots exiting above their corresponding vertebrae.  Symptoms include radiating arm pain, sensory disturbances, and weakness corresponding to the affected dermatomes ((Table 3)). Diagnostic tests include the Spurling test (positive when axial compression combined with head rotation reproduces symptoms) and cervical distraction (positive when traction produces symptom relief). ## Cervical facet syndrome Cervical facet syndrome involves inflammation and pain at facet joints, typically due to trauma, degenerative changes, or posture-related stress.  Symptoms include localized neck pain exacerbated by extension and rotation. ## Cervical spinal stenosis Cervical spinal stenosis involves narrowing of the cervical spinal canal or intervertebral foramina, leading to nerve root or spinal cord compression.  Symptoms include neck pain, radiculopathy, myelopathy, gait disturbances, and upper extremity weakness.  Flexion typically alleviates symptoms, whereas extension exacerbates them. ## Whiplash injury Whiplash results from rapid flexion-extension injury, causing soft-tissue damage, muscle strain, ligamentous sprain, facet dysfunction, and somatic dysfunctions.  Symptoms include neck pain, headache, stiffness, and possible neurologic signs. # Vertebral somatic dysfunctions Cervical vertebral somatic dysfunction involves restricted vertebral movements.  Palpation of the articular pillars allows assessment of rotational components of dysfunction (as opposed to palpation of transverse processes in lumbar and thoracic vertebrae). The diagnosis of upper cervical somatic dysfunctions involves identifying restrictions at the AA and OA joints.  Common OMT modalities include direct muscle energy and high-velocity, low-amplitude (HVLA), both involving positioning the head and neck against the restrictive barrier and applying postisometric relaxation (muscle energy) or a thrust (HVLA) through the barrier.  Cervical HVLA is contraindicated in patients with vertebrobasilar insufficiency (due to risk for ischemic stroke) and in cases of ligamentous instability in patients with severe rheumatoid arthritis or Down syndrome (due to risk for spinal cord trauma). ## Occipitoatlantal dysfunction To diagnose OA joint dysfunction, the physician presses anteriorly on the occiput where it articulates with C1.  If there is restriction in right rotation, the possible diagnoses include posterior occiput left and anterior occiput right.  **Tenderness** is used to distinguish between these 2 diagnoses ((Table 4)): - **Posterior occiput right**:  Tenderness greater on the right. - **Anterior occiput left**:  Tenderness greater on the left. ## Atlantoaxial dysfunction To diagnose AA joint dysfunction, the physician presses anteriorly on the articular pillar of C1.  For example, if there is restriction of left rotation (right articular pillar more posterior), then the atlas is rotated right.  Given that this finding could indicate either the right atlas being more posterior or the left atlas being more anterior, the presence of tenderness identifies the dysfunctional side ((Table 5)): - **Posterior atlas right**:  Tenderness on the right articular pillar. - **Anterior atlas left**:  Tenderness on the left articular pillar. The opposite applies for restriction of right rotation (ie, posterior atlas left vs anterior atlas right). ## C2-C7 dysfunctions Diagnosis of C2-C7 dysfunctions is more straightforward than that of OA and AA dysfunctions.  Instead of pressing anteriorly on the articular pillars, the physician exerts a lateral translational force to determine movement.  Lateral translation to the left (ie, left translation) produces right sidebending, whereas right translation produces left sidebending.  Therefore: - Restriction in translation to the left indicates right sidebending (and rotation). - Restriction in translation to the right indicates left sidebending (and rotation). For example, a restriction in translation of C3 to the right (indicating sidebent right) worsening with flexion indicates C3 is extended, rotated right, and sidebent right (ERRSR). # Nonvertebral somatic dysfunctions ## Tender points Tender points in the cervical region arise from dysfunctional neuromuscular reflexes due to strain, injury, or chronic dysfunction.  Common locations include: - Suboccipital muscles:  Often associated with tension headaches. - Upper trapezius:  Related to stress and poor ergonomics. - Levator scapulae insertion:  Often associated with prolonged computer use. - Scalenes:  Can refer pain down the arm, mimicking radiculopathy. Treatment is counterstrain, which involves placing the patient in a position of ease to diminish tenderness and reflexive muscle tension.  Counterstrain is discussed in detail in a separate article. ## Somatosomatic reflexes Chronic sensory input from cervical somatic dysfunction or injury can result in persistent hypertonicity, tenderness, and vertebral immobility.  Coexisting thoracic and rib somatic dysfunctions should be addressed first because they can manifest as suboccipital or cervical paravertebral hypertonicity.  Targeted therapy to the cervical spine can be performed afterward.  Techniques such as facilitated positional release, direct inhibitory pressure, and counterstrain are effective in normalizing contributing abnormal reflex loops. ## Viscerosomatic reflexes Cervical somatic dysfunctions may reflect underlying visceral pathologies, particularly upper respiratory, cardiac, or gastrointestinal conditions, via viscerosomatic reflexes.  For example, the **vagus nerve** exits the cranium via the jugular foramen and travels posterior to the occipital condyles before reaching various target tissues.  Somatic dysfunction of the OA and AA joints can impair its normal function.  A commonly used OMT technique is **suboccipital release**, a form of myofascial release that restores optimal function of the vagus nerve.  The technique is performed as follows: 1. The physician is seated at the head of table with the patient supine. 2. The occiput is cradled, with fingertips contacting suboccipital muscles. 3. Gentle superior traction is applied to the occiput with fingertips. 4. This position is held for 90-120 seconds while tissue softens. 5. Gentle occipital decompression can be applied. In addition, suboccipital release can be performed in the absence of OA dysfunction (eg, for tension headaches). # Summary The cervical spine (C1-C7) is characterized by anteriorly positioned transverse processes, necessitating palpation of the articular pillars for diagnosing somatic dysfunctions.  The laws of spinal motion (Fryette) do not apply to cervical vertebrae.  The occipitoatlantal joint primarily allows flexion and extension, with rotation and sidebending in opposite directions (Opposite Always) in both neutral and nonneutral dysfunctions, whereas the atlantoaxial joint predominantly permits rotation.  Accurate diagnosis of somatic dysfunction at the occipitoatlantal and atlantoaxial levels relies heavily on identifying tenderness at the involved articular pillars to distinguish anterior from posterior vertebral dysfunction.  From C2-C7, facet joints oriented at 45 degrees facilitate coupled sidebending and rotation in the same direction.  C2-C7 dysfunctions are diagnosed via lateral translational testing: restriction in left translation implies right sidebending and rotation. ​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​
