articles.title: Cranial Osteopathy
articles.markdown: # Cranial Osteopathy # Introduction Cranial osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) uses gentle manual techniques to influence the motion of cranial bones, dural membranes, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fluctuation, and the sacrum.  An understanding of the mechanics of the **sphenobasilar synchondrosis (SBS)** and the craniosacral cycle is important.  This article explores cranial mechanics, the diagnosis of SBS dysfunctions, and cranial OMT techniques. # The SBS and the craniosacral cycle The SBS is the junction of the sphenoid with the basilar part of the occipital bone at the cranial base and allows for extremely subtle movements during the craniosacral cycle.  The sacral base (upper sacrum) is linked to the SBS via a continuous layer of dura that extends along the spinal canal.  Biomechanical forces generated by the inherent motion of the brain and spinal cord cause rhythmic movement of the dura and CSF (ie, **cranial rhythmic impulse** \[CRI\]).  These forces are transmitted between the cranium and sacrum, resulting in craniosacral flexion and extension. During **craniosacral flexion**, the SBS moves cephalad (superiorly), producing the following effects ((figure 1)): - The spinal dura is pulled upward.  Because the dura is attached to the sacral base, the **sacrum counternutates** (rotates backward), resulting in **posterior** movement of the **sacral base**. - The temporal and parietal bones (paired bones) externally rotate.  This decreases the anteroposterior (AP) diameter and increases the transverse diameter of the cranium, resulting in "shortening and widening" of the head. During **craniosacral extension**, the SBS moves caudad (inferiorly), producing the following effects ((Figure 2)): - The spinal dura is pushed downward.  Because the dura is attached to the sacral base, the **sacrum nutates** (rotates forward), resulting in **anterior** movement of the sacral base. - The temporal and parietal bones (paired bones) internally rotate.  This increases the AP diameter and decreases the transverse diameter of the cranium, resulting in "lengthening and narrowing" of the head. # Cranial vault hold The cranial vault hold is a technique used to diagnose dysfunctions at the SBS.  It involves specific hand contacts that allow evaluation of inherent cranial mobility and alterations in the CRI.  The cranial vault hold is performed as follows: 1. The patient lies supine with the physician seated at the head of the table. 2. The physician cradles the patient's head with both hands. 3. The fingers are spread to contact specific areas of the cranium: - The **little fingers** rest along the **occipital** base. - The ring fingers contact the temporal bones at the mastoid processes. - The middle fingers rest on the temporal bone in front of the ear. - The **index fingers** rest at the **greater wings of the sphenoid**. 4. The physician then carefully feels for subtle motion patterns. # SBS dysfunction The cranial vault hold is used to diagnose SBS dysfunctions, both symmetric (flexion, extension) and asymmetric (sidebending/rotation, vertical strain, lateral strain, compression). ## Flexion and extension dysfunctions Flexion and extension dysfunctions are characterized by disruption of normal craniosacral flexion and extension where 1 of these movements is limited.  This occurs due to impaired SBS movement about the **transverse axis**.  Because craniosacral flexion and extension are linked to sacral movement, sacral changes are also noted on palpation.  Findings include: - **Flexion dysfunction**:  The sphenoid and occiput move **cephalad** (superiorly).  The head remains shortened and widened.  Bilaterally **shallow sacral sulci** are present. - **Extension dysfunction**:  The sphenoid and occiput move **caudad** (inferiorly).  The head remains lengthened and narrowed.  Bilaterally **deep sacral sulci** are present. ## Torsion dysfunction Torsion dysfunction is characterized by twisting of the sphenoid and occiput as they **rotate in opposite** directions about the AP axis.  As a result, 1 side of the sphenoid moves superiorly while the other side moves inferiorly.  Diagnostic nomenclature is based on the movement of the **greater wing** of the sphenoid ((Figure 3)).  During the vault hold, the **index finger elevates** while the **little finger depresses** on the side of torsion.  Elevation of the right greater wing indicates right torsion, whereas elevation of the left greater wing indicates left torsion. ## Sidebending/rotation dysfunction Sidebending/rotation dysfunction involves simultaneous, coupled movements of the sphenoid and occiput that: - **Sidebend away** from each other (due to rotation in the same direction about 2 vertical axes). - **Rotate in the same direction** (due to rotation in the same direction about the AP axis). Diagnosis is made based on the side of convexity (fullness and widening) during the vault hold, with the side of fullness indicating the side of dysfunction.  Left sidebending/rotation dysfunction is characterized by a more inferior occiput and more inferior greater wing of the sphenoid on the left ((Figure 4)).  Right sidebending/rotation dysfunction involves the opposite pattern. ## Vertical strain Vertical strains occur when the sphenoid and occiput move in **opposite vertical directions**.  This occurs when these structures **rotate in the same direction** about 2 transverse axes ((Figure 5)).  In a superior vertical strain, the sphenoid moves superiorly relative to the occiput; in an inferior vertical strain, the sphenoid moves inferiorly.  On cranial vault examination, the index and little fingers move in opposite directions vertically. ## Lateral strain Lateral strains occur when the sphenoid and occiput move in **opposite lateral directions**.  This occurs when these structures **rotate in the same direction** about 2 vertical axes ((Figure 6)).  In a right lateral strain, the sphenoid moves to the right relative to the occiput; in a left lateral strain, the sphenoid moves to the left.  On cranial vault examination, the head feels shaped like a parallelogram (ie, one of the physician's arms pronates while the other supinates). ## Compression Compression of the SBS occurs when the sphenoid and occiput are pushed together (typically following **trauma**) along the AP axis.  This eliminates normal flexion, extension, and torsion motion ((Figure 7)).  The head feels dense and rigid under the hands, often with a significant **decrease in CRI amplitude and/or frequency**. # Diagnostic algorithms Applying the algorithms in the following flowcharts can aid in diagnosis ((Figure 8)), ((Figure 9)), ((Figure 10)). # Cranial osteopathic techniques ## Compression of the fourth ventricle Compression of the fourth ventricle (CV4) is performed by gently cradling the occiput with the thenar eminences while allowing the fingers to rest lightly along the sides of the cranium.  The physician applies **gentle medial and upward pressure** toward the foramen magnum, encouraging a still point—a palpable cessation of the CRI—followed by a softening and return of normal motion.  CV4 is commonly utilized to help reduce sympathetic overactivity, **promote parasympathetic tone**, and facilitate overall autonomic balance. It is often indicated for patients experiencing headaches, stress, or insomnia, and after significant trauma such as childbirth.  By influencing CSF flow and enhancing the craniosacral rhythm, CV4 may support CNS homeostasis and improve systemic health.  In neonates and infants, CV4 may also be employed to promote calming and assist in conditions related to nervous system dysregulation. ## V-spread technique V-spread is performed by placing two fingers in a V shape over a cranial suture while applying gentle pressure at a distant point with the opposite hand to **encourage suture release**.  Micromovements are induced to restore physiologic motion between cranial bones. It is commonly used to treat suture dysfunctions from trauma, birth, or mechanical compression.  V-spread enhances venous and lymphatic drainage and can help with sinus congestion, cranial nerve entrapments, and facial pain.  It is particularly effective in infants due to their flexible cranial sutures. ## Occipital condyle decompression Occipital condyle decompression is performed by gently cradling the occiput with the index fingers while supporting the patient's head in a supine position.  Gentle **lateral and cephalad pressure** is applied along the condyles until a softening or release of tension is palpated.  This technique is particularly indicated in neonates who exhibit **difficulty latching** during breastfeeding (after ruling out anatomic causes such as cleft palate, cleft lip, or maternal nipple inversion). During the birth process, compressive forces on the occiput may distort the condyles, leading to functional impairments of the cranial nerves that exit through the hypoglossal canal and jugular foramen.  Dysfunction can affect: - The **hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)**:  Impaired tongue movement. - The glossopharyngeal (CN IX) and vagus (CN X) nerves:  Impaired swallowing, gag reflex, and autonomic regulation. ## Venous sinus drainage Venous sinus drainage is performed by sequentially applying gentle traction and pressure over key cranial sutures and sinus regions (occipital, transverse, straight, sagittal, and cavernous sinuses) to **enhance venous outflow from the cranium**. Indications include cranial congestion, headache, chronic sinusitis, and posttraumatic brain injuries.  By promoting venous drainage, this technique can reduce intracranial pressure, improve cerebral perfusion, and facilitate overall cranial homeostasis.  It is also beneficial in neonates after complicated deliveries where cranial molding may impair venous return. ## Temporal rocking Temporal rocking is performed by placing the fingertips lightly over the squamous portions of the temporal bones and applying gentle alternating pressure to encourage balanced motion.  The physician follows the natural external and internal rotation of the bones without forcing movement. This technique is used to address **dysfunctions affecting the middle and inner ear** (eg, tinnitus, vertigo, eustachian tube dysfunction).  In infants, temporal rocking can help correct compressive birth forces impacting the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) and improve middle ear drainage, reducing the risk of otitis media. # Summary Cranial osteopathy is a specialized form of osteopathic manipulative treatment used to influence cranial bone motion, dural tension, cerebrospinal fluid flow, and sacral dynamics via the sphenobasilar synchondrosis.  At the core of cranial mechanics is the craniosacral cycle, wherein rhythmic pulsations from the brain and spinal cord generate coordinated movements in the cranium and sacrum, detectable as the cranial rhythmic impulse.  The cranial vault hold is the key diagnostic technique used to assess sphenobasilar synchondrosis mobility and identify dysfunctions—categorized as flexion/extension, torsion, sidebending/rotation, vertical strain, lateral strain, or compression—based on bone movement patterns and changes in cranial rhythmic impulse. Treatment methods include compression of the fourth ventricle (to restore autonomic balance), V-spread (to improve suture mobility and drainage), occipital condyle decompression (to relieve cranial nerve dysfunction in infants), venous sinus drainage (to enhance intracranial circulation), and temporal rocking (to support auditory and vestibular health).  These techniques are especially beneficial in neonates and individuals with cranial trauma, nervous system imbalance, or cranial nerve impairments, with the goal of restoring physiologic motion and systemic equilibrium. ​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​

articles.title: Chapman Points
articles.markdown: # Chapman Points # Introduction Chapman points are small, palpable, tender nodules located in specific anatomic regions, representing reflexes linked to visceral dysfunction.  These points may be helpful in osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) as diagnostic and therapeutic indicators.  Understanding and effectively addressing Chapman points can support visceral diagnoses.  This article details the anatomic distribution, diagnostic significance, and therapeutic approaches to Chapman points throughout the body. # Pathophysiology Chapman points are characteristically discrete, **firm** nodules approximately **2-3 mm** in diameter.  Typically located within the deep fascial layers, periosteum of bones, tendinous attachments, or subcutaneous tissue, these points reflect **viscerosomatic reflexes** mediated primarily by the sympathetic nervous system.  Dysfunction or pathology in a visceral organ leads to localized lymphatic congestion and increased fascial tension, manifesting as **exquisitely tender** nodules in corresponding anatomic areas. # Location of Chapman points In general, each organ has an **anterior** ((Figure 1)) and a **posterior** ((Figure 2)) Chapman point.  The anterior Chapman points for the colon can be visualized by "dividing" it midway through the transverse colon and allowing it to "fall" and overlay over the iliotibial bands ((Figure 3)). The following sections list the Chapman points for various regions of the body.  Minor variations exist between sources, occasionally differing by one segmental level (eg, T1 vs T2).  For clinical and examination purposes, such precise differentiation is generally not required ((Figure 4)). # Head and neck ## Sinuses - Anterior:  Midclavicle. - Posterior:  C2. ## Tonsils - Anterior:  Between ribs 1 and 2 near sternum. - Posterior:  C1 posterior arch. ## Middle ear - Anterior:  Superior clavicle at crossing of first rib. - Posterior:  C1. # Thorax ## Esophagus/thyroid/bronchi - Anterior:  Second to third intercostal space (ICS) near sternum. - Posterior:  T2. ## Heart - Anterior:  Second to third ICS near sternum (left side). - Posterior:  Between T2 and T3 (left transverse processes \[TPs\]). ## Bronchi - Anterior:  Second ICS near sternum. - Posterior:  T2. ## Lungs - Anterior:  Third to fourth ICS (upper lungs) and fourth to fifth ICS near sternum. - Posterior:  T3-T4 (upper) and T4-T5 (lower). # Gastrointestinal tract ## Stomach - Anterior:  Fifth to seventh ICS on left. - Posterior:  T5-T7 on left. ## Liver and gallbladder - Anterior:  Fifth to seventh ICS on right. - Posterior:  T5-T7 on right. ## Spleen - Anterior:  Ribs 7-8 (left) at costochondral junction (CCJ). - Posterior:  T7-T8 on left. ## Pancreas - Anterior:  Ribs 7-8 (right) at CCJ. - Posterior:  T7-T8 on right. ## Small intestine - Anterior:  Near the CCJ, ribs 8-9 (duodenum), ribs 9-10 (jejunum), ribs 10-11 (ileum). - Posterior:  T8-T9 (duodenum), T9-T10 (jejunum), T10-T11 (ileum). ## Appendix - Anterior:  Tip of the right twelfth rib. - Posterior:  Right T11-T12 TP. ## Colon - Anterior:  Iliotibial bands (mapped along pattern of colon). - Posterior:  L2-L4 TP. # Genitourinary ## Kidneys - Anterior:  1 inch lateral and 1 inch superior to umbilicus. - Posterior:  T12-L1. ## Adrenal glands - Anterior:  2 inches superior and 1 inch lateral to umbilicus. - Posterior:  T11-T12. ## Bladder - Anterior:  Periumbilical region. - Posterior:  L2. ## Urethra - Anterior:  Pubic symphysis. - Posterior:  L3. ## Prostate - Anterior:  Lateral femur along the posterior iliotibial band. - Posterior:  Between L5 TP and posterior superior iliac spine. ## Ovaries/testes - Anterior:  Pubic symphysis/anterior pubic bone. - Posterior:  T9-T11. ## Uterus - Anterior:  Medial edge of obturator foramen. - Posterior:  L5. # Therapeutic applications Integrating Chapman points into clinical practice enhances diagnostic clarity and therapeutic precision.  Using these points as part of a comprehensive osteopathic examination facilitates early detection and management of visceral dysfunction.  Effective management of Chapman points involves a gentle, rotary stimulation technique directly applied to the identified nodule.  This treatment aims to: - Alleviate tenderness. - Decrease lymphatic congestion. - Normalize sympathetic nervous system function. The therapeutic steps include: 1. Precise palpation and identification of the Chapman point. 2. Application of gentle rotary pressure using fingertip pads for 10-30 seconds. 3. Reassessment posttreatment for reduced tenderness and decreased nodule size. Chapman point therapy synergistically complements other OMT techniques, including myofascial release, lymphatic pump techniques, and muscle energy treatments. # Summary Chapman points are small, palpable nodules associated with viscerosomatic reflexes that serve both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes in osteopathic manipulative treatment.  Located in predictable anterior and posterior anatomic regions, these 2- to 3-mm, tender nodules reflect dysfunction in visceral organs through the sympathetic nervous system, often due to lymphatic congestion and fascial tension.  Their precise locations correspond to various systems—including respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary—enhancing diagnostic accuracy for visceral dysfunction.  In addition to treating the associated underlying medical condition, Chapman points are managed using gentle rotary pressure, which helps reduce tenderness, restore autonomic balance, and improve lymphatic flow. ​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​

articles.title: Visual Pathway
articles.markdown: # Visual Pathway # Introduction The visual pathway is the neural system responsible for transmitting visual information from the retina to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe.  It is essential for the perception of form, color, motion, and spatial orientation.  Visual processing begins with optical refraction by the cornea and lens, followed by the conversion of light into electrical signals by the retinal photoreceptors.  These signals are then relayed through a series of precisely organized neural structures, including the optic nerves, optic chiasm, optic tracts, lateral geniculate nuclei, optic radiations, and, finally, the visual cortex. # The eye ## Refraction of light Refraction is the bending of light as it passes through media of different optical densities.  It is essential for vision because it allows incoming light rays, which enter the eye from various angles, to be focused precisely onto the retina.  A sharp image is formed only when light converges accurately on the retinal photoreceptors, particularly in the fovea centralis.  Without proper refraction, light scatters and is improperly focused, resulting in a blurred image. The eye has several structures that bend and focus light onto the retina ((Figure 1)): - **Cornea**:  The eye's first and most powerful refractive surface, the cornea is the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye, which has a fixed curvature and contributes approximately 70% of the eye's total refractive power. - **Aqueous humor**:  This clear fluid within the anterior chamber contributes minimally to refraction but helps transmit light between the cornea and lens. - **Lens**:  The second major refractive structure of the eye, the lens has an adjustable curvature that allows for accommodation, the process by which the lens changes its shape to focus on objects at varying distances. - **Near vision**:  Ciliary muscle contracts → zonular fibers relax → lens thickens and becomes more convex → increases refractive power for focusing on near objects. - **Distance vision**:  Ciliary muscle relaxes → zonular fibers tighten → lens flattens → decreases refractive power for distant objects. After light passes through the lens and vitreous compartment, the image created on the retina is inverted and reversed ((Figure 2)).  This means that the temporal (lateral) retinas process images from the nasal (medial) visual field, and the nasal retinas process images from the temporal visual field. ## Refractive errors Visual impairments due to refractive errors include: - **Myopia (nearsightedness)** ((Figure 3)):  Light focuses in front of the retina, causing poor distance vision. - **Hyperopia (farsightedness)** ((Figure 4)):  Light focuses behind the retina, causing poor near vision. - **Astigmatism** ((Figure 5)):  Irregular curvature of the cornea or lens leads to a distorted, blurred image. - **Presbyopia:**  Age-related loss of lens elasticity results in impaired accommodation, especially for near focus (eg, reading). # The retina ## The neural sensor Located at the back of the eye, the retina converts light into electrical signals that are then sent to the brain via the optic nerve.  It contains layers of specialized cells that sequentially process visual information ((Figure 6)). - **Photoreceptors**:  Located in the outermost layer of the retina, photoreceptors hyperpolarize in response to light and modulate downstream neurons. - **Rods**:  Highly sensitive to light; provide night vision and low-resolution, monochromatic (no color) vision.  Rods are concentrated in the peripheral retina. - **Cones**:  Enable daytime and color vision (red, green, blue); responsible for high visual acuity.  Cones are concentrated in the fovea centralis. - **Bipolar cells**:  Transmit signals from photoreceptors to ganglion cells. - **Ganglion cells**:  Receive input from bipolar cells and generate action potentials.  Axons of ganglion cells form the optic nerve. - **Horizontal and amacrine cells**:  Modulate and integrate signals to enhance contrast, motion detection, and spatial resolution. ## Special regions of the retina - **Macula lutea**:  The central area of the retina with a high density of cones; specialized for high-acuity central vision. - **Fovea centralis**:  The center of the macula; a cone-only region with the sharpest visual resolution. - **Optic disc**:  Site where ganglion cell axons converge to form the optic nerve; no rods or cones are present, resulting in a physiologic "blind spot" ((Figure 7)). ## Retinal pathology - **Central retinal artery occlusion**:  Reduction or complete cessation of retinal perfusion leads to retinal ischemia and the sudden onset of painless monocular vision loss. - **Age-related macular degeneration**:  Progressive loss of central vision impairs reading and facial recognition; peripheral vision is preserved. - **Retinal detachment**:  Separation of the neurosensory retina (eg, photoreceptors) from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium (which provides oxygen and nutrients) impairs the function of retinal cells, often presenting with flashes of light and floaters.  It can lead to permanent photoreceptor degeneration and vision loss if not corrected. # Neural visual pathway Neural signals travel along the following visual pathway:  Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tracts → lateral geniculate nucleus → optic radiations → primary visual cortex ((Figure 8)).  Lesions along this pathway produce various types of visual deficits based on the location and the nerve fibers that are affected. ## Optic nerve (CN II) - Formed by retinal ganglion cell axons.  Lesions in the optic nerve (eg, central retinal artery occlusion, optic neuritis) cause **monocular blindness (anopia)** ((Figure 9)). ## Optic chiasm - Fibers from the nasal half of the retina (which process the temporal visual field) cross at the optic chiasm, but the temporal retinal fibers (which process the nasal visual fields) remain ipsilateral.  The hemivisual fields of each eye are processed on the contralateral side of the brain (eg, left visual field of the left and right eye is processed in the right hemisphere) ((Figure 10)). - Lesions at the optic chiasm (eg, compression by a pituitary adenoma ((Figure 11))) cause a **bitemporal hemianopia** ((Figure 12)). ## Optic tracts - The optic tracts carry contralateral visual field information from the optic chiasm to the lateral geniculate nucleus. - Lesions in the optic tract (eg, occlusion of the anterior choroidal artery) cause a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia** (loss of the same visual field in both eyes) ((Figure 13)). ## Lateral geniculate nucleus - The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) is a 6-layered visual relay center within the posterolateral thalamus that sends fibers to the visual cortex via optic radiations. - Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or tumor involving the LGN) cause a **contralateral homonymous visual field deficit**. ## Optic radiations - **Inferior optic radiations**:  Carry information from the superior visual field (inferior retina) through the temporal lobe (Meyer loop) to the visual cortex.  Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or mass involving the temporal lobe) cause a **contralateral homonymous superior quadrantanopia** ("pie in the sky") ((Figure 14)). - **Superior optic radiations**:  Carry information from the inferior visual field (superior retina) through the parietal lobe to the visual cortex.  Lesions in this region (eg, stroke or mass involving the parietal lobe) cause a **contralateral homonymous inferior quadrantanopia** ("pie on the floor") ((Figure 15)). Large infarctions involving the territory supplied by the middle cerebral artery can damage both the upper and lower limbs of the optic radiations, resulting in homonymous hemianopia. ## Primary visual cortex - Located in the occipital lobe and is retinotopically organized (eg, specific retinal areas map to specific areas of the visual cortex). - Macular vision is processed by the posterior cortex. - Peripheral vision is processed by the anterior cortex. - Lesions in this region (eg, occlusion of the posterior cerebral artery) cause a **contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing** (the cortical structures responsible for macular vision are dual-supplied from the middle and posterior cerebral arteries). After visual information is received in the occipital cortex, it is relayed along distinct pathways to association cortices for higher-order processing ((Figure 16)).  The ventral (P) pathways project to the occipitotemporal association cortex for the identification of letters, colors, shapes, and faces (ie, what is it?).  The dorsal (M) pathways project to the parietooccipital association cortex for processing of motion and spatial relationships (ie, where is it?). # Summary Vision begins when light is refracted by the cornea and lens and focused onto the retina, where rods and cones convert light into neural signals.  These signals travel via ganglion cells into the optic nerve, cross partially at the optic chiasm, and continue through the optic tracts, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations to reach the primary visual cortex.  Lesions along this pathway produce characteristic visual field defects ((Figure 17)). ​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​

articles.title: Thyroid Physiology And Diagnostic Testing
articles.markdown: # Thyroid Physiology And Diagnostic Testing # Introduction The thyroid is a small endocrine gland that plays an important role in regulating the basal metabolic rate.  Thyroid disorders are very common globally and can include hyperthyroidism (overproduction of thyroid hormone), hypothyroidism (underproduction of hormone), and a variety of neoplastic and inflammatory conditions. # Embryology The thyroid is primarily an endodermal derivative.  In utero, the thyroid gland forms from an outpouching of pharyngeal epithelium at the base of the tongue ((Figure 1)).  It then descends to the base of the anterior neck via the thyroglossal duct, which extends from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue to the superior midline border of the thyroid ((Figure 2)).  Normally, the duct then atrophies.  Occasionally, failure of normal migration can leave residual deposits of ectopic thyroid tissue along the route of descent, and residual patency of the duct can manifest as a thyroglossal duct cyst. As the cells migrate to the lower neck, they also fuse with parafollicular C cells from the ultimobranchial body of the 4th pharyngeal arch to form the mature thyroid glandular structure ((Figure 3)). # Anatomy The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped gland that sits on the midline in the lower neck, anterior to the trachea and inferior to the thyroid cartilage ((Figure 4)).  It is composed of 2 lobes with a central isthmus; most patients have a posterior extension from each lobe (tubercle of Zuckerkandl).  The gland is supported by the trachea via the lateral suspensory ligament and is typically mobile, rising with the thyroid cartilage during swallowing.  The parathyroids are a set (usually 4) of small glands that lie immediately posterior to the thyroid lobes. Blood supply to the thyroid is primarily via the paired superior and inferior thyroidal arteries ((Figure 5)).  Innervation to the thyroid is scant, primarily consisting of small sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers that regulate blood flow to the thyroid.  However, the recurrent laryngeal nerve passes through the thyroid, and the superior laryngeal nerve runs in close proximity; these nerves can be injured during thyroid dissection or thyroidectomy. The fundamental unit of thyroid microanatomy is the thyroid follicle ((figure 6)), spherical structures consisting of a core of glycoprotein colloid, which serves as substrate for synthesis of thyroid hormone, surrounded by cuboidal epithelium.  The reticular tissue between follicles is highly vascular with a dense network of capillaries.  The interfollicular space also contains the parafollicular C cells, which secrete calcitonin. # Thyroid hormone physiology Synthesis of thyroid hormone begins with thyroglobulin, a large glycoprotein produced in thyroid follicular cells and secreted into the follicular lumen ((Figure 7)).  The follicular cells also transport inorganic iodide from the bloodstream into the lumen.  There, thyroid peroxidase (TPO) oxidizes iodide to iodine, and covalently links it to tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin (ie, organification), forming mono- and diiodotyrosine.  TPO then couples the iodinated tyrosine residues to form triiodothyronine (T3) and tetraiodothyronine (T4, also referred to as thyroxine), which are collectively termed thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormone is stored in the thyroid follicles while still bound to thyroglobulin.  In preparation for release, it is taken up into follicular cells, liberated from thyroglobulin by proteolytic enzymes, and transported into the follicular capillaries.  Most thyroid hormone is released in the form of T4, with only a small amount of T3 released.  T3 (the more active form of thyroid hormone) is then produced by deiodination of T4 in peripheral tissues.  Most thyroid hormone in circulation is bound to plasma proteins, primarily thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, and albumin.  A much smaller free thyroid hormone pool is metabolically active. Thyroid hormone acts on an intranuclear receptor that is ubiquitous in tissues throughout the body.  It acts to stimulate the basal metabolic rate, increasing energy consumption and thermogenesis.  It also increases expression of catecholamine receptors, amplifying adrenergic effects. # Regulation of thyroid endocrine function Thyroid hormone synthesis and release are regulated primarily by thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), which is secreted by thyrotroph cells of the anterior pituitary ((Figure 8)).  Release of TSH is stimulated in turn by thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus.  Production of both TRH and TSH is suppressed by negative feedback from thyroid hormone. In addition to T4 and T3, a small amount of thyroid hormone is released as reverse T3 (rT3), an inactive isomer.  Conversion of T4 to rT3 also occurs in peripheral tissues; increased rT3 conversion, as can occur in severe illness, leaves less T4 available for deiodination to active T3, which serves as a secondary check on thyroid hormone status. # Effect of pregnancy Pregnancy requires increased thyroid hormone production to meet metabolic demands.  Alterations to thyroid hormone levels occur through 2 primary mechanisms: - Estrogen stimulates the synthesis of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) and decreases TBG clearance, leading to higher circulating TBG levels and an increased pool of bound thyroid hormone.  T4 production subsequently increases to maintain free hormone levels ((Figure 9)). - hCG (which shares a common alpha subunit with TSH and a similar beta subunit) directly stimulates thyrotropin receptors on thyroid follicular cells, resulting in increased T4 production.  TSH levels typically fall due to negative feedback of thyroid hormone on pituitary TSH release. # Laboratory testing ## TSH Serum TSH is the primary laboratory test used in diagnosis and management of thyroid conditions.  Abnormalities include the following: - TSH is increased in primary hypothyroidism, central/secondary hyperthyroidism, and under-replacement in thyroid hormone therapy. - TSH is decreased/suppressed in primary hyperthyroidism, central hypothyroidism, and over-replacement in thyroid hormone therapy. Because the pituitary response to changes in thyroid physiologic status is rapid and vigorous, TSH is generally the most sensitive marker in thyroid disease, with levels rising or falling before thyroid hormone levels are outside their laboratory reference ranges.  The correlation between serum TSH and thyroid metabolic status is logarithmic, with changes at the lower end of the reference range representing a greater change in status than a proportional change at the upper end of the range. ## Thyroxine (T4), free and total The bulk of circulating thyroid hormone is in the form of T4.  Levels are elevated in primary and central hyperthyroidism, and decreased in primary and central hypothyroidism.  Because free T4 is the metabolically active fraction and is less affected by plasma binding protein levels, many experts prefer free T4 over total T4 measurement for clinical decision making. ## Triiodothyronine (T3) Serum T3 is often used in evaluation of hyperthyroidism; elevated levels serve to confirm an elevated T4 measurement.  However, TSH, which is elevated in primary hypothyroidism, increases the share of thyroid hormone released as T3, and serum T3 levels are often normal in mild to moderate hypothyroid states.  Therefore, T3 is not recommended in evaluation of hypothyroidism. ## Thyroglobulin A small amount of thyroglobulin is released with thyroid hormone from thyroid follicular cells.  Excessive thyroid hormone production in hyperthyroidism (eg, Graves disease) is typically associated with elevated serum levels of thyroglobulin.  Thyroglobulin levels can be strikingly elevated when hyperthyroidism is due to destruction of thyroid follicles with release of preformed thyroid hormone (eg, painless thyroiditis, subacute \[granulomatous\] thyroiditis).  Also, because thyroglobulin is made exclusively in the thyroid, patients who undergo total thyroidectomy (eg, for thyroid cancer) should have no detectable thyroglobulin in circulation; measurable levels suggest the presence of residual or recurrent neoplastic tissue. ## Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies (Anti-TPO) Anti-TPO is classically used as a marker for chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis and related conditions (eg, painless and postpartum thyroiditis).  In these disorders, high anti-TPO levels are associated with increased risk for progression of subclinical hypothyroidism (ie, elevated TSH with normal free T4 levels) to overt hypothyroidism.  Anti-TPO is not specific to these disorders, however, and also can be seen in Graves disease and other autoimmune endocrinopathies. ## Thyrotropin (TSH) receptor antibodies (TRAb) Autoantibodies against the TSH receptor can activate the receptor independent of TSH (ie, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin).  These antibodies are the hallmark of Graves disease and are a sensitive marker for diagnosis. # Imaging ## Ultrasound Because the thyroid occupies a relatively superficial position in the anterior neck, it is readily accessible to ultrasound imaging.  Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice in evaluating thyroid nodules, and ultrasound characteristics (eg, size, echotexture, calcification) can be used to determine the risk for malignancy and need for tissue sampling.  Ultrasound is also commonly used to guide fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid. Ultrasound with Doppler can assess blood flow in the thyroid, which correlates roughly with metabolic activity and can clarify the differential diagnosis in hyperthyroidism.  Graves disease, which is characterized by increased thyroid hormone synthesis, typically shows increased blood flow; destructive thyroiditis, which causes release of preformed hormone with decreased new hormone synthesis, shows decreased flow.  Thyroid scintigraphy (see below) is usually preferred for this purpose but is contraindicated in pregnant women, in whom ultrasound is preferred. ## Nuclear medicine Radioactive iodine uptake scintigraphy is widely used in the evaluation of hyperthyroidism.  This imaging modality uses a radioiodine tracer to assess uptake and organification of iodine in the thyroid.  Typical patterns include the following: - Diffusely increased uptake ((Figure 10)) throughout the thyroid gland suggests Graves disease. - Focal uptake ((Figure 11)) with decreased uptake in the remainder of the gland suggests hypermetabolic thyroid nodules (toxic adenoma or toxic multinodular goiter). - Decreased uptake ((Figure 12)) throughout the gland suggests destructive thyroiditis or exogenous thyroid hormone intake. # Summary The thyroid gland synthesizes hormones that regulate the body's metabolic rate.  These hormones are produced through a multi-step process that utilizes iodine, and their release is controlled via a feedback loop involving the pituitary gland.  Thyroid-stimulating hormone, produced by the pituitary, is the primary screening tool for diagnosing thyroid conditions.  Imaging techniques such as ultrasound and radioactive iodine uptake scans can further pinpoint the cause of the thyroid dysfunction, such as Graves disease or thyroid nodules. ​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​

articles.title: Thermoregulation
articles.markdown: # Thermoregulation # Introduction Thermoregulation maintains core body temperature within a narrow range (36.5-37.5 C \[97.7-99.5 F\]), despite environmental variation, through the integration of peripheral thermal sensing, central processing in the hypothalamus, and autonomic and behavioral responses that adjust heat production and dissipation.  The process reflects a negative feedback loop organized around a hypothalamic set point. # Thermal compartments and heat balance Body temperature varies across compartments due to differences in perfusion and exposure: - **Core compartment** (brain and visceral organs):  Core temperature is tightly regulated because enzymatic and cellular processes are temperature sensitive. - **Peripheral compartment** (skin and extremities):  Peripheral temperature may fluctuate, serving as a buffer between the core and the environment. Total body heat content is determined by the balance between heat production and heat loss: - **Heat production**:  Determined by several factors, including basal metabolic activity (major contributor at rest), skeletal muscle activity, shivering, and nonshivering thermogenesis (described later). - **Heat loss**:  Occurs through 4 major mechanisms: - Radiation:  Transfer of infrared heat to surrounding surfaces (dominant at rest). - Conduction:  Direct heat transfer to objects in contact. - Convection:  Heat transfer via moving air or fluid. - Evaporation:  Heat loss through vaporization of water (sweat, respiration). # Mechanisms: Feedback loop ## Peripheral and central thermal sensing Thermal inputs originate from peripheral and central receptors: - **Peripheral thermoreceptors**:  Located in skin, these receptors detect environmental temperature and allow anticipatory adjustments before core temperature changes. - **Central thermoreceptors**:  Located in the hypothalamus, spinal cord, and viscera, these receptors respond to core temperature changes. There are more cold-sensing than warm-sensing receptors, so responses are biased toward protection against heat loss. ## Central integration The hypothalamus integrates thermal signals and compares them to the hypothalamic set point, with the following locations playing important roles: - Preoptic/anterior hypothalamus:  Promotes heat dissipation. - **Posterior hypothalamus**:  Promotes heat conservation and production. Deviations from the hypothalamic set point trigger coordinated outputs through autonomic, endocrine, and somatic pathways to ensure a narrow physiologic temperature range ((Figure 1)). ## Effector mechanisms **Heat dissipation** Increases in body temperature stimulate: - **Diaphoresis** (sweating):  Evaporation of water from the skin is the most effective mechanism for releasing excess heat.  (Sweating, with production of the hypotonic fluid from eccrine glands, is mediated by sympathetic cholinergic fibers, an exception to the usual adrenergic sympathetic signaling.) - **Peripheral vasodilation** and shunting of blood and heat from internal organs to the skin (eg, through splanchnic vasoconstriction):  Heat dissipation from the skin occurs via conduction, convection, and radiation. - **Behavioral changes**:  Examples include voluntary decisions to seek shade or cooler environments. **Heat conservation and production** Decreases in body temperature stimulate: - **Shivering**:  Oscillatory skeletal muscle contraction generates rapid heat production. - **Nonshivering thermogenesis**:  Heat is generated from brown adipose tissue (eg, mainly adjacent to the heart and great vessels).  Upregulation of the mitochondrial uncoupling protein dissipates the proton gradient as heat (ie, instead of ATP) ((Figure 2)). - **Peripheral vasoconstriction**:  Blood shunting toward internal organs conserves heat. - **Behavioral thermoregulation**:  Examples include voluntary decisions to keep moving or to seek shelter. **Endocrine contributions** Beyond these relatively rapid responses, hormonal systems provide sustained regulation.  In particular, **thyroid hormone** increases basal metabolic rate and heat production via enhanced mitochondrial activity.  Cold exposure stimulates the hypothalamic release of thyroid-releasing hormone, increasing thyroid hormone production over time.  Conversely, heat-loss mechanisms include decreased thyroid hormone formation. Other hormones involved in thermoregulation include: - **Catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine)**:  Stimulate glycogenolysis, lipolysis, and thermogenesis. - **Cortisol**:  Has permissive effects on metabolism during prolonged stress. # Adaptations ## Fever and set point regulation Fever reflects a regulated increase in the hypothalamic set point, typically in response to exogenous or endogenous pyrogens that stimulate production of prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus.  The elevated set point activates heat-conserving mechanisms (vasoconstriction, shivering), initially producing a sensation of cold and chills during the febrile episode.  Once the set point returns to normal (eg, after antipyretics), heat-dissipating mechanisms (sweating, vasodilation) are activated, producing a sensation of warmth during defervescence. ## Acclimatization Repeated heat exposure induces adaptive changes that improve thermoregulation, including: - Earlier onset and increased rate of sweating. - Reduced sweat sodium concentration due to aldosterone-mediated reabsorption. - Expansion of plasma volume, improving cardiovascular stability. These adaptations enhance heat dissipation and reduce the risk of heat-related illness. # Clinical correlations The following scenarios are described in more detail in separate articles. - **Hypothermia**:  Hypothermia occurs when heat loss exceeds production; it leads to impaired enzymatic function, decreased cardiac output, and risk of arrhythmias. - **Hyperthermia (heat stroke)**:  Heat-dissipating mechanisms fail without a change in hypothalamic set point; this can result in multiorgan dysfunction. # Summary Thermoregulation depends on the integration of peripheral and central temperature sensing with hypothalamic control of a defined set point.  Heat balance is achieved by modulating heat production (metabolism, shivering) and heat loss (radiation, evaporation, skin blood flow).  Rapid neural responses are complemented by slower endocrine adjustments that sustain temperature control.  Fever represents an upward resetting of the set point mediated by inflammatory signaling. ​‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌

articles.title: Renal Anatomy And Physiology
articles.markdown:
# Renal Anatomy And Physiology

# Introduction

The kidneys are a pair of bean-shaped organs responsible for maintaining systemic homeostasis.  Their key functions include filtration and waste excretion, sodium and water balance, electrolyte and acid-base handling, and various endocrine roles (eg, vitamin D activation).  This review explores structural and functional characteristics of the kidney, from its embryologic development to the molecular mechanisms underlying filtration and reabsorption.  Endocrine functions are discussed in separate articles.

# Embryology and gross morphology

## Embryology

The definitive kidney, or metanephros, originates from the intermediate mesoderm.  Its development proceeds through a series of stages (pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros) during the fourth week of embryologic development.  The metanephros arises from the reciprocal interaction between the ureteric bud (which forms the collecting system) and the metanephric mesenchyme (which differentiates into nephrons) ((Figure 1)).

## Gross morphology

Each adult kidney sits within the retroperitoneal space ((Figure 2)), shielded by a fibrous renal capsule and surrounded by perirenal fat.  This fatty cushion provides both mechanical protection and thermal insulation.  Each kidney receives blood flow from its respective renal artery and is drained by the renal veins.  The left renal vein is longer, making the left kidney preferred for renal transplant because the greater length simplifies the surgical procedure ((Figure 3)).

Internally, the kidney can be divided into 2 primary regions ((Figure 4)):

-   **Renal cortex**:  This outer granular layer contains glomeruli and most metabolically active regions of the nephron (eg, early proximal tubule) with a rich vascular network.
-   **Renal medulla**:  This inner region contains renal pyramids and houses the loops of Henle, vasa recta, and collecting ducts.  Each pyramid terminates at a renal papilla, which projects into a minor calyx.  The renal papillae serve as the exit points where collecting ducts converge to drain urine into the minor calyces, which join to form major calyces that in turn converge into the renal pelvis.

Some individuals are born with a solitary functioning kidney, as in the case of unilateral renal agenesis (failure of the ureteric bud to develop).  Although most of these people remain asymptomatic due to compensatory hyperfiltration by the remaining kidney, they face an elevated risk for chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to hyperfiltration injury.

# The nephron

The nephron is the fundamental functional unit of the kidney, responsible for transforming filtered blood (the filtrate) into urine ((Figure 5)).  Each kidney contains approximately 1 million nephrons, each of which consists of a renal corpuscle (site of filtrate formation) and tubule (site of filtrate refinement).

## Renal corpuscle: Filtrate formation

The renal corpuscle forms the kidney's filtration apparatus ((Figure 6)) and consists of:

-   **Glomerulus**:  A specialized capillary network supplied by the afferent arteriole.
-   **Bowman capsule**:  A double-walled epithelial structure enclosing the glomerulus, consisting of simple squamous epithelium (parietal layer) and specialized podocytes with interdigitating foot processes connected by slit diaphragms (visceral layer) interspersed by proteins (eg, nephrin, podocin).

Within the renal corpuscle, blood is filtered through the glomerular capillaries into the Bowman space (confined space within the capsule), forming the filtrate that ultimately becomes urine.  The filtration occurs across the **glomerular filtration barrier**, which progressively increases in selectivity (based on particle size) as substances pass through its 3 layers:

-   **Fenestrated endothelium**:  Fenestrated endothelium forms the innermost layer of the glomerular capillaries, permitting the passage of many plasma components through pores (70-100 nm in diameter).  Fluid, dissolved solutes, and plasma proteins are allowed through, whereas blood cells are not.
-   **Glomerular basement membrane (GBM)**:  This middle layer is composed of type IV collagen and heparan sulfate, serving as the most significant physical barrier.  The GBM prevents entry of molecules >40-50 nm.
-   **Podocyte foot processes**:  These processes form the outermost layer and contain small slit diaphragms (25-60 nm in diameter) that restrict the passage of proteins larger than approximately 70 kDa.

In addition to the size barriers, **negatively charged glycoproteins** in all 3 layers add an electrostatic filter that repels larger, negatively charged solutes (eg, albumin) while not affecting small solutes (eg, electrolytes).  This intricate filtration system comprising physical and electrochemical barriers ensures that essential plasma proteins remain in circulation while waste products, electrolytes, and excess fluid are filtered ((Figure 7)).

## Renal tubules: Filtrate refinement

Once the glomerular filtrate is formed, it enters the tubular system, where its composition is adjusted through tubular reabsorption (movement of substances from tubular lumen to blood) and secretion (movement from blood to tubular lumen).  The result—the net sum of filtration, reabsorption, and secretion—is excretion, the forming of the final urine.  The functionally distinct tubular segments include:

-   **Proximal convoluted tubule** (PCT)
    -   Lined by cuboidal epithelial cells with a prominent brush border and abundant mitochondria, optimizing it for extensive solute reabsorption.
    -   Reabsorbs 65%-70% of filtered Na⁺ (eg, via Na+/H+ exchangers), in addition to glucose (via sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 \[SGLT-2\] ((Figure 8))), bicarbonate ((Figure 9)), phosphate (regulated by parathyroid hormone), and Ca2+.
    -   Secretes organic anions (eg, penicillin) via organic anion transporters and reabsorbs uric acid.  Both functions are inhibited by probenecid, a gout medication with a uricosuric effect (probenecid should be avoided in patients taking penicillin) ((Figure 10)).
    -   Renal glucose handling follows a titration curve:  At plasma glucose <200 mg/dL, nearly all filtered glucose is reabsorbed.  Beyond the transport maximum, excess glucose spills into urine (glucosuria) ((Figure 11)).
-   **Loop of Henle**
    -   Descending limb:  Passively reabsorbs water, concentrating tubular fluid.
    -   Thick ascending limb (TAL):  Impermeable to water, it actively transports Na+, K+, and Cl− into the medullary interstitium via Na+\-K+\-2Cl− cotransporters.  This creates a medullary concentration gradient, allowing water reabsorption and urine concentration (discussed later).
    -   Reabsorbs Mg2+ and Ca2+ via paracellular pathways.
-   **Distal convoluted tubule** (DCT)
    -   This segment adjusts sodium and calcium concentrations (eg, via Na+\-Cl− cotransporters) under regulation by parathyroid hormone.
-   **Collecting duct** (CD)
    -   The nephron's final segment, the CD, determines urine concentration and composition.
    -   Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) regulates water reabsorption via aquaporin-2 channels, concentrating urine when present and allowing dilution in its absence ((Figure 12)).
    -   Principal cells secrete K+ (via ROMK channels) and reabsorb Na+ (via ENaC), modulated by aldosterone.  Intercalated cells maintain acid-base balance by secreting H+ (via H+\-ATPase) and modulating bicarbonate transport.  Both are regulated by aldosterone ((Figure 13)).
    -   Urea passively diffuses out of the inner medullary CD, contributing to the medullary osmotic gradient.

The following is a summary of electrolyte handling through the tubular segments:

-   Sodium:  Reabsorbed in PCT (65%), TAL (25%), and DCT/CD (10%).
-   Potassium:  Reabsorbed in PCT/TAL; secreted in CD (regulated by aldosterone).
-   Phosphate:  Reabsorbed in PCT (inhibited by parathyroid hormone).
-   Calcium:  Reabsorbed in PCT (60%), TAL (20%), and DCT (20%).
-   Magnesium:  Primarily reabsorbed in TAL (70%).

There are 2 types of nephrons specialized for different purposes.  **Cortical nephrons** make up the majority of nephrons and are optimized for solute reabsorption (ie, contain short loops of Henle) into peritubular capillaries.  **Juxtamedullary nephrons** extend deep into the medulla and are therefore critical for concentrating urine through the countercurrent multiplication system.

The countercurrent multiplication system ((Figure 14)) establishes a **medullary concentration gradient** in the renal medulla to facilitate water reabsorption.  It relies on the unique structure of the loop of Henle.  The descending limb is permeable to water but not solutes; this allows water to leave the tubules, increasing tubular fluid osmolarity.  In contrast, the ascending limb is impermeable to water but actively transports sodium, potassium, and chloride into the medullary interstitium, reducing tubular fluid osmolarity while increasing medullary solute concentration.  This countercurrent flow amplifies the osmotic gradient, which is essential for the CD to reabsorb water under the influence of ADH, ultimately concentrating the urine.  The vasa recta, a specialized capillary network, helps maintain this gradient by preventing the washout of solutes from the medulla.

# Vascular architecture

Blood enters the kidneys via the renal artery, which divides into interlobar arteries, then arcuate arteries, and, finally, cortical radial arteries.  These give rise to afferent arterioles, forming the glomerular capillary network.  After blood is filtered through the glomerulus, it exits via the efferent arterioles, forming peritubular capillaries (in cortical nephrons) or the vasa recta (in juxtamedullary nephrons) ((Figure 15)).  The blood is finally collected from the peritubular network into cortical radial veins, which coalesce into arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, and, finally, the renal vein.

The renal cortex receives approximately 90%-95% of renal blood flow, whereas the renal medulla receives the remaining 5%-10%.  This makes the medulla very sensitive to hypoxia, as demonstrated by the injury pattern seen in ischemic acute tubular necrosis, with the outer medullary cells being most affected ((Figure 16)).

# Glomerular filtration

## Net filtration pressure

The net filtration pressure, which governs fluid movement across the glomerular filtration barrier, is a result of pressure gradients formed by Starling forces and is calculated by subtracting the oncotic pressure gradient from the hydrostatic pressure gradient (ie, net filtration pressure = \[Pc − Pi\] − \[πc − πi\]) ((Figure 17)):

-   The hydrostatic pressure gradient (Pc − Pi) is the difference between the hydrostatic pressures in the intraglomerular capillaries and the Bowman space.  Hydrostatic pressure in the capillaries is higher than that in the Bowman space and provides the driving force for fluid efflux from the capillaries.
-   The oncotic pressure gradient (πc − πi) is the difference between the oncotic pressures in the intraglomerular capillaries and the Bowman space.  Oncotic pressure is driven chiefly by large plasma proteins (eg, albumin), which do not freely filter across the glomerular capillary basement membrane due to both size and charge barriers.  The high oncotic pressure in the capillaries counteracts the capillary hydrostatic pressure and decreases net fluid efflux from the capillaries.

## Renal clearance and renal plasma flow

Renal **clearance** is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a given substance by the kidneys per unit time (usually expressed in mL/min).  It reflects the kidney's efficiency in removing a substance from the bloodstream.  Renal clearance of any substance (S) can be calculated as:

Clearance = (\[Urine concentration of S\] × \[Urine flow rate\]) / (Plasma concentration of S)

Renal clearance can vary from 0 to >600 mL/min, depending on the substance.  For example, under normal physiologic conditions, clearance of albumin and glucose is 0 (albumin is not filtered; glucose is filtered and then completely reabsorbed).  In contrast, maximum clearance is demonstrated by **para-aminohippurate** (PAH), which is freely filtered in the glomerulus and also actively secreted in the proximal tubule (ie, tubular fluid concentration increases along the nephron segments ((figure 18))).  PAH is nearly completely cleared in 1 renal pass, and its clearance therefore approximates the **renal plasma flow** (RPF), which is the volume of plasma passing through the kidney per unit of time (approximately 625 mL/min).

In contrast to PAH clearance, inulin clearance, described in the next section, is the gold standard for measuring the glomerular filtration rate ((Figure 19)).

## Glomerular filtration rate

The **glomerular filtration rate** (GFR) represents the volume of plasma filtered per minute, typically 90-120 mL/min in healthy adults.  GFR represents the sum of filtration rates across all nephrons and is most accurately measured through **inulin clearance**.  Inulin, an exogenous substance, is an ideal marker because it is freely filtered by the glomerulus and not reabsorbed, secreted, or metabolized by the renal tubules.  As a result, the amount of filtered inulin exactly equals the amount excreted in urine.  However, this method is labor intensive, requiring continuous infusion and multiple blood and urine samples, limiting its clinical use.

In clinical practice, GFR is typically estimated using the serum concentration of **creatinine**, a waste product generated during muscle metabolism of creatine.  Creatinine is produced at a relatively constant rate proportional to muscle mass and is freely filtered by the glomerulus without being reabsorbed (and is only slightly secreted).  The **estimated GFR** (eGFR) is calculated using formulas (eg, CKD-EPI, MDRD) that incorporate serum creatinine alongside variables such as age, sex, and race.

The relationship between serum creatinine and GFR is nonlinear.  A useful clinical rule is that each 50% reduction in GFR correlates with a doubling of serum creatinine.  For example, if a serum creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL corresponds to a GFR of 100 mL/min, a decline in GFR to 50 mL/min raises serum creatinine to 2.0 mg/dL.  Further reductions to 25, 12.5, and 6.25 mL/min would yield serum creatinine levels of 4.0, 8.0, and 16.0 mg/dL, respectively.  This curvilinear relationship means that in early kidney disease even minor increases in serum creatinine reflect substantial declines in GFR ((Figure 20)).  Consequently, serum creatinine alone is an insensitive marker for detecting early CKD, underscoring why GFR—rather than creatinine concentration alone—is used for CKD staging and management.

## Creatinine clearance

Alternatively, **creatinine clearance** (CrCl) provides another approximation of GFR.  CrCl can be measured directly using a 24-hour urine creatinine collection or estimated using the Cockcroft-Gault formula (which incorporates age, weight, sex, and serum creatinine).  However, unlike inulin, a small fraction of creatinine is actively secreted by the proximal tubules, leading to an overestimation of GFR by approximately 10%-20% when using uncorrected CrCl.  Although this overestimation makes CrCl less suitable for precise CKD diagnosis and staging, it remains widely used for medication dosing adjustments because drug dosing studies and guidelines were historically developed using CrCl measurements.

## Advanced biomarkers

Given that both eGFR and CrCl rely on serum creatinine, both have limitations in individuals with low muscle mass (eg, malnutrition, lower extremity amputation) or high- or low-protein diets.  In such cases, advanced biomarkers are helpful.  For instance, cystatin C, a small protein produced by all nucleated cells (ie, not affected by muscle mass or dietary protein) and freely filtered by the glomerulus, offers a more reliable biomarker.

# Renal hemodynamics

## Renal blood flow and filtration fraction

RPF (approximated by PAH clearance) can be used to calculate the following:

-   Renal blood flow (RBF):  Defined as the volume of whole blood (plasma plus blood cells) passing through the kidneys per unit time.  RBF = RPF/(1 − hematocrit).  RBF reflects overall renal perfusion (approximately 25% of cardiac output, or 1.25 L/min) and is influenced by systemic hemodynamics (eg, blood pressure, vascular resistance).
-   Filtration fraction (FF):  Expressed as the ratio of GFR to RPF.  It is the portion of RPF that is filtered across the glomerular capillaries.  Normally, FF is approximately 20%, meaning that 20% of the RBF is filtered.  The remaining 80% of the RBF exits the efferent arterioles and joins the peritubular capillary blood flood.

## Mechanisms regulating GFR and RBF

Both GFR and RBF are influenced by the vascular tone of both the afferent and the efferent arterioles, as shown in the following table ((Table 1)).

# Juxtaglomerular apparatus

The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) is a specialized structure located where the DCT contacts the afferent and efferent arterioles ((Figure 21)).  The JGA is critical for regulating RBF and glomerular filtration and consists of the following components:

-   **Macula densa**:  Chemoreceptor cells that sense sodium chloride (NaCl) concentration in the tubular fluid via Na+\-K+\-2Cl− transporters.
-   **Juxtaglomerular cells**:  Modified smooth muscle cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole that secrete renin in response to decreased blood pressure, reduced NaCl, or sympathetic stimulation.
-   **Extraglomerular mesangial cells**:  Cells that facilitate communication within the JGA through gap junctions, fine-tuning the feedback response.

In addition to regulating RBF and GFR (discussed in the next section), the JGA also plays a key role in the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system** (RAAS) by releasing renin in response to a variety of renal stimuli, including reduced afferent arteriolar pressure, reduced sodium delivery, and increased sympathetic drive.  Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II by ACE.  Angiotensin II causes systemic vasoconstriction (increasing blood pressure), promotes aldosterone release (increasing blood volume), and stimulates thirst ((Figure 22)).

# Regulation of renal blood flow

## Normal renal autoregulation

Normally, the kidneys maintain **stable RBF and GFR** over a wide range of mean arterial pressures (MAPs) (80-180 mm Hg) ((Figure 23)).  This process, called renal autoregulation, is accomplished through dynamic adjustments in **afferent arteriole** resistance via the following mechanisms:

-   **Myogenic response**:  Rising arterial pressure stretches afferent arteriolar smooth muscle, triggering vasoconstriction (through opening of stretch-activated calcium channels).  This reduces blood flow into the glomerulus, preventing abrupt increases in glomerular pressure.  Conversely, dropping arterial pressure triggers afferent vasodilation, increasing RBF (and hence GFR).
-   **Tubuloglomerular feedback**:  Increased arterial pressure leads to higher filtration of NaCl, which is delivered to the macula densa.  This triggers the paracrine release of vasoconstrictors (eg, adenosine), causing afferent arteriole constriction to limit blood flow.  In contrast, as pressures drop, reduced NaCl delivery releases vasodilators (eg, prostaglandins, nitric oxide) to maintain RBF and GFR.

## Failure of renal autoregulation

Under extreme deviations in MAP (<80 mm Hg or >180 mm Hg), renal blood flow autoregulation is unable to maintain stable RBF and GFR, as demonstrated in the following scenarios:

-   ↓↓ **MAP**:  Autoregulatory vasodilation is overwhelmed, unable to sufficiently elevate RBF and GFR.  Although compensatory prostaglandins (eg, prostaglandin E₂) dilate the afferent arteriole to preserve GFR, prolonged/severe hypotension exhausts this safeguard, causing prerenal acute kidney injury (AKI).
-   ↑↑ **MAP**:  Excessive pressure overwhelms autoregulatory vasoconstriction, exposing glomeruli to systemic hypertension.  This leads to hyperfiltration, glomerular damage, proteinuria, and inflammation (due to mesangial stretch), culminating in acute hypertensive nephrosclerosis.

## Clinical applications

In addition to extreme MAP deviations, renal autoregulation can be disrupted in various clinical scenarios, including:

-   ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs):  These inhibit angiotensin II, which normally maintains GFR via efferent constriction during reduced MAP (eg, volume depletion).  As MAP decreases, patients on these drugs are prone to prerenal AKI due to afferent vasodilation ((Figure 24)).  However, in patients whose volume status is stable, these medications protect glomerular capillaries (eg, diabetic nephropathy) by reducing intraglomerular hypertension, slowing disease progression despite a minor GFR decline.
-   NSAIDs:  By inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis (eg, PGE₂), these medications prevent afferent arteriole dilation during hypoperfusion.  In states of low effective arterial blood volume (EABV) (eg, volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis), this causes unopposed vasoconstriction and AKI ((Figure 25)).
-   SGLT-2 inhibitors:  Blocking SGLT-2 in the proximal tubule reduces glucose and sodium reabsorption, increasing solute delivery to the macula densa.  This enhances tubuloglomerular feedback, causing afferent vasoconstriction, lowering intraglomerular pressure, and reducing hyperfiltration ((Figure 26)).  This renoprotective effect mimics those of ACE inhibitors and ARBs but targets afferent (rather than efferent) arterioles.
-   Nephrotoxic agents:  Intraarterial iodinated contrast may cause AKI via afferent vasoconstriction (and direct tubular toxicity), especially in CKD.  Calcineurin inhibitors (eg, tacrolimus) can also induce afferent vasoconstriction.
-   Hepatorenal syndrome:  Advanced cirrhosis leads to severe splanchnic vasodilation and reduced EABV.  Compensatory RAAS hyperactivity (from renal hypoperfusion) causes intense renal vasoconstriction, overwhelming autoregulatory mechanisms and impairing renal function.

Beyond these acute disruptions, chronic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus also significantly impact renal autoregulation.  In chronic hypertension, prolonged high pressure shifts the autoregulatory range upward, making the kidneys reliant on high perfusion.  A sudden MAP drop (eg, from overtreatment) can cause AKI.  Diabetes mellitus promotes persistent afferent dilation (via multiple mechanisms), increasing glomerular hyperfiltration.  Over time, this damages the glomerular basement membrane, leading to proteinuria and nephropathy.  Both conditions impair perfusion stability, heightening AKI risk during hemodynamic stress.

# Summary

The kidneys maintain homeostasis through intricate filtration, reabsorption, and secretion mechanisms.  Cortical nephrons dominate solute reabsorption, whereas juxtamedullary nephrons establish the medullary osmotic gradient via countercurrent multiplication (allowing water reabsorption with concentration of urine).

The glomerular filtration barrier combines size-selective (eg, glomerular basement membrane, podocytes) and charge-selective (ie, negatively charged glycoproteins) layers to exclude plasma proteins.  Tubular segments use specialized transporters to adjust filtrate composition, modulated by various hormones (eg, antidiuretic hormone, aldosterone).

Renal hemodynamics are autoregulated via myogenic responses and tubuloglomerular feedback, maintaining the glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow across a wide range of mean arterial pressures (80-180 mm Hg).  Clinical biomarkers (eg, creatinine, cystatin C) and clearance techniques (eg, inulin clearance) quantify renal function.  Pharmacologic agents (eg, ACE inhibitors, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors) target glomerular pressure to mitigate hyperfiltration injury.  Disrupted autoregulation (eg, NSAIDs, hypotension) precipitates acute kidney injury, underscoring the kidney's vulnerability to hemodynamic perturbations.
