Pancreatic enzymes are secreted in inactive forms to prevent autodigestion.  Enteropeptidase (also called enterokinase), a duodenal brush border enzyme, activates trypsin from its inactive precursor, trypsinogen.  Once active, trypsin cleaves peptide bonds in dietary proteins and activates the other pancreatic enzymes .

›Bile and fat digestion

Efficient digestion of dietary lipids requires both pancreatic enzymes and bile.

Bile is synthesized by hepatocytes in the liver and stored in the gallbladder (other accessory organs for digestion).  In the gallbladder, bile is concentrated through the reabsorption of water and electrolytes.  When fats enter the duodenum, CCK stimulates gallbladder contraction and bile release into the intestinal lumen.

Bile contains bile salts, which are amphipathic molecules that function as detergents.  These molecules emulsify large fat droplets into smaller particles, greatly increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase activity.  Pancreatic lipase then hydrolyzes triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides, which combine with bile salts to form micelles that facilitate lipid absorption by intestinal epithelial cells .

›Small intestinal digestion and absorption

The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption.  The mucosal surface is optimized to provide maximal surface area for absorption.  The intestinal lining contains complex circular folds with villi (finger-like structures that project into the lumen).  The primary mucosal cell is the enterocyte, a specialized columnar epithelial cell with a brush border (microvilli) that further increases absorptive surface area .  Enzymes concentrated in the brush border of the enterocytes complete the digestion of carbohydrates and proteins into absorbable molecules .

The small intestine is composed of 3 physiologically distinct segments, each of which emphasizes absorption of specific nutrients :

  • Duodenum: In addition to receiving bile and pancreatic juice, the duodenum serves as a site for absorption of certain metals (eg, iron, magnesium, copper), some water-soluble vitamins (eg, thiamine, niacin, folate), and fat-soluble vitamins (vitamins A, D, E, and K).
  • Jejunum:  The jejunum serves as the primary site for macronutrient absorption (ie, monosaccharides, lipids, amino acids), as well as absorption of many micronutrients, including a wide variety of vitamins and minerals.
  • Ileum:  The ileum serves as the primary site for reabsorption of bile acids, as well as absorption of cobalamin (vitamin B12).  Additional absorption of certain micronutrients that were not completely absorbed in the jejunum may also occur in the ileum.

Major absorption mechanisms include:

  • Monosaccharides transported via sodium-dependent cotransporters.
  • Amino acids and peptides transported through specialized carriers.
  • Fatty acids and monoglycerides absorbed from micelles.

After absorption, nutrients follow different pathways.  Water-soluble nutrients enter the portal circulation and travel to the liver.  Lipids are packaged into chylomicrons and transported via the lymphatic system.

›Colonic digestive phase

The colon does not play an active role in chemical digestion of macronutrients, although colonic bacteria break down some nondigestible fiber into short-chain fatty acids (ie, via colonic fermentation).  Colonic bacteria also contribute to the absorbable pool of certain vitamins (eg, vitamin K, biotin).  However, the colon is responsible for absorption of the remaining water and electrolytes from chyme, desiccating the chyme to produce solid stool.

›Neural and hormonal regulation of digestion and gut motility

Neural

Neural control of digestion involves both extrinsic and intrinsic gut neurons:

  • Enteric nervous system (intrinsic innervation): Network of neurons in the walls of the gastrointestinal tract, primarily in the myenteric and submucosal plexuses.  Provides autonomous control of motility (eg, peristalsis, segmentation, churning), secretory activity, and blood flow .
  • Autonomic nervous system (extrinsic innervation): Both parasympathetic (via vagus and pelvic nerves) and sympathetic (via splanchnic nerves) nervous systems influence motility, secretory activity, and segmental blood flow.  Generally, parasympathetic activity increases motility and blood flow, whereas sympathetic activity does the opposite.

Neural regulation of digestion is often described in 3 overlapping phases:

  • Cephalic phase: The sight, smell, or thought of food activates vagal pathways that stimulate salivation and gastric activity in preparation for meals.
  • Gastric phase:  The presence of food in the stomach triggers local and long-distance reflexes to increase acid secretion and motility.
  • Intestinal phase:  The passage of food into the intestine triggers feedback slowing of gastric emptying and modulates pancreatic and gallbladder activity.

As food passes down the esophagus, vagally stimulated enteric neurons release nitric oxide, which induces relaxation of the fundus of the stomach to accommodate the incoming food bolus.  Specialized gastric pacemaker cells (interstitial cells of Cajal) initiate pacesetter potentials (slow waves), which generate circumferential contractions of the gastric smooth muscle (peristalsis).  Gastric peristalsis facilitates food mixing and propulsion toward the pylorus.

Hormonal: Incretin hormones

Among the digestive regulatory hormones, incretins (insulin-secreting hormones) are released by the gut mucosa after feeding to regulate postprandial glucose metabolism.  The two primary incretins are glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and gastric inhibitory peptide (GIP) (also known as glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide).

  • GLP-1 is secreted primarily by L cells in the distal small bowel and colon in response to luminal sugars .  It increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion by pancreatic beta cells, potentiating the effects of glucose on insulin secretion.  It also slows gastric motility, thereby increasing satiety.
  • GIP is secreted primarily by K cells in the upper small bowel and also potentiates insulin secretion.

GLP-1 and GIP are rapidly degraded by dipeptidyl peptidase-4 and cleared by the kidneys.

›Summary

Digestion involves the mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into absorbable molecules.  It starts in the mouth with chewing, mixing of food with saliva, and breaking down of starch and triglycerides by salivary enzymes.  Food moves to the stomach, where gastric acid and pepsin begin protein digestion as contractions form chyme.  In the duodenum, intestinal hormones such as secretin (stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate) and cholecystokinin (stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzymes) regulate secretions.  The pancreas supplies enzymes for carbohydrate, protein, and fat hydrolysis.  Liver-produced bile emulsifies lipids for effective pancreatic lipase action.  Most digestion and nutrient absorption occur in the small intestine via brush border enzymes and specialized transport.  Finally, the colon absorbs water and electrolytes, yielding solid stool.

​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​

articles.title: Physiology: Core Principles
articles.markdown: # Physiology: Core Principles # Introduction Physiology examines how living systems behave across different levels of biologic organization, from cells to tissues to organs, with an emphasis on functional relationships and adjustments to disturbances.  This article describes core principles of physiology using day-to-day examples and applications. # Homeostasis and allostasis ## Homeostasis Homeostasis, a core physiologic process, is the maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions despite external variability.  Variables such as body temperature, plasma osmolality, blood glucose, and arterial pressure are regulated within ranges compatible with cellular function.  Regulatory systems continuously adjust physiologic processes to counteract imbalances ((Figure 1)).  For example, a rise in body temperature detected by the hypothalamus leads to vasodilation and perspiration, bringing body temperature down to a normal range ((Figure 2)). ## Allostasis **Allostasis** describes regulation through adaptive change that prepares the organism for expected challenges.  During exercise, sympathetic activation increases heart rate, ventilation, and glucose mobilization before large disturbances in oxygen delivery or metabolic substrates occur. Homeostasis corrects deviations after they arise, whereas allostasis aims to accommodate anticipated demands.  However, persistent or excessive allostatic responses may impose physiologic cost (allostatic load). # Feedback regulation Physiologic regulation relies heavily on **feedback control systems**, particularly negative feedback. ## Negative feedback In a **negative feedback** loop, a change in a variable activates responses that **oppose** the initial disturbance.  At the cellular level, a stimulus causes a cellular response that inhibits continuation of the initial stimulus ((Figure 3)).  For example, when blood pressure rises, stretch-sensitive baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch increase firing.  This signal reduces sympathetic output and enhances parasympathetic activity, lowering heart rate, contractility, and vascular resistance.  The resulting decrease in pressure diminishes baroreceptor activation, completing the feedback loop.  Negative feedback stabilizes physiologic variables and limits excessive responses. The efficiency of a homeostatic system in maintaining stability is expressed by the gain, calculated as the correction applied divided by the remaining error: **gain = correction / remaining error**, where correction = (initial disturbance – remaining error).  The gain measures how effectively a negative feedback mechanism brings a physiological parameter (eg, blood pressure, temperature) back to its set point.  If blood pressure initially drops by 20 mm Hg upon standing (ie, initial disturbance = 20 mm Hg), but the baroreceptor feedback mechanism corrects it to a drop of 10 mm Hg (ie, remaining error = 10 mm Hg), then the gain = (20 – 10) / 10 = 2.  A gain of 2 means the system corrected twice as much disturbance as was left uncorrected. Positive feedback In contrast, positive feedback amplifies an ongoing process.  Such loops are uncommon in steady-state regulation but play roles in rapid transitions (eg, escalating oxytocin release and uterine contractions during parturition ((Figure 4))). ## Feedforward control Physiologic systems also use **feedforward control**, in which regulatory responses are initiated before the controlled variable changes.  Anticipatory increases in heart rate and ventilation at the onset of exercise arise from central neural commands and sensory input from muscles and joints.  These mechanisms reduce the magnitude of disturbances that would otherwise require slower feedback correction. # Physiologic variation and genotype-phenotype relationships Genetic differences influence the structure and function of proteins, receptors, enzymes, and regulatory pathways, producing variability in physiologic traits.  For example, polymorphisms affecting hemoglobin structure influence oxygen affinity and erythrocyte behavior.  Differences in enzyme activity affect drug metabolism and metabolic pathways.  This is why reference intervals (eg, for laboratory tests or blood pressure) represent distributions derived from populations. # Physiology across the life cycle Physiologic function changes across developmental stages. In the **fetal environment**, gas exchange, nutrient delivery, and waste removal occur through the placenta.  The fetal circulation contains shunts (eg, ductus arteriosus, foramen ovale) that direct blood flow to optimize oxygen delivery from placental blood.  At birth, rapid cardiopulmonary transitions close these pathways and establish pulmonary respiration. In the **neonatal period**, thermoregulation, renal concentrating ability, and metabolic control remain immature.  High metabolic demand and limited energy reserves influence responses to stress and illness. During **childhood and adolescence**, endocrine regulation drives growth, skeletal maturation, and sexual development.  Pubertal activation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis alters hormone profiles and body composition. In **adulthood**, mature physiologic systems respond to changes in lifestyle and environment to maintain homeostasis.  With **healthy aging**, gradual structural and functional changes occur across organ systems.  Examples include reduced maximal cardiac output due to decreased beta-adrenergic responsiveness, diminished renal filtration rate, reduced lung elastic recoil, and changes in immune function.  Although baseline function often remains adequate for everyday activities, physiologic reserve declines, reducing the ability to respond to stressors such as illness or extreme environmental conditions. # Adaptation to environmental challenges Adaptations to environmental challenges may occur acutely (minutes to hours) through regulatory responses or chronically (weeks to months) through structural and biochemical changes. At **high altitude**, reduced atmospheric oxygen pressure lowers arterial oxygen tension.  Immediate responses include hyperventilation and increased sympathetic activity.  Over time, erythropoietin-mediated increases in red blood cell production, enhanced capillary density, and alterations in oxygen transport improve tissue oxygenation. Exposure to **microgravity** (spaceflight) removes the hydrostatic gradients normally imposed by gravity.  Fluid shifts toward the thorax and head initially increase central blood volume.  Over time, cardiovascular deconditioning, reduced plasma volume, and skeletal muscle atrophy occur.  These changes resemble the physiologic effects of prolonged bed rest, which serves as a terrestrial model for microgravity. Acute **exercise** increases oxygen consumption, cardiac output, ventilation, and skeletal muscle blood flow to meet metabolic demands.  With training, repeated exposure induces long-term adaptations (eg, increased mitochondrial density in muscle, improved capillary supply, enhanced stroke volume) that support improved performance. # Physiology and pathophysiology Understanding normal physiology provides the framework for interpreting disease.  Pathophysiology examines how disturbances in normal regulatory mechanisms produce clinical disorders.  For example, knowledge of normal insulin signaling and glucose metabolism clarifies how impaired insulin secretion or resistance leads to hyperglycemia in diabetes mellitus.  Conversely, the study of disease often reveals underlying physiologic principles that are difficult to observe in healthy systems.  Hormone deficiencies and receptor abnormalities have clarified endocrine feedback regulation.  Therefore, physiology and pathophysiology provide complementary perspectives on the same biologic processes. # Summary Physiology examines how biologic systems maintain function by regulating internal variables within viable ranges while adapting to perturbations.  Homeostasis stabilizes parameters via negative feedback, whereas allostasis anticipates demands but can impose cumulative strain if persistent.  Regulation also includes limited positive feedback (eg, parturition) and feedforward control that reduces anticipated disturbances.  Adaptation to environmental stressors occurs through acute responses and longer-term structural changes (eg, altitude acclimatization, exercise training).  These principles form the basis for understanding disease pathophysiology, which reflects disruption of normal regulatory mechanisms. ​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌

articles.title: Muscle Physiology
articles.markdown:
# Muscle Physiology # Introduction Skeletal muscle function depends on the coordinated interaction of electrical, chemical, and mechanical processes.  At the core of this physiology is the excitation-contraction coupling mechanism, through which an action potential triggers calcium release and ultimately leads to muscle contraction.  Neuromuscular transmission, sarcolemmal excitability, and intracellular calcium dynamics are tightly integrated to ensure precise regulation of force generation.  Cardiac and smooth muscle, which contract involuntarily (unlike skeletal muscle), share some similarities with skeletal muscle but exhibit differences in structure and regulation. # Skeletal muscle structure Skeletal muscle is composed of long, cylindrical multinucleated cells called **muscle fibers**, which are formed by the fusion of myoblasts during development.  Each muscle fiber is surrounded by a plasma membrane known as the **sarcolemma** and contains numerous **myofibrils**, which are the contractile elements of the cell.  Myofibrils are organized into repeating structural units called **sarcomeres**, giving skeletal muscle its characteristic striated appearance ((Figure 1)).  These sarcomeres are aligned end-to-end along the length of the myofibril and serve as the fundamental unit of muscle contraction. A sarcomere is composed of overlapping filaments of **actin** and **myosin** as well as structural and binding proteins (eg, titin, alpha-actinin).  A single sarcomere is defined as the distance between 2 Z lines.  Thin filaments (actin, tropomyosin, troponin) are bound to structural proteins at the Z line.  The unbound ends of the actin filaments project into the middle of the sarcomere, where they interact with thick filaments (myosin) during muscle contraction.  The organization of the filaments gives rise to distinct bands and lines that can be seen on electron microscopy ((Figure 2)): - The Z line (Z disc) defines the lateral boundaries of each sarcomere and is the anchoring point for thin filaments.  The Z line is typically darker than the remainder of the sarcomere. - The M line, where myosin filaments anchor to structural elements, lies in the center of the sarcomere. - The I band is the light region of the sarcomere in which actin does not overlap with myosin. - The A band corresponds to a dark region of myosin filaments in the sarcomere.  In this region, there are myosin filaments overlapped with actin filaments as well as nonoverlapped myosin filaments. - The H band is the region in which myosin does not overlap with actin. During muscle contraction, the thin filaments slide over the thick filaments toward the M line, reducing the length of the H and I bands.  The A band always remains the same length. # Muscle fiber types and metabolism Muscle fibers are arranged into a motor unit composed of the same fiber type, with each unit innervated by a single motor neuron.  Skeletal muscle fibers are categorized into 2 major types: type I (slow-twitch) and type II (fast-twitch) ((Table 1)). ## Type I (slow-twitch) fibers Type I (slow-twitch) fibers specialize in stamina by using **oxidative** phosphorylation in the mitochondria for steady and sustained ATP production.  Type I fibers perform actions requiring low-level **sustained** force (eg, postural maintenance) and function primarily via **aerobic** metabolism, meaning they have high concentrations of myoglobin (oxygen storage) and mitochondria (aerobic respiration).  The high myoglobin content gives these fibers a **red** color. ## Type II (fast-twitch) fibers Type II (fast-twitch) fibers are specialized for generating **rapid** forceful movements; however, they fatigue quickly.  These fibers derive energy in the form of ATP mainly via glycogenolysis and subsequent anaerobic **glycolysis**.  The lower quantities of mitochondria and myoglobin lead to a **pale** color. Histologically, these motor units form a characteristic mixed checkerboard pattern of type I and type II fibers (lost during denervation and revenrvation as adjacent fibers become innervated by the same neuron). # Muscle contraction ## Overview - Muscle contraction begins with a neural signal that initiates an action potential in the motor neuron. - The action potential leads to acetylcholine (ACh) release at the neuromuscular junction. - ACh binding to nicotinic receptors initiates an end-plate potential and muscle fiber depolarization. - Depolarization spreads along the sarcolemma and into transverse tubules, triggering calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). - Intracellular calcium binds to troponin C, allowing for actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling. - ATP is required for both cross-bridge cycling and calcium reuptake into the SR during relaxation. ## Excitation and action potential generation Skeletal muscle is activated by lower motor neurons originating from the anterior horn of the spinal cord.  The motor neuron action potential leads to calcium influx at the axon terminal, promoting ACh vesicle fusion and release into the synaptic cleft.  ACh binds to postsynaptic nicotinic receptors (ionotropic or ligand-gated channels), causing sodium influx and potassium efflux.  The resultant end-plate potential, if suprathreshold, triggers a muscle action potential. Muscle action potentials differ from neuronal action potentials in several key ways: - **More negative resting membrane potential** (~–90 mV vs ~–70 mV in neurons). - **Slightly longer duration**, which helps coordinate contraction. - **Propagate into the fiber via transverse tubules (T-tubules)**, not just along the surface. Sodium, potassium, and chloride are the main ions that determine the membrane potential.  Under normal physiologic conditions, there is a low concentration of sodium and chloride ions in the cell and high concentration of potassium in the cytoplasm.  Conversely, the extracellular space has a high concentration of sodium and chloride ions and low concentration of potassium ions.  When a specific ion channel opens, the respective ions will flow across the membrane in a direction that brings the resting membrane potential closer to that ion's equilibrium potential. Like neurons, muscle action potentials are initiated by depolarization and rely on voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels for rapid upstroke and repolarization.  However, in skeletal muscle, the action potential propagates not only along the sarcolemma but also deep into the fiber via T-tubules, which are invaginations of the plasma membrane ((Figure 3)).  T-tubules are closely associated with the SR, a specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum that stores and releases calcium ions.  The T-tubules contain voltage-gated L-type calcium channels (dihydropyridine receptors \[DHPRs\]) that play a key role in the next step of muscle contraction, called excitation-contraction coupling. ## Excitation-contraction coupling **Excitation-contraction coupling** (ECC) refers to the process by which the electrical signal (muscle action potential) is translated into a mechanical response (contraction).  In skeletal muscle, this process works as follows: - The action potential in the T-tubules activates DHPRs, which undergo a conformational change. - DHPRs are mechanically linked to ryanodine receptor 1 (RyR1) on the SR membrane, and the conformational change in the DHPR triggers them to open.  This causes calcium release into the cytosol from the SR without requiring extracellular calcium influx. - Intracellular calcium binds to troponin C, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose myosin-binding sites on actin. - Actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling begins, powered by ATP hydrolysis, and results in contraction. This tightly coordinated process ensures that every muscle fiber contracts uniformly in response to a single neural signal. ## Actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling Once calcium is released into the cytosol during ECC, it initiates a sequence of molecular interactions between actin and myosin filaments within the sarcomere.  This process, known as **cross-bridge cycling**, is driven by calcium binding and ATP hydrolysis and is responsible for the actual shortening of skeletal muscle fibers during contraction.  The actin-myosin interaction cycle consists of several ATP-dependent steps ((Figure 4)): - **Rest**:  At rest, the myosin head is charged by ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) from previously bound and hydrolyzed ATP.  However, calcium-modulated regulatory complexes of troponin-C and tropomyosin block the myosin binding sites on actin. - **Cross-bridge formation**:  When calcium binds to troponin-C, troponin-tropomyosin complexes shift to expose the myosin binding sites; the myosin head then binds actin perpendicularly, forming a cross-bridge ((Figure 5)). - **Power stroke**:  The bound head releases Pi and bends the cross-bridge at a 45-degree angle, increasing filament overlap and shortening the sarcomere length.  Once the process is completed, ADP is released. - **Cross-bridge dissociation**:  A new ATP molecule must bind the myosin head to dissolve the crossbridge, returning the head to its original position to restart the cycle. - **Cross-bridge cycling**:  Continues while calcium and ATP are readily available; cycling across multiple myosin heads leads to increased or sustained contraction. Muscle relaxation occurs when the stimulus for contraction ceases and calcium is actively removed from the cytosol.  Intracellular calcium is removed primarily via 2 pumps: - **Na+/Ca2+ exchange pump (NCX)**:  NCX uses the large extracellular Na+ concentration gradient to pump Ca2+ out of the cell and, in the process, removes one intracellular Ca2+ in exchange for 3 extracellular Na+ ions. - **Sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+\-ATPase pump (SERCA)**:  SERCA is a Ca2+\-ATPase pump that actively transfers Ca2+ from the cytosol to the lumen of SR at the expense of ATP hydrolysis. The decline in cytosolic calcium causes tropomyosin to recover actin's binding sites, halting cross-bridge cycling and allowing the muscle to relax. # Muscle proprioceptors Proprioceptors are specialized sensory receptors that provide the CNS with information about body position, movement, and muscle tension.  In skeletal muscle, the 2 primary proprioceptors are muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) ((Figure 6)). ## Muscle spindles Muscle spindles (intrafusal muscle fibers) are stretch-sensitive receptors embedded within the muscle belly, parallel to the extrafusal (force-generating) muscle fibers.  They are innervated by group Ia and group II sensory axons and are sensitive to changes in muscle length.  Muscle spindles mediate the stretch (myotatic) reflex, which is commonly tested during the neurologic examination (deep tendon reflexes).  When a muscle is stretched, monosynaptic reflex activation of the alpha motor neuron (of the same muscle) results in contraction that resists the stretch. ## Golgi tendon organs GTOs are located at the junction between muscle fibers and tendons, innervated by group Ib afferent sensory axons.  GTOs are connected in series with contracting extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers.  When a muscle actively contracts against resistance, the increase in tension is transmitted through the tendon, activating the GTOs.  The Ib sensory axons from the GTOs contact inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which in turn synapse with the alpha motor neurons that innervate the same muscle.  Therefore, the Golgi tendon circuit is a negative feedback system that regulates and maintains muscle tension.  When a muscle exerts too much force, the GTOs inhibit contraction of the muscle, causing sudden muscle relaxation.  This prevents damage to the musculoskeletal system. Together, muscle spindles and GTOs continuously modulate reflexes and motor output, allowing for coordinated movement, posture maintenance, and injury prevention. # Skeletal muscle vs cardiac and smooth muscle Whereas skeletal muscle is under voluntary control and contracts in response to somatic motor neuron stimulation, cardiac and smooth muscle differ in both structure and regulation: ## Cardiac muscle Cardiac muscle is also striated but contracts **involuntarily**.  In contrast to skeletal muscle ECC, cardiac ECC requires **extracellular calcium**.  During the action potential, calcium enters the myocyte through L-type calcium channels (DHPRs) in the T-tubules.  This influx triggers **calcium-induced calcium release** from the SR via RyR2, making both extracellular and intracellular calcium essential for contraction ((Figure 7)). ## Smooth muscle Smooth muscle is **nonstriated** and contracts **involuntarily**.  It lacks organized sarcomeres and T-tubules.  Contraction is initiated by intracellular calcium increases, which can come from the SR or extracellular space.  Calcium binds **calmodulin** (calcium-modulated protein) because smooth muscle cells lack troponin.  Calmodulin activates myosin light-chain kinase to enable actin-myosin interaction. # Neuromuscular disorders Several clinical conditions arise from abnormalities in muscle excitation or contraction: ## Myasthenia gravis Autoantibodies target nicotinic ACh receptors, reducing the number of functional receptors available for synaptic transmission.  This leads to decreased end-plate potentials and impaired muscle activation, particularly with sustained or repeated use, resulting in fluctuating weakness that classically affects ocular, bulbar, and proximal limb muscles. ## Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome Antibodies inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic terminal of motor neurons, impairing calcium influx and reducing ACh release into the synaptic cleft.  The decreased neurotransmitter availability weakens neuromuscular transmission, typically producing proximal muscle weakness and autonomic symptoms that may improve with repeated stimulation due to calcium buildup. ## Malignant hyperthermia Genetic mutations in RyR1 render the channel abnormally sensitive to certain anesthetic agents (eg, succinylcholine), resulting in uncontrolled calcium release from the SR.  The excess cytosolic calcium causes sustained muscle contraction and a hypermetabolic state with severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, acidosis, and potentially life-threatening complications if untreated. ## Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy This condition is caused by mutations in proteins involved in sarcolemmal stability and ECC (eg, caveolin, dysferlin).  Disruption of the T-tubule network and associated signaling leads to impaired propagation of depolarization across the muscle fiber.  As a result, calcium release becomes asynchronous, reducing coordinated contraction and causing progressive weakness in the shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles. # Summary Skeletal muscle contraction is a multistep process dependent on action potential generation, intracellular calcium dynamics, and ATP-driven mechanical events.  The integration of electrical signaling and molecular motor activity enables skeletal muscle to generate controlled force.  The main steps involve the triggering of the muscle action potential by acetylcholine in the neuromuscular junction, depolarization spreading through the sarcolemma into T-tubules, excitation-contraction coupling, and actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling.  Cardiac and smooth muscle differ in both structure and regulation. ​‌​‌​‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​‌​‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌​​​​‌

articles.title: Hypothalamic-Pituitary Hormones
articles.markdown: # Hypothalamic-Pituitary Hormones # Introduction The hypothalamic-pituitary axis is a core component of the endocrine system, responsible for regulating various physiologic processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and stress responses.  The hypothalamus, located at the base of the brain, controls the release of hormones from the pituitary gland, which is divided into anterior and posterior lobes.  The anterior pituitary releases several hormones that regulate peripheral endocrine glands, whereas the posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus.  The interplay between these 2 organs maintains homeostasis in the body.  This article examines the hormones produced by both the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland and their functions, regulatory mechanisms, and physiologic effects. # Hypothalamic hormones The hypothalamus produces releasing and inhibiting hormones that control the secretion of hormones from the anterior pituitary.  These hormones help regulate a variety of bodily functions, including reproduction, stress response, and metabolism. ## Gonadotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) is part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis** in women ((Figure 1)) and men ((Figure 2)), influencing secretion of **gonadotropins**, including luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), from the anterior pituitary. - GnRH and gonadotropins regulate the function of the gonads (testes, ovaries) and reproductive processes, including production of **sex hormones** (testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone), spermatogenesis, and ovulation. - Prepubertal GnRH secretion is **low and constant**, which suppresses anterior pituitary gonadotropin secretion and gonadal sex hormone production.  Puberty is marked by a transition to **pulsatile** GnRH secretion, which stimulates increased gonadotropin secretion (resulting in increased LH, FSH, and sex hormones). **Regulation** - **Positive feedback**:  Leading up to ovulation, a sustained increase in estrogen levels leads to positive stimulation of GnRH secretion (ie, GnRH and LH surge). - **Negative feedback**:  Elevated sex hormone levels generally inhibit GnRH secretion; this effect occurs consistently with testosterone and progesterone, but the effects of estrogen in women depend on the current phase of the menstrual cycle (see below). **Clinical applications** - **Central hypogonadism**:  Suppression of GnRH can occur in states of stress or undernutrition (eg, via suppressive effects of elevated corticotropin-releasing hormone and cortisol, discussed in the next section), leading to low GnRH and hypogonadism (eg, decreased LH, estrogen, testosterone). - **Hyperprolactinemia**:  Elevated prolactin levels suppress GnRH secretion ((Figure 3)), leading to hypogonadism (low LH, FSH, estrogen). - **Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism**:  Primary ovarian insufficiency or testicular failure lowers sex hormone production, which leads to hypogonadism with elevated GnRH secretion (high LH and FSH with low estrogen or testosterone). - **Polycystic ovary syndrome**:  Polycystic ovary syndrome is characterized by excessively rapid pulsatile secretion of GnRH leads to a persistent imbalance in LH relative to FSH production, resulting in increased ovarian and peripheral androgen production. ## Corticotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) is part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis** ((Figure 4)), stimulating the anterior pituitary to release **adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)**, which subsequently stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce **corticosteroids** (eg, glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids). - Corticosteroids (especially cortisol) are involved in the body's response to stress and immune function; mineralocorticoids contribute to salt and volume homeostasis.  Corticosteroids also play a crucial role in regulating circadian rhythms. **Regulation** - **Positive feedback**:  Secretion of CRH is triggered by inflammatory cytokines (eg, infection), circadian rhythms, and limbic system input in states of high physiologic or psychologic stress (eg, trauma, hypoglycemia) via input from the suprachiasmatic nucleus; CRH secretion is highest in the early morning and is lowest at night. - **Negative feedback**:  High cortisol levels lower CRH and ACTH secretion ((Figure 5)). **Clinical correlations** - **Adrenal insufficiency**:  Adrenal insufficiency is characterized by low cortisol due to either primary adrenal failure or secondary (ie, central) suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.  In primary adrenal insufficiency, cortisol is low and ACTH/CRH are high due to loss of negative feedback.  Glucocorticoid use can lead to iatrogenic central suppression, with atrophy of hypothalamic CRH-releasing neurons causing low ACTH/CRH and cortisol. - **Cushing syndrome**:  Cushing syndrome refers to the clinical manifestations of prolonged, excessive cortisol exposure.  It can result from an adrenal source, such as an autonomously functioning adrenal adenoma, which leads to elevated cortisol and suppressed ACTH and CRH (due to negative feedback).  Alternately, it may arise from a central (ACTH-dependent) source, most commonly Cushing disease, which describes an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma that causes elevated ACTH and cortisol, with suppressed CRH (due to negative feedback). ## Thyrotropin-releasing hormone **Function** - Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), part of the **hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis** ((Figure 6)), stimulates the release of **thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)** from the anterior pituitary.  TSH in turn stimulates the thyroid gland to produce and release **thyroid hormones** (T3 and T4). - Thyroid hormones are critical for regulating metabolism, growth, and development, affecting nearly every tissue in the body. **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  TRH (and TSH) secretion is suppressed by increased levels of T3 and T4.  Other inhibitors of TRH include high dopamine levels, and starvation or critical illness (due to decreased leptin levels, high cortisol, and cytokine release), - **Positive feedback**:  Cold exposure, increased leptin, estrogen levels, and alpha-adrenergic stimulation (eg, norepinephrine) increase TRH levels. **Clinical applications** TRH is not routinely measured in clinical practice. - **Hyperthyroidism**:  Hyperthyroidism may result from central causes (eg, TSH-secreting tumors) with high TSH and T3/T4 or, more commonly, from primary hyperthyroidism with high T3/T4 and low TSH (feedback inhibition). - **Hypothyroidism**:  Hypothyroidism may be due to primary thyroid dysfunction (eg, Hashimoto disease) with low T3/T4 and high TSH (from negative feedback) or due to central inhibition (in which TSH and T3/T4 are both low). - **Euthyroid sick syndrome**:  In critical illness, caloric deprivation along with glucocorticoid and inflammatory cytokine release induce several changes in thyroid physiology (known as euthyroid sick syndrome \[ESS\]).  TRH suppression causes low-normal TSH levels, and decreased peripheral 5′-deiodination of T4 to T3 causes low T3; free T4 levels are initially normal.  If the underlying illness continues, T4 and TSH levels may eventually decrease, mimicking central hypothyroidism.  Because ESS typically improves with recovery, thyroid function testing in acutely ill, hospitalized patients is generally not recommended. ## Growth hormone–releasing hormone and somatostatin **Function** Growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH) and somatostatin are important regulators of the **growth hormone (GH) axis** ((Figure 7)) involving GH and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which mediate growth, cell repair, and metabolism.  GHRH stimulates somatotrophs of the anterior pituitary to **release GH**.  In contrast, somatostatin is the primary inhibitor of GH secretion, counteracting the effects of GHRH.  Somatostatin also inhibits the release of other hormones (eg, TSH, insulin). **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  Elevated levels of IGF-1 inhibits GHRH release from the hypothalamus (and GH secretion from the anterior pituitary). - Other regulators:  Somatostatin suppresses GH release, whereas factors such as sleep, exercise, stress, and hypoglycemia stimulate GHRH and GH secretion. **Clinical applications** - **Dwarfism**:  Dwarfism is characterized by GH deficiency. - **Acromegaly**:  Acromegaly is characterized by GH excess. ## Dopamine **Function** - Dopamine inhibits the release of **prolactin** from the anterior pituitary.  Prolactin is primarily involved in milk production in lactating women, and dopamine prevents excessive secretion of prolactin when not needed. **Regulation** - Dopamine secretion is modulated by feedback from prolactin levels.  Elevated prolactin can reduce dopamine release, allowing prolactin levels to rise further. - **Estrogen** can increase the secretion of prolactin, especially during pregnancy. **Clinical correlations** - **Prolactin-secreting tumors**:  Pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas) autonomously secrete prolactin, bypassing hypothalamic dopamine inhibition.  Elevated prolactin can cause galactorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and infertility. - **Dopamine antagonist medications**:  Antipsychotics and other dopamine D2 receptor blockers inhibit hypothalamic dopamine action, removing suppression of prolactin secretion.  This can lead to medication-induced hyperprolactinemia with symptoms similar to those seen in prolactinoma. # Pituitary hormones The anterior and posterior pituitary release several hormones that influence the function of other endocrine glands and target tissues throughout the body.  These hormones include ACTH, TSH, GH, LH, FSH, prolactin, and vasopressin. ## Adrenocorticotropic hormone **Function** - Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete **cortisol** and other corticosteroids.  Cortisol is vital for managing the body's response to stress, regulating metabolism, immune response, and inflammation. **Regulation** - **Negative feedback**:  Suppression of ACTH (and CRH) secretion can occur with high cortisol levels (or in the setting of long-term exogenous glucocorticoid therapy). ## Thyroid-stimulating hormone **Function** - Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) stimulates the thyroid gland to produce and release **thyroid hormones** (T3 and T4).  These hormones regulate metabolism, thermogenesis, and overall growth and development. **Regulation** - Like ACTH secretion, TSH secretion is regulated by **negative feedback** from thyroid hormones.  Elevated levels of T3 and T4 inhibit TRH release from the hypothalamus and TSH secretion from the pituitary. ## Growth hormone **Function** - Growth hormone (GH) stimulates growth, particularly in bones and muscles, and regulates metabolism.  It promotes protein synthesis, lipolysis, and the growth of long bones and cartilage, mainly through the action of IGF-1. **Regulation** GH secretion is regulated by **both** positive and negative feedback mechanisms: - **Positive feedback** occurs via GHRH, which stimulates GH release. - **Negative feedback** occurs through IGF-1, which inhibits both GHRH release and GH secretion. ## Prolactin **Function** - Prolactin is essential for **milk production** in the mammary glands during lactation.  It also plays a role in regulating reproductive function, immune modulation, and metabolism. **Regulation** - Prolactin release is primarily inhibited by dopamine.  During pregnancy, estrogen increases prolactin levels, preparing the mammary glands for lactation. ## Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone **Function** - Luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) are **gonadotropins** responsible for regulating reproductive functions.  In women, LH triggers ovulation and the formation of the corpus luteum, whereas FSH stimulates the growth of ovarian follicles.  In men, LH stimulates testosterone production from Leydig cells and FSH supports spermatogenesis. **Regulation** - In women, **estrogen** and **progesterone** mediate negative feedback on LH and FSH release, but during the menstrual cycle, rising estrogen levels mediate **positive feedback** by triggering the **LH surge**, which leads to ovulation. ## Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) **Function** - Antidiuretic hormone (ADH), also called vasopressin, regulates water balance by promoting water reabsorption in the kidneys.  It also plays a role in constricting blood vessels to maintain blood pressure. **Regulation** - ADH release is primarily regulated by **osmotic pressure** and **blood volume**.  When plasma osmolarity increases (indicating dehydration), ADH release is stimulated to conserve water.  Conversely, low blood volume or blood pressure also triggers ADH secretion. ## Oxytocin **Function** - Oxytocin is involved in uterine contractions during labor and facilitates milk ejection during breastfeeding.  It also has a role in social bonding, emotional responses, and maternal behaviors. **Regulation** - Oxytocin operates through **positive feedback** during labor.  The stretching of the cervix during labor stimulates oxytocin release, which intensifies uterine contractions, leading to further cervical dilation and more oxytocin release. # Summary The hypothalamic-pituitary axis plays a central role in regulating numerous physiologic functions, including metabolism, growth, reproduction, and stress response.  The hypothalamus produces hormones that either stimulate or inhibit the release of pituitary hormones, which in turn regulate the activity of peripheral endocrine glands.  Feedback mechanisms, primarily negative feedback, maintain hormonal balance, although positive feedback plays a role in certain physiologic processes such as ovulation and labor.  Disruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis can lead to a variety of endocrine disorders. ​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​‌​​​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌​​​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​

articles.title: Endocrinology: Core Principles
articles.markdown: # Endocrinology: Core Principles # Introduction The endocrine system participates in cellular communication and regulation of responses in the body, typically over chronic periods.  It uses hormones, chemical messengers carried in the bloodstream for long-distance communication among the body's cells.  This article provides an overview of the endocrine system, with an emphasis on functional aspects.  The individual hormones and associated disorders are described in separate articles. # Hormones Hormones are signaling molecules secreted from endocrine tissues into the circulation.  They can be classified based on their structure (peptide hormones, steroid hormones, and amino acid–derived hormones, described later) or their influence on other hormones: - **Tropic** hormones target endocrine tissues to influence secretion of other hormones (eg, adrenocorticotropic hormone, produced by the anterior pituitary, stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol). - In contrast, **direct** hormones act directly on target cells to produce nonendocrine responses (eg, prolactin, released by the anterior pituitary, promotes milk secretion). Some hormones (eg, growth hormone) act as both a tropic hormone (eg, stimulate the liver to release hormones) and a direct hormone (stimulates tissues to uptake glucose). # Endocrine glands Endocrine glands lack ducts and secrete hormones into the bloodstream.  The major endocrine glands are shown in the figure ((Figure 1)).  The **hypothalamic-pituitary axis** is a core component of the endocrine system; it is responsible for regulating various physiologic processes, including growth, metabolism, reproduction, and stress responses.  The hypothalamus, located at the base of the brain, controls the release of hormones from the pituitary gland, which is divided into anterior and posterior lobes.  The anterior pituitary releases several hormones that regulate peripheral endocrine glands (eg, thyroid, adrenal glands, gonads), whereas the posterior pituitary stores and releases hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus.  The interplay between these 2 organs maintains homeostasis in the body. # Hormone transport Hormones travel to target cells via the blood; therefore, a hormone's solubility affects how it is transported and how it exerts its physiologic effects. ## Peptide hormones Peptide hormones are produced in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and stored in vesicles until a signal causes them to be released.  They typically possess an overall charge at physiologic pH, making them water soluble **(hydrophilic)**.  Therefore, they can circulate largely in a free form (ie, unbound to proteins) in the bloodstream; however, they cannot cross the hydrophobic lipid layer of the target cell plasma membrane and rely on intracellular molecules to transmit a signal to the interior of a cell.  They are relatively fast acting with relatively short-lived results. ## Steroid hormones Steroid hormones are procured in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.  Because they are derived from cholesterol, they are lipophilic **(hydrophobic)** and can diffuse through the secreting cell's membrane.  They are bound predominantly to protein carriers to increase their solubility.  Their hydrophobicity facilitates diffusion through target cell plasma membranes, after which the hormones bind receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus to regulate gene expression ((Figure 2)).  They are slower acting with longer-lasting results. ## Amino acid–derived hormones Amino acid–derived hormones can function similarly to peptide and steroid hormones, depending on their structure and regulation.  For example, the catecholamine hormones epinephrine and norepinephrine behave like peptide hormones, whereas thyroid hormones behave like steroid hormones. # Endocrine signaling Endocrine signaling is 1 of the 3 broad ways (autocrine, paracrine, endocrine) in which cell signaling occurs ((Figure 3)).  The reception of a signal by a target cell is the first step in endocrine signaling. Receptors for peptide hormones are located in the plasma membrane because peptide hormones are charged and cannot readily cross the phospholipid bilayer; these receptors are often coupled with a G protein.  The peptide hormone serves as a first messenger, which binds its receptor and triggers a **second messenger** (eg, cyclic adenosine monophosphate), another molecule inside the target cells that transmits the signals (often through phosphorylation) ((Figure 4)).  Signal amplification can occur along this signaling cascade due to the production of hundreds of secondary messengers. Because steroid hormones are lipophilic, they diffuse directly across the plasma membrane and bind **intracellular receptors** in the cytosol or the nucleus, typically without using second messengers.  The steroid hormone–receptor complex usually acts as a **transcription factor** and binds DNA, resulting in increased or decreased transcription of target genes.  Often, 2 steroid hormone–receptor complexes bind together (ie, dimerize) prior to DNA binding. # Regulatory organization and feedback Endocrine function is organized primarily into regulatory axes that link the hypothalamus, pituitary gland, and peripheral endocrine organs (eg, hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal, hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal).  Hypothalamic hormones stimulate the anterior pituitary to release tropic hormones, which in turn regulate hormone secretion from peripheral glands. Hormone secretion within these axes is governed primarily by feedback mechanisms.  In **negative feedback**, the final hormone produced by a peripheral gland suppresses further secretion of hypothalamic and pituitary hormones, stabilizing circulating hormone levels ((Figure 5)).  For example, thyroid hormones inhibit the release of both thyrotropin-releasing hormone from the hypothalamus and TSH from the anterior pituitary. Less commonly, **positive feedback** amplifies hormone secretion under specific physiologic conditions ((Figure 6)).  For example, rising estradiol levels during the late follicular phase stimulate a surge in LH, which triggers ovulation. Hormone secretion also follows characteristic temporal patterns.  Some hormones are released in a pulsatile manner (eg, GnRH), whereas others exhibit circadian variation (eg, cortisol, which peaks in the early morning).  These patterns are integral to normal endocrine function and can be disrupted in disease states. # Patterns of endocrine disease Disorders of the endocrine system can be broadly categorized based on abnormalities in hormone production or action. Hormone excess and deficiency can result from dysfunction at different levels of an endocrine axis. - In **primary** disorders, pathology originates in the peripheral endocrine gland itself, leading to altered hormone production. - In **secondary** or tertiary (central) disorders, abnormalities in the pituitary or hypothalamus result in inappropriate regulation of peripheral glands. These distinctions tend to produce predictable patterns of hormone levels due to feedback mechanisms.  For example, primary gland failure leads to reduced end-hormone levels with compensatory elevation of tropic hormones, whereas central dysfunction results in low levels of both. In some conditions, circulating hormone levels are normal or elevated, but target tissues fail to respond appropriately.  This end-organ resistance may result from defects in hormone receptors or downstream signaling pathways (eg, insulin resistance). # Evaluation of endocrine disorders Evaluation of endocrine disorders follows from axis physiology and feedback relationships.  Initial testing measures both the peripheral (end) hormone and its corresponding pituitary tropic hormone to determine whether feedback is intact: - In primary gland dysfunction, reduced end-hormone production removes negative feedback, resulting in elevated tropic hormone levels (eg, primary hypothyroidism: low T4, high TSH). - Conversely, excess end hormone suppresses tropic hormone secretion (eg, primary hyperthyroidism: high T4, low TSH). - In central (pituitary or hypothalamic) disorders, both tropic and end-hormone levels are inappropriately low or inappropriately normal relative to each other (eg, secondary hypothyroidism: low T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH). When baseline measurements do not clearly localize the defect, dynamic testing is used to assess how the system responds to perturbation. - **Stimulation tests** are used when hormone deficiency is suspected, evaluating whether a gland can increase hormone production when appropriately stimulated (eg, cosyntropin stimulation test: failure of cortisol to rise indicates adrenal insufficiency). - **Suppression tests** are used when hormone excess is suspected, evaluating whether normal feedback can reduce hormone secretion (eg, dexamethasone suppression test: failure to suppress cortisol suggests Cushing syndrome). # Summary The endocrine system coordinates long-range cellular communication through hormones released into the bloodstream, with effects determined by hormone structure, transport, and receptor signaling.  Peptide hormones are water soluble and act via cell-surface receptors and second messengers, whereas steroid and thyroid hormones are lipophilic, circulate protein-bound, and regulate gene transcription through intracellular receptors.  Endocrine function is organized into hypothalamic–pituitary–target gland axes governed primarily by negative feedback, with additional modulation by pulsatile and circadian secretion.  Disorders arise from hormone excess or deficiency or from end-organ resistance and can be localized within an axis by interpreting feedback relationships.  Evaluation relies on paired measurement of tropic and end hormones, with dynamic stimulation or suppression testing used to assess glandular reserve or autonomy when baseline findings are inconclusive. ​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌

articles.title: Cardiovascular Hemodynamics
articles.markdown:
# Cardiovascular Hemodynamics # Basics of cardiovascular blood flow The cardiovascular system consists of a continuous circuit of blood vessels that supply oxygen and nutrients to the organs and tissues of the body.  The system is powered by 2 pumps: - The right ventricle (RV) powers the relatively low-pressure pulmonary circulation. - The left ventricle (LV) powers the relatively high-pressure systemic circulation. The parameters that govern cardiovascular blood flow are defined as follows. ## Stroke volume and cardiac output

Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate

Cardiac index = cardiac output / total body surface area

- **Stroke volume** is the volume of blood ejected from the RV or the LV with each contraction.  It is typically measured in milliliters.  The normal stroke volume for an adult at rest is approximately 70 mL. - **Cardiac output** is the amount of blood ejected from the RV or the LV per unit of time.  It is the product of stroke volume and heart rate and is typically measured in liters per minute.  The normal cardiac output for an adult at rest is approximately 5-6 L/min. - **Cardiac index** is a representation of cardiac output adjusted per body size; it is equal to cardiac output divided by total body surface area.  The normal cardiac index for an adult at rest ranges from 2.5-4.0 L/min/m2. - Because the RV and LV are connected in series, all blood passing through one ventricle must pass through the other ventricle at the same rate (otherwise blood will back up).  Therefore, under normal conditions, the cardiac output of the RV is the same as the cardiac output of the LV. ## Modified Ohm law

Voltage = current × resistance →

Pressure = cardiac output × resistance

- Ohm law (V \[voltage\] = I \[current\] × R \[resistance\]) was developed to describe energy flow through an electrical circuit, but the concept applies to all types of energy flow.  According to Ohm law, a voltage difference between points A and B drives electrical flow (current) against resistance between the 2 points. - In the modified Ohm law that describes cardiovascular hemodynamics, voltage is analogous to pressure and current is analogous to blood flow, such that the law becomes **P (pressure) = CO (cardiac output) × R (resistance)**.  In the circulatory system, blood flows from an area of higher pressure to an area of lower pressure, with the magnitude of flow inversely related to resistance. - Pressure and resistance are relatively low in the pulmonary circulation and relatively high in the systemic circulation.  Cardiac output is the same in both circulations. ## Resistance - Resistance is required to maintain pressure in the cardiovascular system. - **Systemic vascular resistance (SVR)** is created primarily by the systemic arterioles, and **pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR)** is created primarily by the pulmonary arterioles.  These arterioles can vasodilate and vasoconstrict to adjust resistance. ## Ejection fraction

Stroke volume = LV end-diastolic volume − LV end-systolic volume

LV ejection fraction = stroke volume / LV end-diastolic volume

- LV **stroke volume** is often calculated by subtracting the volume of blood in the LV at the end of contraction (ie, LV end-systolic volume) from the volume of blood in the LV at the beginning of contraction (ie, LV end-diastolic volume). - **Ejection fraction** ((Figure 1)), the relative volume of blood ejected from the LV with each contraction, is calculated by dividing stroke volume by the LV end-diastolic volume.  For instance, in a patient with LV end-diastolic volume of 150 mL and stroke volume of 75 mL, the ejection fraction is 50%.  An LV ejection fraction of 50%-70% is considered normal. ## Stroke volume:  Preload, contractility, and afterload Stroke volume is determined by 3 parameters ((Figure 2)):  preload, contractility, and afterload. **Preload** is the volume of blood in the ventricle at the end of diastole; it depends on venous return from the systemic circulation and the effectiveness of diastolic filling.  In a normally functioning heart, LV preload is directly related to RV preload, and the term "preload" usually refers to LV preload, which is synonymous with LV end-diastolic volume.  Stroke volume is directly related to preload according to the Frank-Starling law (as preload increases, stroke volume increases), which is discussed below. Factors that increase preload include: - Increased total blood volume. - Systemic venous vasoconstriction to mobilize blood from the venous capacitance system. Factors that decrease preload include: - Decreased total blood volume. - Systemic venous vasodilation. **Contractility**, also referred to as inotropy, is the intrinsic force of myocardial contraction and is determined by intracellular calcium concentration.  Stroke volume is directly related to contractility. Factors that increase contractility are primarily those that increase intracellular calcium and include: - Increased sympathetic tone. - Positive inotropic pharmacologic interventions (eg, digoxin, beta-1 agonists). Factors that decrease contractility are primarily those that decrease intracellular calcium and include: - Decreased sympathetic tone. - Negative inotropic pharmacologic interventions (eg, beta blockers, nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers). - Dilated cardiomyopathy and other disorders that impair cardiac sarcomere function (independent of intracellular calcium). **Afterload** is the pressure that the LV must contract against.  In contrast with preload, afterload is represented as pressure rather than volume; systolic blood pressure is generally indicative of LV afterload.  Stroke volume is inversely related to afterload:  As afterload increases, stroke volume decreases. Factors that increase afterload include: - Peripheral arteriolar vasoconstriction (increased SVR). - Increased contractility. - Increased preload. Factors that decrease LV afterload include: - Peripheral arteriolar vasodilation (decreased SVR). - Decreased contractility. - Decreased preload. ## Frank-Starling law The Frank-Starling law ((Figure 3)) of the heart states that, as LV preload increases, stroke volume increases accordingly to maintain forward blood flow (ie, "**the heart gives what it gets**").  The underlying mechanism is that increased preload causes increased myocardial stretching (ie, increased tension), which allows for more forceful contraction to expel the additional preload.  The increased force of contraction is entirely due to increased myocardial stretching and does not involve an increase in myocardial contractility (ie, there is no change in intracellular calcium concentration). ## Determinants of arterial blood pressure

Systolic blood pressure = diastolic blood pressure + pulse pressure

**Diastolic blood pressure (DBP)** is the baseline hydrostatic pressure in the arterial system and is directly related to SVR and arterial blood volume.  **Pulse pressure** is the amount that arterial pressure increases above DBP during LV contraction; it is directly related to stroke volume and inversely related to aortic compliance, which is generally constant but gradually decreases with advancing age. **Systolic blood pressure** is the sum of DBP and pulse pressure ((Figure 4)).  For example: - An isolated increase in SVR increases DBP and secondarily increases systolic blood pressure, with pulse pressure remaining unchanged. - An isolated increase in stroke volume increases pulse pressure and systolic blood pressure, with DBP remaining unchanged. Increased heart rate slightly increases DBP by mobilizing a higher percentage of blood volume from the venous capacitance system to the arterial circulation (increased arterial blood volume). ## Vascular compartments - The systemic veins act as a capacitance system ((Figure 5)), storing up to 90% of intravascular blood volume.  Vasodilation of the capacitance venules increases venous storage, whereas vasoconstriction reduces storage and mobilizes blood to the right side of the heart (increases venous return). - The pressure in the **systemic venous system** is referred to as **central venous pressure** (CVP) and is roughly 6-8 cm H2O (~5-6 mm Hg). - Blood that is mobilized from the venous system to the right atrium fills the RV during diastole.  Right atrial pressure and RV end-diastolic pressure are roughly equivalent ((Figure 6)) to CVP. - During RV systole, blood is ejected into the pulmonary arteries and delivered to the lungs for oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange.  The pulmonary arterioles create PVR and maintain pressure in the pulmonary circulation.  **RV systolic pressure** and **pulmonary artery systolic pressure** are roughly equivalent (~25 mm Hg). - After traveling through the pulmonary capillaries, blood travels through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium and then fills the LV during diastole.  Left atrial pressure is often estimated during right heart catheterization ((Figure 7)) by the measurement of **pulmonary capillary wedge pressure** (PCWP).  Left atrial pressure and LV end-diastolic pressure are roughly equivalent to PCWP (~8 mm Hg). - During LV systole, blood is ejected into the aorta and delivered to the organs and tissues of the body.  Vasodilation and constriction of the systemic arterioles regulate SVR to maintain systemic blood pressure and modulate flow to specific organs and tissues (eg, skeletal muscle vs intestines).  LV systolic pressure and systemic arterial systolic pressure are roughly equivalent (~120 mm Hg). - After passing through the systemic capillaries, blood returns to the venous capacitance system, where it can be mobilized again as venous return to the right atrium. # Blood pressure regulation ## Blood volume regulation via the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system Blood volume is determined primarily by total body **sodium** because the osmotic activity of sodium keeps water in the intravascular space.  Blood volume is regulated by the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system** (RAAS), a hormonal cascade ((Figure 8)) and feedback loop that culminates in aldosterone-mediated sodium and water reabsorption by the kidneys.  The juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA) ((Figure 9)) of the kidneys controls the RAAS by stimulating renin release in response to the following stimuli: - Decreased pressure in the renal afferent arterioles. - Decreased total sodium delivery to the macula densa. - Increased sympathetic drive to the JGA. As the JGA senses reduced blood volume, aldosterone secretion from the adrenal cortex ((Figure 10)) increases and blood volume increases.  During periods of adequate blood volume and blood pressure, renin activity (and downstream aldosterone activity) is inhibited ((Figure 11)). In addition to stimulating aldosterone secretion, angiotensin II also induces systemic vasoconstriction to help increase blood pressure. ## Baroreceptor reflex The baroreceptor reflex regulates blood pressure by stimulating autonomic-mediated changes in heart rate, contractility, and peripheral vasoconstriction to compensate for changes in blood pressure.  The **carotid and aortic arch baroreceptors** ((Figure 12)) are stretch-sensitive mechanoreceptors that increase their firing rate in response to arterial distension.  They transmit impulses to the solitary nucleus of the medulla, which then modulates sympathetic and parasympathetic (vagal) output in response to the baroreceptor firing rate. - With an abrupt **decrease** ((Figure 13)) in cardiac output and blood pressure, reduced stretch of the arterial walls leads to reduced baroreceptor firing and decreased activation of the solitary nucleus.  This causes an increase in sympathetic outflow with a corresponding reduction in parasympathetic tone, leading to vasoconstriction (increased peripheral resistance) and increased heart rate and contractility (increased cardiac output), minimizing the drop in blood pressure. - Conversely, an abrupt **increase** ((Figure 14)) in blood pressure leads to increased stretch of the arterial walls and increased baroreceptor firing.  In response, increased activation of the solitary nucleus causes reduced sympathetic tone and a corresponding increase in parasympathetic outflow, leading to alleviated vasoconstriction (decreased peripheral resistance) and decreased heart rate and contractility (decreased cardiac output), minimizing the rise in blood pressure. ## Valsalva maneuver The Valsalva maneuver ((Figure 15)) relies on changes in intrathoracic pressure to modulate baroreceptor reflex activity and create a brief surge in blood pressure.  It has 2 phases. During the initial **strain phase** of the Valsalva maneuver, air is inspired and then an exhale is held against a closed glottis.  This increases intrathoracic pressure and facilitates the following: - Increased intrathoracic pressure is transmitted directly to the aortic wall, causing a slight initial increase in blood pressure. - The increased intrathoracic pressure restricts venous return to the right atrium, which in turn leads to reduced cardiac output. - The baroreceptor reflex senses the reduced cardiac output (via a reduction in blood pressure) and triggers a compensatory sympathetic increase in heart rate and SVR to raise cardiac output and blood pressure. Once the exhale strain is released, the **relaxation phase** begins and facilitates the following: - With intrathoracic pressure released, pressure on the aortic wall decreases, causing a brief drop in blood pressure.  In addition, venous return is no longer restricted, and it surges into the right atrium and pulmonary circulation. - The increased venous return is ejected by the LV into the previously increased SVR, causing a surge in systemic blood pressure (ie, blood pressure "overshoot"). - The baroreceptor reflex senses the surge in blood pressure and triggers a compensatory surge in vagal tone to reduce SVR and return hemodynamics to baseline. Examples of clinical applications of the Valsalva maneuver include: - Heart murmur identification:  The reduction in venous return (ie, preload) during the strain phase can be used to help identify certain heart murmurs that are affected by changes in preload (eg, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, mitral valve prolapse). - Supraventricular tachycardia termination:  The surge in vagal tone toward the end of the relaxation phase can slow conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node and can sometimes terminate AV node–dependent paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias. # Left ventricular pressure–volume loops The LV pressure–volume loop ((Figure 16)) follows the cardiac cycle and illustrates the interactions between preload, contractility, and afterload.  At point 1, the LV is full of blood and begins isovolumetric contraction until the aortic valve opens at point 2, causing blood to eject into the aorta and LV volume to decrease.  LV contraction ends at point 3, and LV pressure rapidly decreases to point 4, where the mitral valve opens and LV diastolic filling begins again. ## Main parameters on the pressure-volume loop On the LV flow–volume loop, the following parameters are represented as follows: - **Preload** (end-diastolic volume) is the volume at point 1.  Shifting of point 1 to the right indicates an increase in preload, and shifting of point 1 to the left indicates a decrease in preload. - **Afterload** is generally represented by the peak pressure generated during blood ejection.  An increase in the peak pressure represents an increase in afterload, and a decrease in peak pressure represents a decrease in afterload. - **Contractility**, the intrinsic force the myocardium contracts with, is represented by the line tangent to point 3.  A shift in the contractility line up and to the left indicates increased contractility, and a shift down and to the right indicates decreased contractility. - **Stroke volume** is the difference in volume from end-diastole (point 1) to end-systole (point 3).  Stroke volume can increase or decrease due to changes in the other parameters. - **Compliance** is the slope of the diastolic filling line from point 4 to point 1 (ie, increase in pressure per increase in volume).  An increase in the slope of the line represents decreased compliance, and a decrease in the slope of the line represents increased compliance.  Unlike the other parameters, compliance is typically constant in the short term and is not subject to change. A primary change in one parameter leads to an immediate secondary change in other parameters (not considering baroreceptor-mediated reflex effects).  The immediate effects of primary changes are as follows. ## Preload - An isolated increase in preload occurs with an increase in blood volume (eg, infusion of normal saline).  Increased preload ((Figure 17)) leads to an increase in stroke volume and a slight increase in afterload. - An isolated decrease in preload occurs with a decrease in blood volume (eg, blood loss, dehydration).  Decreased preload ((Figure 18)) leads to a decrease in stroke volume and a slight decrease in afterload. ## Afterload - An isolated increase in afterload occurs with clamping of the abdominal aorta.  Increased afterload ((Figure 19)) leads to decreased stroke volume. - An isolated decrease in afterload occurs with a primarily arterial vasodilator such as hydralazine.  Decreased afterload ((Figure 20)) leads to increased stroke volume. ## Contractility - An isolated increase in contractility occurs with a positive inotrope such as digoxin or a primarily beta-1 agonist (eg, dobutamine).  Increased contractility ((Figure 21)) leads to an increase in stroke volume and a slight increase in afterload. - An isolated decrease in contractility occurs with a negative inotrope such as a primarily beta-1 antagonist (eg, metoprolol) or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (eg, verapamil).  Decreased contractility ((Figure 22)) leads to a decrease in stroke volume and a slight decrease in afterload. # Cardiac function–vascular function curves (Guyton curves) The cardiovascular system is a closed circuit:  Blood ejected from the LV (cardiac output) returns to the right atrium (venous return) before passing through the lungs and being ejected once again.  Cardiac function–vascular function curves (Guyton curves) ((Figure 23)) illustrate the relationship between cardiac output and venous return. - **Cardiac function curve**:  As right atrial pressure (an indication of preload) increases, **cardiac output** increases due to myocardial fiber stretching and a corresponding increase in stroke volume.  This curve is essentially a Frank-Starling curve, representing constant LV contractility (inotropy) along the curve.  Changes in contractility shift the curve to the left or the right. - **Vascular function curve**:  As right atrial pressure increases, **venous return** to the right atrium decreases as a reduced pressure gradient drives blood return to the right atrium.  Changes in blood volume, venous capacitance, and SVR shift the curve to the left or the right. - The **intersection point** of the curves represents the **steady-state** equilibrium of right atrial pressure and cardiac output/venous return for a given set of cardiac and vascular parameters. ## Shifting of the curves Shifting ((Figure 24)) of the cardiac function curve is facilitated by a change in contractility.  Shifting of the venous return curve is facilitated by a change in blood volume, venous capacitance, or SVR. ## Cardiac function curve - **Increased contractility** ((Figure 25)), as occurs with a positive inotrope (eg, digoxin), shifts the cardiac function curve to the **left** and creates a new steady-state equilibrium point at an increased cardiac output and a reduced right atrial pressure. - **Decreased contractility** ((Figure 26)), as occurs with a negative inotrope (eg, verapamil), shifts the cardiac function curve to the **right** and creates a new equilibrium point at a reduced cardiac output and an increased right atrial pressure. ## Vascular function (venous return) curve - **Increased** venous return ((Figure 27)) shifts the venous return curve to the **right** and creates a new equilibrium point at an increased venous return and an increased right atrial pressure.  Factors that increase venous return include: - **Increased blood volume**, as occurs with an infusion of normal saline. - **Decreased venous capacitance**, as occurs with a venous vasoconstrictor.  This mobilizes blood from the venous capacitance system to the right atrium. - **Decreased SVR**, as occurs with an arteriolar vasodilator.  This allows blood to return to the right atrium more easily. - **Decreased** venous return ((Figure 28)) shifts the venous return curve to the **left** and creates a new equilibrium point at a decreased venous return and a decreased right atrial pressure.  Factors that decrease venous return include: - Decreased **blood volume**, as occurs with dehydration or blood loss. - Increased **venous capacitance**, as occurs with a venous vasodilator (eg, nitroglycerin). - Increased **SVR**, as occurs with an arteriolar vasoconstrictor. - Changes in blood volume and venous capacitance cause the entire venous return curve to shift left or right.  Changes in SVR (arteriolar vasoconstriction or vasodilation) cause the venous return curve to pivot left or right at the x-axis, meaning that the curve appears steeper or flatter but the right atrial pressure at the *x*\-axis (ie, where cardiac output/venous return are zero) does not change.  This is because blood volume is mostly (90%) held in the venous (vs arterial) system, so when the system is stagnant (ie, cardiac output/venous return = 0), blood volume delivered to the right atrium is not significantly affected by changes in SVR. # Catheter-based cardiovascular pressure charts Catheter-based pressure charts reflect measurements made by introducing a catheter into the blood and and obtaining hemodynamic measurements at various points (eg, heart chambers).  They illustrate normal cardiovascular pressures ((Figure 29)) throughout the cardiac cycle and show how valvular disruptions affect cardiovascular pressures: - Aortic stenosis ((Figure 30)) restricts blood flow from the LV to the aorta and creates an abnormal pressure gradient between LV systolic pressure and aortic systolic pressure. - Aortic regurgitation ((Figure 31)) creates a backflow of blood from the aorta to the LV during diastole, which leads to a progressive decrease in aortic pressure and an increase in LV pressure during diastole. - Mitral stenosis ((Figure 32)) restricts blood flow from the left atrium to the LV to increase left atrial pressure and create an abnormal pressure gradient between left atrial pressure and LV diastolic pressure. -
